title: View of database that appears to an application program is
subject: Data Base Management System
text: The view of a database that is presented to an application program is known as:
solution:
Concept

In the three-schema approach, a database can be described at internal, conceptual, and external levels.

An external-level description exposes only the data and relationships needed by a particular user or application while hiding the rest of the database design.

Application

The stem asks for the name of this application-specific external description. That description is a subschema, because it selects the relevant part of the broader database schema for one application program.

Contrast

  • Schema: the overall formal organization of database data, relationships, and constraints.

  • Virtual table: a query-defined relation, commonly called a view in SQL.

  • Index table: an access structure used to locate records efficiently.

Cross-check

Cross-check: replacing “application program” with “external view” preserves the same three-schema-level meaning, which points to subschema rather than a query result or an access structure.

Result

Therefore, the required term is subschema.

optionFeedback.html: Schema denotes the formally described organization of data, relationships, and constraints in a database.
Subschema denotes a defined subset of a broader schema tailored to the needs of a particular user or application program.
Virtual table denotes a relation produced by a stored query, generally without existing as an independently stored base table.
Index table denotes an auxiliary access structure that associates search-key values with record locations or data pages.

title: Consider the following statements and chose the correct option(s): (MSQ)
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following statements and choose the correct option(s):
S1: The conceptual schema insulates users from the changes in the external schema. This property is referred to as logical data independence
S2: The physical schema insulates users from the changes in the logical structure of data or changes in the choice of relation stored. This property is called Physical data independence.
solution:
Answer: Both statements are false.

Reason:

  • Why the statement about the conceptual schema is false: Logical data independence means that changes to the conceptual schema (the logical structure of the database) should not require changes to the external schemas (user views). The original statement reverses this direction by saying the conceptual schema insulates users from changes in the external schema, which is incorrect.

  • Why the statement about the physical schema is false: Physical data independence means that changes to the internal/physical schema (storage details, file organization, indexing) should not require changes to the conceptual schema or external views. The original statement incorrectly states that the physical schema insulates users from changes in the logical structure, reversing the correct relationship.

Therefore, both given statements are false.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The conceptual schema does not insulate users from changes in the external schema. Logical data independence means that changes to the conceptual schema (the logical structure) should not force changes to the external schemas (user views). The original statement reverses the direction of insulation.

Incorrect. Physical data independence means that changes to the internal/physical schema (storage, file organization, indexes) should not require changes to the conceptual schema (logical structure) or external views. The statement claims the physical schema insulates users from changes in the logical structure, which reverses the relationship.

Correct. The statement about the conceptual schema is false because logical data independence means external schemas (user views) are insulated from changes to the conceptual schema, not the other way around.

Correct. The statement about the physical schema is false because physical data independence means changes to the internal/physical schema should not affect the conceptual schema or user views; the original statement reverses this direction.

title: Which one of the following statement is not correct?

options.html: Data models provide necessary means to achieve data abstraction.

Database approach doesn’t support data independence between data and programs.
Database approach supports multiple views of the data.

solution: Step 1: Understand that data models are used to abstract data from physical storage, allowing users to interact with data at a conceptual level. This supports data abstraction. Step 2: A self-describing database system stores metadata about its structure, enabling it to manage data independently. This is a key feature of the database approach. Step 3: The database approach supports data independence, meaning changes in data storage do not affect programs. This allows flexibility in database design. Step 4: Multiple views allow different users to see data in ways that suit their needs, which is a supported feature in database systems.

optionFeedback.html: Data models are designed to abstract data from physical storage details, allowing users to interact with data at a conceptual level. This option correctly describes the role of data models in achieving data abstraction.
A self-describing database system stores metadata about its structure, enabling it to manage data independently. This is a key feature of the database approach.
The database approach is designed to support data independence, allowing changes in data storage without affecting programs. This option incorrectly denies that support.
Multiple views allow different users to see data in ways that suit their needs, which is a supported feature in database systems. This option correctly identifies that support.
This option indicates no attempt, so no feedback is needed for correctness. It is not a statement to be evaluated for truth.

title: What does the term “Tuple Cardinality” refer to in database
subject: Data Base Management System
text: What does the term “Tuple Cardinality” refer to in a database ?

options.html: The number of keys in a table
The number of rows in a table
The number of tables in a database
The number of columns in a table

solution: The correct option is B: The number of rows in a table. In a relational database, a "tuple" represents a single row or record in a table. "Cardinality" refers to the total count of these unique data rows. Therefore, tuple cardinality is simply the total number of rows.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. "Keys" (like Primary, Foreign, or Candidate keys) are specific constraints or attributes used to uniquely identify records, not the measure of tuple cardinality.
Correct. As defined in the relational model, rows are called tuples, and the total count of rows present in a table at any given time is called its cardinality.
Incorrect. The total number of tables represents the size or complexity of the database schema, which has no direct relation to the tuple cardinality of an individual table.
Incorrect. The number of columns (attributes) in a relational table is called the Degree or Arity of the table, not its cardinality.

title: Which of the following is an example of relational DBMS
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following is an example of a relational DBMS?
solution:
Concept

A relational database management system stores structured data in related tables and uses a relational query language to retrieve and combine rows. Keys, constraints, and joins express relationships while preserving data integrity.

Application

MySQL implements this table-and-relation model: it provides SQL queries, primary and foreign keys, constraints, and joins. These features make MySQL the relational DBMS among the listed technologies.

Contrast

  • MongoDB stores BSON-like documents in collections and is designed around a document data model.

  • Cassandra is a distributed wide-column database optimized for partitioned, highly available workloads.

  • Hadoop is an ecosystem for distributed storage and processing, with components such as HDFS and MapReduce; it is not itself a DBMS.

Result

Therefore, the relational DBMS in the given set is MySQL.

optionFeedback.html: MySQL organizes structured records in tables and uses SQL joins and keys to connect related data.
MongoDB stores BSON-like documents in collections and uses embedded documents and references to model related data.
Cassandra stores partitioned rows in wide-column tables and distributes replicas across nodes for availability.
Hadoop stores files across HDFS nodes and processes distributed datasets through frameworks such as MapReduce.

solution: In a relational database, the structure of data is defined by its schema. The schema specifies tables, columns, relationships, and constraints that organize how data is stored and accessed.

optionFeedback.html: To identify the overall database design, consider what defines relationships and constraints across all tables instead.
A tuple represents a single row of data within the table structure.
An index improves query performance but does not define the data structure itself. Review how tables, columns, and relationships organize information logically within a database system.
A query is an operation to retrieve data, not the structure itself.

title: Which of the following is the main function of DBMS
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following is the main function of a DBMS ?
solution: A Database Management System (DBMS) is software designed to manage and organize data efficiently. Its primary role involves storing data securely in structured formats, which corresponds to option A. Beyond storage, a DBMS allows users and applications to modify data through operations like insertion, updating, or deletion, fulfilling option B. Additionally, it enables users to query and retrieve specific information from the database using languages like SQL, covering option C. Since a DBMS integrates storage, manipulation, and retrieval into a unified system to ensure data integrity and accessibility, all listed functions are essential. Therefore, the correct choice is Option D (All of these), as it comprehensively captures the core responsibilities of a DBMS rather than isolating individual tasks.

optionFeedback.html: Data storage is indeed a core function of a DBMS. However, this option only covers one aspect and ignores other critical roles like data retrieval or security management.

Data manipulation is essential for interacting with stored data, yet it does not represent the complete scope of DBMS capabilities. Review if this option covers all key responsibilities like storage and security.

While data retrieval is a valid DBMS function, it is only one part of the system's overall purpose. Check if other listed options like storage or security are also core functions before selecting this answer.
Correct. A DBMS handles storage, retrieval, security, and more.

title: Three-tier structure of DBMS in ANSI-SPARC, extended SPARC is
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Three-tier structure of DBMS in ANSI-SPARC, extended SPARC is _________
solution:
The correct option is B (Standard planning and requirement committee).

The question asks for the expansion of SPARC within the context of the ANSI-SPARC architecture, which defines the classic three-tier (three-schema) structure of a Database Management System (DBMS).

  • Full Form: ANSI stands for American National Standards Institute, and SPARC stands for Standards Planning And Requirements Committee.

  • Historical Context: In 1975, the ANSI/X3/SPARC study group proposed a framework for database management systems to achieve data independence.

  • Three-Tier Architecture: This framework divides a database system into three abstraction levels to separate the user applications from the physical database:

    1. External Level (View Schema): What the individual users see.

    2. Conceptual Level (Logical Schema): The community view of the entire data structure, detailing what data is stored and their relationships.

    3. Internal Level (Physical Schema): How the data is physically stored on the storage disk.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The 'S' stands for 'Standards', not 'System'. This is a common distractor designed to confuse the technical term with generic system terminology.
Correct. "Standards Planning And Requirements Committee" is the official and precise historical designation of the ANSI committee that proposed the 3-level database architecture.
Incorrect. Both 'System' and 'Reassessment' are incorrect words in this acronym. The correct words are 'Standards' and 'Requirements' respectively.
Incorrect. The word 'System' is used incorrectly instead of 'Standards', and 'Review' is used incorrectly instead of 'Requirements'.

title: Data inconsistency can be prevented by preventing
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Data inconsistency can be prevented by preventing
solution:
Concept. Data redundancy means the same fact is physically stored in more than one place in a database. Data inconsistency is the state in which those duplicate copies hold different (conflicting) values for what should be a single fact, so the database no longer agrees with itself.

Why redundancy is the root cause: inconsistency can only occur when there is more than one copy to disagree. If a fact is stored only once, there is no second copy that can fall out of step when an update happens.

Application.

  1. Suppose a customer's address is duplicated across several tables.

  2. An update changes the address in one table but, by oversight, not in the others.

  3. The copies now disagree — the database is inconsistent.

  4. Remove the duplication (store the address exactly once, e.g. through normalization), and there is no second copy to update, so the inconsistency can never arise.

Cross-check / contrast.

  • Redundancy — the duplication itself; eliminating it (normalization) is the standard way to prevent inconsistency.

  • Metadata — "data about data" (schema, definitions, constraints); it describes the data rather than being the stored payload.

  • Deadlocks — a concurrency-control problem where transactions wait on each other forever; a locking/scheduling issue.

  • Multiprogramming — running several programs concurrently on the CPU; an operating-system scheduling idea.

Result: data inconsistency is prevented by preventing redundancy.

optionFeedback.html: Redundancy is the duplication of the same fact across multiple storage locations. When one copy is updated and another is missed, the copies hold conflicting values — and that drift is exactly the inconsistency in question. Keeping each fact in a single place through normalization removes the second copy that could ever disagree.

Metadata is "data about data" — the schema, definitions and constraints that describe how a database is organized. It is descriptive information about structure rather than the stored records themselves, and reducing it does not change whether the actual data values agree with one another.

A deadlock is a concurrency problem in which two or more transactions each hold a lock the other needs and wait on one another forever, so progress halts. Avoiding it is a matter of lock ordering and transaction scheduling — a runtime liveness concern about how transactions execute, separate from the values that records store.

Multiprogramming means keeping several programs in memory and switching the CPU among them to raise utilization. It is an operating-system scheduling idea about how processes share the processor, a concern at the level of running programs rather than the values held in a database's records.

title: Information about the structure of Database is stored in
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Information about the structure of a database is stored in ______.
solution:
Concept

A DBMS stores both user data and metadata. User data consists of the records being managed, whereas metadata is “data about data”: it defines the schema objects and rules that give the database its structure.

The DBMS maintains this metadata in a system-managed catalog so that components such as the query processor can discover table definitions, column types, indexes, constraints, views, and privileges.

Application

The standard name for that metadata repository is the data dictionary, also called the system catalog. Therefore, information describing the structure of a database is stored in the Data Dictionary.

Contrast

  • Data File: stores database blocks containing rows, index entries, and other user or system data.

  • Data Components: is a generic phrase for constituent elements and does not name a specific catalog repository.

  • Data Model: is an abstract framework for representing structures, relationships, constraints, and operations.

Cross-check: when a table is created or altered, the DBMS updates its catalog entry; it does not redefine the database’s data model or turn the schema definition into an ordinary data row. This confirms Data Dictionary as the required repository.

optionFeedback.html: Database systems manage data files through storage units such as tablespaces; their size, placement, and growth are controlled by storage configuration.
Database products commonly expose data-dictionary views through system schemas; administrators query these views subject to catalog-access privileges.
In data-architecture discussions, data components may include data sources, storage services, processing services, and interfaces grouped within a system.
Data models are discussed at conceptual, logical, and physical levels, with each level expressing a different degree of abstraction.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q71
subject: Data Base Management System
text: DBMS stands for
solution:
Concept

An acronym is formed from the established name of a concept, not merely from any phrase whose initial letters happen to match.

In computing, a database is an organized collection of related data, and the software that defines, stores, retrieves, updates, and controls that data is called a database management system.

Application

Applying that standard terminology, DBMS expands to Database Management System: “Database” names the managed data collection, “Management” names the operations and controls, and “System” names the software as a whole.

Contrast

  • Data Backup Management System concerns backup copies, retention, and recovery rather than the general management of a database.

  • Data Base Modeling System concerns schema and data-model design rather than the complete database-management software layer.

  • Digital Base Management Structure is not the established computing term for software that manages databases.

Cross-check

Standard computing references define a DBMS as software that enables users to create, maintain, and control access to a database, which matches the expansion Database Management System.

Result: DBMS stands for Database Management System.

optionFeedback.html: The phrase “Data Backup Management System” describes software focused on organizing backup copies, retention, and recovery operations.
The phrase “Database Management System” describes software used to define, store, retrieve, update, and control access to a database.
The phrase “Data Base Modeling System” describes a tool focused on designing data models, entities, relationships, or schemas.
The phrase “Digital Base Management Structure” describes an organizational structure for managing a digital base or repository.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2019 — Q1
subject: Data Base Management System
text: The collection of information stored in a database at a particular moment is called its:
solution:
Concept

A database has two different aspects: its relatively stable structure and its changing data state.

The structure is described by a schema, whereas the data present at one specific time forms a database instance.

Application

The stem asks for the collection of information stored at a particular moment. That wording refers to the data state at that instant, so the required term is instance.

Contrast

  • view: a query-defined presentation of selected data.

  • instance: the database state at a particular time.

  • scheme: an ordinary word for a plan; schema is the DBMS term for structure.

  • None of these: unnecessary because instance is among the listed terms.

Cross-check

If rows are inserted or deleted, the instance changes, while the schema can remain unchanged. This confirms that the time-specific collection of stored information is the database instance.

Therefore, the answer is instance.

optionFeedback.html: In database terminology, a view is associated with a query-defined presentation of selected data.
In database terminology, an instance is associated with the current state of stored data and may change over time.
In ordinary terminology, a scheme denotes an organized plan or arrangement.
None of these is a set-referential choice used when no listed term supplies the requested concept.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2019 — Q11
subject: Data Base Management System
text: In MS Access, the “Lookup Wizard” is used to:
solution:
Concept

A lookup field lets a user choose a displayed value while Access stores the bound value defined by the field’s row source.

The Lookup Wizard configures that row source from another table or query, or from an explicit list entered during setup, and sets the related field properties.

Application

Here the intended source-paper wording is “select a value from another table.” The wizard can read the display values from that table or from a query based on it, so this wording matches its standard table-based use.

Contrast

  • “Select values from an Excel sheet” describes importing or linking external spreadsheet data, not the Lookup Wizard’s table-field setup.

  • “Select from previous values” is not the wizard’s standard description: a value list must be explicitly supplied, while arbitrary earlier entries are not reused automatically.

  • “None of these” does not apply because the table-based action is explicitly supported.

Cross-check

Microsoft’s Lookup Wizard instructions begin with the choice to get values from another table or query and then ask the user to select that source.

Result

Therefore, the Lookup Wizard is used to select a value from another table.

optionFeedback.html: The proposed source is another table, represented inside Access as a table or query.
The proposed source is an Excel sheet, represented in Access through an external-data import or link.
The proposed source is earlier field entries, represented as ordinary stored records.
The proposed response is set-level, representing the listed actions collectively.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q29
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following is NOT a database object in Microsoft Access?
solution:
Concept

A database object is a named, reusable component that stores data or presents, retrieves, or automates work on that data.

Classification questions require distinguishing an item’s primary function from the wider system in which it participates; sharing a context does not make two items members of the same category.

Application

Microsoft Access exposes tables, queries, forms, reports, macros, and modules as database objects. Classify each offered value by its role: data storage, data retrieval, formatted presentation, or a rule connecting stored data.

Contrast

  • Tables store records in rows and fields.

  • Queries retrieve, filter, calculate, or modify data.

  • Reports format and summarize data for viewing or printing.

  • Relationships define how fields in different tables correspond and may enforce referential integrity.

Result

Therefore, Relationship is the offered value that is not a database object in Microsoft Access.

optionFeedback.html: A relationship records how corresponding fields in distinct record sets are linked and can enforce referential integrity across their records.
A table stores records in rows and fields, providing the persistent data structure used by the database.
A query retrieves, filters, calculates, or modifies data by applying specified criteria to one or more data sources.
A report formats and summarizes data for structured viewing, presentation, or printing.

title: UGC NET Paper 1 December 2024 (9 January 2025 Shift 1) — Q41
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Choose the correct statements in the context of DBMS.

A. DBMS is a software to create and manage databases.

B. Database schema is the design of the database.

C. Foreign key in a relation is used for unique identification of tables.

D. Primary key is used to relate two tables or relations.

E. SQL stands for Structured Query Language.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Concept: A database management system (DBMS) is the software layer through which databases are created, stored, queried and administered, and a schema is the design-time description of such a database — its relations, attributes, data types and constraints. Inside the relational model the two key constructs have opposite jobs: a primary key is the attribute (or attribute set) whose value uniquely identifies each tuple of its own relation, while a foreign key is an attribute of one relation that must draw its values from the primary key of another relation, and is therefore the construct that links two relations. SQL is the standard declarative language in which relational data is defined and queried.

Application to the given statements:

  1. Statement A restates the definition of a DBMS as software for creating and managing databases, which is exactly what the term denotes.

  2. Statement B restates the definition of a schema as the design of the database, which is exactly what a schema records.

  3. Statement C gives unique identification to the foreign key. Unique identification of a tuple within its own relation is the primary key’s job, so this statement puts the primary key’s role on the foreign key.

  4. Statement D gives the linking of two relations to the primary key. Linking is achieved when a foreign key in one relation references another relation’s primary key, so this statement puts the foreign key’s role on the primary key. Statements C and D are the two halves of the same swap.

  5. Statement E gives the standard expansion of SQL, Structured Query Language, which is the accepted full form.

Cross-check — primary key versus foreign key:

Aspect

Primary key

Foreign key

Purpose

Uniquely identify each tuple of its own relation

Reference another relation and link the two

Uniqueness

Values must be unique

Values may repeat

NULLs

Not allowed

Allowed unless otherwise constrained

Enforces

Entity integrity

Referential integrity

Result: the statements that hold are A, B and E, so the correct selection is “A, B and E only”. The remaining two statements are wrong only because the roles of the primary key and the foreign key have been interchanged; correcting the swap makes both of them true.

optionFeedback.html: This grouping is built from the statement defining a DBMS as software for creating and managing databases, the statement defining a schema as the database design, and the statement assigning unique identification of tables to the foreign key; it excludes the statement assigning the relating of two tables to the primary key and the statement expanding SQL as Structured Query Language.

title: Which of the following focuses on actual storage and organisation
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following focuses on actual storage and organisation of data on disk blocks?
solution: The physical schema defines how data is actually stored on the storage medium, including disk blocks and indexing structures. Unlike conceptual schemas which focus on logical relationships, or external schemas for user views, the physical layer manages implementation details.

optionFeedback.html: External schemas define how individual users perceive data rather than physical storage details. This level focuses on user-specific views and security, not disk block organization or implementation specifics required for storage management within the database system architecture.

Conceptual schemas describe the logical structure and relationships between data entities. They remain independent of physical storage mechanisms, so they do not address actual disk block organization or hardware-specific implementation details within the broader database system.

Physical schema specifically addresses how data is physically stored on storage media within the database system architecture. It typically manages disk block organization and file structures, which is distinct from logical relationships or external user views.

External schemas define user-specific views, while conceptual schemas outline logical structures without physical details. Neither of these levels addresses actual disk block organization or storage implementation directly within the database system architecture, which is managed by the physical storage level instead.

title: Data inconsistency can be prevented by preventing
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Data inconsistency can be prevented by preventing
solution:
Concept. Data redundancy means the same fact is physically stored in more than one place in a database. Data inconsistency is the state in which those duplicate copies hold different (conflicting) values for what should be a single fact, so the database no longer agrees with itself.

Why redundancy is the root cause: inconsistency can only occur when there is more than one copy to disagree. If a fact is stored only once, there is no second copy that can fall out of step when an update happens.

Application.

  1. Suppose a customer's address is duplicated across several tables.

  2. An update changes the address in one table but, by oversight, not in the others.

  3. The copies now disagree — the database is inconsistent.

  4. Remove the duplication (store the address exactly once, e.g. through normalization), and there is no second copy to update, so the inconsistency can never arise.

Cross-check / contrast.

  • Redundancy — the duplication itself; eliminating it (normalization) is the standard way to prevent inconsistency.

  • Metadata — "data about data" (schema, definitions, constraints); it describes the data rather than being the stored payload.

  • Deadlocks — a concurrency-control problem where transactions wait on each other forever; a locking/scheduling issue.

  • Multiprogramming — running several programs concurrently on the CPU; an operating-system scheduling idea.

Result: data inconsistency is prevented by preventing redundancy.

optionFeedback.html: Redundancy is the duplication of the same fact across multiple storage locations. When one copy is updated and another is missed, the copies hold conflicting values — and that drift is exactly the inconsistency in question. Keeping each fact in a single place through normalization removes the second copy that could ever disagree.

Metadata is "data about data" — the schema, definitions and constraints that describe how a database is organized. It is descriptive information about structure rather than the stored records themselves, and reducing it does not change whether the actual data values agree with one another.

A deadlock is a concurrency problem in which two or more transactions each hold a lock the other needs and wait on one another forever, so progress halts. Avoiding it is a matter of lock ordering and transaction scheduling — a runtime liveness concern about how transactions execute, separate from the values that records store.

Multiprogramming means keeping several programs in memory and switching the CPU among them to raise utilization. It is an operating-system scheduling idea about how processes share the processor, a concern at the level of running programs rather than the values held in a database's records.

title: Database application were directly built on top of file system
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Database application were directly built on top of file system to overcome the following drawbacks of using file-systems:

(a) Data redundancy and inconsistency

(b) Difficulty in accessing data

(c) Data isolation

(d) Integrity problems
solution:
Answer: Database systems address all four listed drawbacks.

Brief explanations of how databases overcome each problem:

  • Data redundancy and inconsistency: File-based systems often store duplicate data across multiple files, causing inconsistent updates. Database systems centralize data, use data modeling and normalization, and provide a single source of truth to reduce redundancy and inconsistency.

  • Difficulty in accessing data: In file-based systems each application must implement its own data access logic. DBMSs provide high-level query languages (such as SQL), APIs, and optimized access methods that make it easier to retrieve and manipulate data.

  • Data isolation: Files may use different formats and be scattered across applications, making combined queries and integration hard. A database offers a unified schema and centralized management, removing isolation and enabling integrated views of the data.

  • Integrity problems: File systems cannot easily enforce global constraints or atomic updates. DBMSs support integrity constraints, transactions (ACID properties), and concurrency control to ensure correctness and consistency of data.

Therefore, all four issues—data redundancy and inconsistency; difficulty in accessing data; data isolation; and integrity problems—are reasons why database applications were built on top of file systems.

optionFeedback.html: This choice mentions only data redundancy and inconsistency. While database systems do resolve redundancy and inconsistency through centralized storage and normalization, they also address other problems listed: they make data easier to access, remove data isolation by providing a unified schema, and enforce integrity. Selecting only this drawback is therefore incomplete.

This choice identifies redundancy and integrity problems, which databases do handle. However, it omits that database systems also simplify data access (for example via query languages and APIs) and eliminate data isolation by integrating data under a common schema. The full set of problems listed is addressed by database systems.

This choice lists redundancy, difficulty in accessing data, and data isolation. Those are valid drawbacks of file-based systems that databases fix. However, it omits integrity problems: database systems enforce integrity through constraints, transactions and concurrency control. The correct view is that databases address all four listed issues.

Correct. Database systems were developed to overcome data redundancy and inconsistency by centralizing and normalizing data; to make data easier to access via query languages and DBMS services; to remove data isolation by integrating data under a common schema; and to prevent integrity problems using constraints, transactions and concurrency control.

title: Which of the following is not Database management system?
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following is not a Database management system?
solution:
A Database Management System (DBMS) is software whose defining job is to store, organize, and manage persistent structured data, and to provide controlled retrieval and query access to it -- whether through SQL (relational/RDBMS) or through document/collection style APIs (non-relational/NoSQL). Any software satisfying this storage-plus-management role qualifies as a DBMS, regardless of which family it belongs to.

  • MySQL is a widely used, open-source Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) -- it stores data in tables and is queried using SQL, so it is a genuine DBMS.

  • MongoDB is a widely used, open-source NoSQL database management system -- it stores data as flexible, JSON-like documents, so it is a genuine DBMS even though it is not relational.

  • Oracle Database is a comprehensive, multi-model enterprise Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) used widely for enterprise data management, so it is a genuine DBMS.

  • Apache Spark is a distributed data-processing and analytics engine -- it computes over data (batch jobs, streaming, machine learning, graph analytics) but has no native persistent storage layer of its own, relying on an external store such as HDFS, Amazon S3, or a database to hold the data it processes. It manages computation, not data storage, so it is not a DBMS.

MySQL, MongoDB, and Oracle only differ along the RDBMS-vs-NoSQL line -- both families still store and manage persistent data, which is the core DBMS capability. Apache Spark sits in an entirely different category: a processing/compute engine rather than a data store, which is the sharper distinction the question is actually testing.

Therefore, Apache Spark is the option that is not a database management system.

MongoDB is a widely used, open-source NoSQL database management system that stores data as flexible, JSON-like documents.

Apache Spark is a distributed data-processing and analytics engine, not a database management system -- it computes over data (batch processing, streaming, machine learning, graph analytics) but has no native persistent storage layer of its own, relying on an external store such as HDFS, Amazon S3, or a database to hold the data it processes.
Oracle Database is a comprehensive, multi-model enterprise Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) widely used for robust enterprise data management.

title: Recursive entity set is It is an entity type with
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Recursive entity set is

S1: It is an entity type with foreign key referring to same table or itself

S2: Recursive entity type occurs in unary relationship

Which of the above statements is/ are correct?
solution:
Key idea: A recursive (self-referential) entity set is an entity type that participates in a relationship with itself and is typically implemented by a foreign key that refers to the primary key of the same table.

  • Statement about implementation with a foreign key referring to the same table: True. A common way to represent a self-referential relationship is to include a foreign key column that points to the primary key of another row in the same table (for example, an employee's manager_id referencing employee_id).

  • Statement that recursive entity types occur in unary (self) relationships: True. A unary relationship involves a single entity type participating more than once in the relationship (for example, an Employee supervises other Employee(s)).

Example: In a supervisor–subordinate scenario, each employee row may have a manager_id that refers to another employee row. This is both a self-referential implementation (foreign key to the same table) and a unary relationship (the Employee entity relates to itself).

Conclusion: Both statements are correct because they describe the same concept from implementation and relationship-perspective.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The statement that a recursive entity set can be implemented by a foreign key referencing the same table is correct, but the other statement is also true: recursive entity types arise from unary (self) relationships. So saying only the first statement is correct is incomplete.

Incorrect. While it is true that recursive entity types occur in unary (self) relationships, the other statement is also correct: such a relationship is often implemented by a foreign key in the table that refers to the primary key of the same table. Therefore selecting only the unary-relationship statement is incomplete.

Correct. A recursive (self-referential) entity set is an entity type that participates in a relationship with itself and can be implemented by a foreign key referring to the same table. This is a unary relationship (one entity type appears on both sides), so both statements are true.

Incorrect. Both statements are true: recursive entity sets are self-referential and commonly implemented via a foreign key that references the same table, and such situations are modeled as unary (self) relationships. Therefore saying neither statement is correct is wrong.

title: An entity in an ER model represents
subject: Data Base Management System
text: An entity in an ER model represents
solution:
Concept: In the Entity-Relationship (ER) model, three distinct constructs describe data. An entity is an identifiable real-world object or concept — a person, place, thing, or event — that exists independently and can be distinguished from every other object. An attribute is a descriptive property that characterizes an entity type (such as a name, age, or price). A relationship is an association that links two or more entities to each other.

Application: The question asks what an entity itself represents. By definition, an entity is the object or concept — for example, a specific student, course, or employee — not the properties describing it and not the associations connecting it to other entities. Among the offered options, the one that names the object or concept itself matches this definition.

Why the other options do not fit:

  • Relationships between entities names a different construct — an association that links entities to each other — not the entity itself.

  • Attributes of an entity type names the descriptive properties that belong to an entity, not the entity.

  • All of these treats entity, attribute, and relationship as equivalent, but the ER model defines them as three separate constructs, so this over-generalizes.

Cross-check: Applying the definition to a concrete case confirms it — in a database of orders, "Order #1042" is the entity (the real-world thing being recorded), "order date" is one of its attributes, and "placed by" (linking the order to a customer) is a relationship, not the entity.

optionFeedback.html: An association between two or more entities is captured as a relationship, representing how those entities interact or connect within the model.
A descriptive property associated with an entity type — for example, a name, age, or price value — used to characterize that entity is captured as an attribute.
An identifiable, real-world object or concept — such as a specific customer, product, or event — that can be distinguished from other objects in the domain.
This option represents a combined selection that groups together the ideas presented in the other three options into one choice.

Incorrect. Gender is a single-valued attribute as it records a single biological or legal category for an individual in standard database schemas.

title: Database Design includes the functions like
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Database Design includes the functions like
solution:
Concept

Database design is the process of organising data into a structured schema before any data is stored. It is not a single action but a set of coordinated functions: deciding what entities to store, describing each entity's attributes, and defining the rules and links that keep the data consistent.

Application

The three statements offered are not alternatives — each names a distinct, necessary stage of the design process:

  • Identifying the different tables decides which real-world entities (e.g. Students, Courses) each become a separate table.

  • Creating fields with their attributes describes each table's columns and their data types, sizes and defaults.

  • Creating validation rules and interrelationships adds the constraints (e.g. NOT NULL, range checks) and the foreign-key relationships that bind the tables together.

Conclusion

Because every one of these is a genuine function of database design, the option that covers all three — "All of the above" — is the complete and correct answer. Choosing only one of them describes a single step rather than the full design activity.

optionFeedback.html: Identifying the different tables is indeed one function of database design, but it is only the first stage — it decides which entities exist without describing their fields or the rules that connect them. A statement covering just this leaves out the rest of the design work.

Creating fields with their attributes is a real part of design — it defines each table's columns and their data types — but on its own it assumes the tables already exist and ignores the validation and relationship work. It describes one step, not the whole activity.

Creating validation rules and interrelationships is a genuine design function — it adds constraints and foreign-key links — but it presupposes that the tables and their fields have already been defined. Taken alone it captures the final stage while omitting the earlier ones.

Database design is the combination of identifying tables, defining their fields with attributes, and setting validation rules and interrelationships. Since all three are functions of the same design process, the choice that encompasses every one of them is the complete description.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q91
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following best explains why a weak entity must always participate in a total participation relationship with its identifying entity?

options.html: Weak entities do not contain any attribute
Weak entities are always stored in a separate table from the identifying entity
Weak entities do not have a primary key of their own

solution:
Concept

In ER modeling, a weak entity type is one that has no key attribute of its own capable of uniquely identifying its instances. It relies on a partial key (discriminator) combined with the primary key of another entity type — called its identifying (or owner) entity — to form a composite identifying key. Because a weak entity's instances cannot be told apart, or even considered to exist, without a linked owner instance, ER modeling rules require the participation of every weak entity type in its identifying relationship to be total (mandatory): each weak-entity instance must be connected to exactly one owner-entity instance.

Application to this question

For this question, the reason total participation is forced is exactly this identification dependency: a weak entity has no independent primary key, so an occurrence of the weak entity that is not linked to an owner occurrence would have no way of being uniquely identified (and, under the existence-dependency view of weak entities, no way of legitimately existing in the database at all). Making the participation partial (optional) would allow such un-linked, unidentifiable rows, which the model must rule out — hence the total-participation constraint is mandatory, not merely a design convention.

Cross-check: why the other reasons offered don't explain it

  • Having zero attributes is not a property of weak entities — a weak entity type still carries its own attribute set, including the partial key used in the composite identifier; attribute count is unrelated to the participation rule on the identifying relationship.

  • Whether the weak entity's rows end up in a table of their own or merged with the owner's table is decided later, during logical/relational schema design; that physical-mapping choice does not drive the conceptual-level participation constraint fixed on the identifying relationship.

  • A weak entity can indeed take part in other relationship sets besides its identifying one, but that is a separate fact about relationship count; it says nothing about why participation in the identifying relationship specifically must be total.

So the total-participation requirement follows specifically from the weak entity's lack of an independent primary key — that is, its identification (and existence) dependency on the owning entity.

optionFeedback.html: A weak entity type's own attribute set includes a discriminator (partial key), which combines with the identifying entity's primary key to form its composite identifying key.
A weak entity type's relation carries a foreign key to its owning entity's table together with its own partial key, forming the composite primary key of that relation.
A weak entity type's composite identifying key is formed by combining its own partial key (discriminator) with the primary key contributed by its identifying (owner) entity.
A weak entity type's identifying relationship with its owner is the specific relationship set that supplies the primary-key component used in its composite identifying key.

text: Let E1 and E2 be two entities in an ER diagram. R1 is a one-to-many relationship between E1 and E2. R1 does not have any attributes on its own, and E2 has only one multivalued attribute. What is the minimum number of tables required to represent this situation in the relational model?
solution:
Answer: Minimum number of tables = 3.

title: Consider the following ER diagram: The minimum no. of tables

text:
Consider the following ER diagram:

The minimum number of tables needed to represent this ER diagram in the relational model is ____.
solution:
CONCEPT

In ER-to-relational mapping, each strong entity set normally becomes a relation. However, two entity sets connected by a one-to-one relationship with total participation on both sides can be merged into one relation without losing information. A weak entity requires its own relation containing the owner entity’s primary key, while its identifying relationship does not require a separate relation.

APPLICATION

  1. R₁ connects A and B with cardinality 1:1, and the double participation lines show total participation on both sides. Therefore, A and B may be merged into one relation containing the attributes of both entities.

  2. C is a weak entity (double rectangle) identified through R₂ (double diamond) by B, with one B related to many C entities. Hence, C needs a separate relation whose key includes the primary key inherited from the merged A–B relation.

  3. Neither R₁ nor R₂ needs a separate relation here: R₁ is absorbed by merging A and B, and R₂ is represented by the owner key stored in the relation for C.

CROSS-CHECK / CONTRAST

Counting three entity sets does not force three tables. The 1:1 total-participation mapping allows A and B to share one table, while the weak entity C remains separate. Thus the schema uses one table for merged A–B and one table for C.

RESULT

Minimum number of tables = 2.

Short answer: The minimized table with attributes A, C, B and primary key (A, C) is correct.

Reasoning:

  • Identify which relationships are identifying and which entities are merged: the relationship labeled S is identifying/associative and can be merged into the relation for the entity that has attribute A.

  • When S is merged into that entity, attribute C is brought into the same relation as a foreign key and, because the relationship is identifying, the primary key becomes the composite (A, C).

  • Attribute B is an attribute of the original entity containing A, so it remains in the same relation as a non-key attribute. Therefore the relation contains A, C, B with primary key (A, C).

Why the other proposed sets are incorrect:

  • Including attribute F (from the other entity E3) in the same relation is incorrect because F belongs to a separate entity that is represented by its own table; merging unrelated entity attributes violates normalization and the diagram's structure.

  • Proposing a standalone relation with only attributes A and E (and key A,E) omits B, which belongs to the entity with A. The relationship mapping must preserve entity attributes appropriately, not drop them.

  • Listing S as only (A,C) ignores the non-key attribute B that must remain with the entity; the minimized relation formed by merging must include that attribute.

Final minimized relations (as derived from the diagram):

  • Relation merging the entity with A and the identifying relationship S: attributes A, C, B; primary key (A, C).

  • Relation representing the entity connected by R: attributes A, E, B; primary key (A, E).

  • Relation for the entity with attributes C and D: attributes C, D; primary key (C).

  • Relation for the entity with attributes E and F: attributes E, F; primary key (E).

title: Consider the following Relationship Entity Diagram(ERD) Which of the following

subtopic: Conversion of ER Diagram into Relational Model
text:
Consider the following Entity–Relationship Diagram (ERD):

Which of the following possible relations will not hold when the ERD is mapped to a relational model?
solution:
Concept

In an ER-to-relational mapping, each strong entity becomes a relation containing its key and the attributes directly attached to that entity.

A many-to-many relationship becomes a separate relation containing the keys of both participating entities plus any attribute attached to the relationship; the entity relations do not absorb a single foreign key for that M:N link.

Application

  1. Map the Person entity as Person (NID, Name), with NID as its key.

  2. Map the Exam entity as Exam (ExamID, ExamName), with ExamID as its key.

  3. The diagram marks Qualification as an M:N relationship between Person and Exam, so map it separately as Qualification (NID, ExamID, QualifiedDate). NID and ExamID reference the participating entity rows, their pair identifies a relationship row, and QualifiedDate describes that relationship.

  4. Exam (ExamID, NID, ExamName) puts a Person key inside the Exam entity relation. A single NID there cannot represent the diagram’s many Person–Exam pairs; those pairs belong in Qualification.

Cross-check and contrast

  • Person (NID, Name) contains exactly the attributes attached to Person.

  • Qualification (NID, ExamID, QualifiedDate) contains both participant keys and the relationship attribute.

  • Exam (ExamID, NID, ExamName) mixes the Person key into the Exam entity while the M:N association is already represented by relationship rows.

  • Exam (ExamID, ExamName) contains exactly the attributes attached to Exam.

Therefore, the relation that will not hold is Exam (ExamID, NID, ExamName).

optionFeedback.html: For the schema Person (NID, Name), NID identifies a Person tuple and Name describes that same tuple. Both attributes are connected to Person in the diagram.

For the schema Qualification (NID, ExamID, QualifiedDate), NID and ExamID identify the participating entity tuples and QualifiedDate describes their association. All three roles come from the M:N relationship mapping.

For the schema Exam (ExamID, NID, ExamName), ExamID identifies an Exam tuple, ExamName describes it, and NID identifies a Person tuple participating through Qualification. These attribute roles come from both an entity and its relationship mapping.
For the schema Exam (ExamID, ExamName), ExamID identifies an Exam tuple and ExamName describes that same tuple. Both attributes are connected to Exam in the diagram.

title: Which of the following is type of relationship in relational

solution: In a relational database, relationships define how data in one table connects to data in another. There are three fundamental types of relationships supported by relational database models: one-to-one, where a single record in Table A relates to only one record in Table B; one-to-many, which is the most common type where a single record in Table A can relate to multiple records in Table B; and many-to-many, where multiple records in Table A can relate to multiple records in Table B. Since options A, B, and C all represent valid relationship types used to structure data effectively in relational systems like SQL databases, the correct choice must include all of them. Therefore, 'All of the above' is the accurate answer as it encompasses every valid relationship type listed in the other options.

optionFeedback.html: One-to-one relationships exist in relational databases where one record links to exactly one other. However, this is not the only valid relationship type available in database design.

Many-to-many is valid but incomplete. Other types like one-to-one and one-to-many are also correct.
Correct. All relationship types (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many) are valid in relational databases.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q143
subject: Data Base Management System
subtopic: Conversion of ER Diagram into Relational Model
text: When converting an E-R diagram to a relational schema, how is a multivalued attribute typically represented in the relational model?

options.html: As a nullable column in the same table
As a separate relation with a foreign key

solution:
Concept

The ER-to-relational mapping algorithm converts each ER construct into relations and columns using type-specific rules: simple attributes become columns of the owning relation; composite attributes are flattened into one column per component sub-attribute; derived attributes are usually dropped (recomputed on demand); and a multivalued attribute -- one that can legitimately hold zero, one, or many values for a single entity instance -- cannot be stored as a single column, because a relational table cell must hold exactly one atomic value (this is the essence of First Normal Form). The mapping rule instead creates a brand-new relation for that attribute, containing a foreign key referencing the primary key of the owning entity's relation, plus the attribute value itself; the primary key of this new relation is the combination {foreign key, attribute value} (or an added surrogate key), so the owning entity can be linked to any number of rows -- one per recorded value.

Application

Take an Employee entity with a multivalued attribute PhoneNumbers. Applying the rule: Employee's simple/composite attributes populate the Employee relation as usual, but PhoneNumbers cannot become a single Employee column, since an employee may have zero, one, or several numbers. So a new relation EmployeePhone(EmpID, PhoneNumber) is created, where EmpID is a foreign key referencing Employee's primary key and {EmpID, PhoneNumber} is the primary key of EmployeePhone. Each phone number the employee has becomes its own row in EmployeePhone, all pointing back to the same EmpID -- exactly the "separate relation with a foreign key" pattern.

Contrast with the other options

  • As a composite attribute -- a composite attribute only regroups the fixed sub-parts of one value (for example, Address into Street, City, and PIN) into columns of the same table; it does not create room for a variable number of value instances.

  • As a nullable column in the same table -- a nullable column still allocates exactly one storage slot per row, so it can hold at most one recorded value (or none); it cannot hold two, three, or an unbounded number of values for the same employee without adding more columns.

  • As an attribute with CHECK constraints -- a CHECK constraint only restricts which values a single column may take; it does not change the table structure to allow more than one value per entity instance.

  • As a separate relation with a foreign key -- matches the derivation above: each value becomes its own row in a child relation keyed back to the parent via a foreign key, which is exactly what the mapping algorithm prescribes for a multivalued attribute.

optionFeedback.html: A composite attribute is one that decomposes into a fixed set of named sub-attributes, each stored as its own column in the same relation -- for example, an Address composite might split into Street, City, and PIN columns.
A nullable column is a single column in the base relation where each row may hold either a value or a NULL marker, representing at most one recorded value per row.
A CHECK constraint is a rule attached to a column that restricts the set of values the column may legally hold, independent of how the value's storage is structured.

title: In Relational Model, which type of constraint does not allow
subject: Data Base Management System
text: In Relational Model, which type of constraint does not allow composite and multivalued attributes?
solution:
In the relational model, every attribute is defined over a domain: the set of atomic (indivisible) and single-valued permissible values for that attribute. A domain constraint requires every attribute's value to be drawn from such an atomic domain, which is exactly what excludes composite attributes (attributes built from sub-parts) and multivalued attributes (attributes holding more than one value at once).

Applying this here: among the given constraint types, only a domain constraint restricts what an attribute's domain may look like at the value level. Because a relational attribute's domain must contain atomic values only, any composite or multivalued attribute coming from an ER design must be decomposed into atomic attributes, or moved into a separate relation, before it can satisfy this constraint. So domain constraints are the rule that disallows them.

The other constraint types govern different things entirely:

  • Entity integrity constraint: requires a relation's primary key to be unique and not NULL. It says nothing about whether an attribute's domain is atomic.

  • Referential integrity constraint: requires a foreign key value to match an existing primary key value in the referenced relation, or be NULL. It governs cross-relation consistency, not attribute structure.

  • Uniqueness (key) constraint: requires values of a candidate-key attribute to be distinct across tuples. It says nothing about atomicity either.

So the constraint that disallows composite and multivalued attributes is the domain constraint.

Final answer: Statements 2, 3, and 4 are true; Statement 1 is false.

  • Statement 1 — (X,Y)→(Z,W) implies X→(Z,W): False. You cannot drop attribute Y without additional dependencies. Decomposition only gives (X,Y)→Z and (X,Y)→W.

  • Statement 4 — (X→Y and Y→Z) implies X→Z: True. This is the transitivity rule for functional dependencies.

Therefore choose the option that lists statements (X,Y)→Z, ((X,Y)→Z and W→Y) implies (X,W)→Z, and (X→Y and Y→Z) implies X→Z as true.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. This choice includes the statement that (X,Y)→(Z,W) implies X→(Z,W), which is false. From (X,Y)→(Z,W) you can derive (X,Y)→Z and (X,Y)→W by decomposition, but you cannot drop Y and conclude X→Z or X→W without additional information.

Incorrect. While (X,Y)→Z (decomposition) and the combination ((X,Y)→Z and W→Y) implying (X,W)→Z are both true, this choice wrongly includes the statement that (X,Y)→(Z,W) implies X→(Z,W), which is false. Also it omits the true transitivity statement X→Z from X→Y and Y→Z.

Correct. The true statements are: (X,Y)→Z (by decomposition); from (X,Y)→Z and W→Y you can derive (X,W)→Z (augment W→Y with X to get XW→XY, then use transitivity); and X→Z follows from X→Y and Y→Z (transitivity).

Incorrect. This choice claims all four statements are true, but the first statement is false: (X,Y)→(Z,W) does not imply X→(Z,W) unless additional dependencies exist. Decomposition only yields (X,Y)→Z and (X,Y)→W.

title: In schema with attributes and following set of functional dependencies
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
In a schema with attributes A, B, C, D, and E, the following set of functional dependencies is given: A → B, A → C, CD → E, B → D, E → A.

Which of the following functional dependencies is NOT implied by the given set?
solution:
Answer: BD → CD

To test whether a functional dependency is implied, compute the closure of its left-hand side.

CD⁺: Start with {C, D}. From CD → E, get E. From E → A, get A. From A → B, get B. So CD⁺ contains A and C; hence CD → AC is implied.

BD⁺: Start with {B, D}. From B → D, no new attribute is added because D is already present. There is no dependency that derives C from B or D. So C is not in BD⁺; hence BD → CD is not implied.

BC⁺: Start with {B, C}. From B → D, get D. Now C and D give E by CD → E, and E → A gives A. So BC⁺ contains C and D; hence BC → CD is implied.

AC⁺: Start with {A, C}. From A → B, get B, and C is already present. So AC⁺ contains B and C; hence AC → BC is implied.

Only BD → CD is not implied, so option B is correct.

optionFeedback.html: Implied. CD⁺ starts with {C, D}. From CD → E, we get E; from E → A, we get A. Since C is already present, CD⁺ contains both A and C. Therefore, CD → AC is implied.
Correct. BD⁺ = {B, D}. The dependency B → D adds only D, which is already present, and no dependency can derive C from B or D. Since C ∉ BD⁺, BD → CD is not implied.
Implied. BC⁺ starts with {B, C}. From B → D, we get D. Now C and D together give E by CD → E, and then E → A. Therefore, BC⁺ contains C and D, so BC → CD is implied.
Implied. AC⁺ starts with {A, C}. From A → B, we get B, and C is already present. Therefore, AC⁺ contains both B and C, so AC → BC is implied.

title: If two attributes, and satisfy the functional dependencies and then
subject: Data Base Management System
text: If two attributes, P and Q, satisfy the functional dependencies P → Q and Q → P, then they exhibit:
solution:
Concept

A functional dependency X → Y means the value of X uniquely determines the value of Y. When a dependency holds in BOTH directions — X → Y and also Y → X — each attribute set determines the other. Two attribute sets that determine each other this way are called equivalent, and the relationship is described as a mutual (reciprocal) functional dependency.

Application

Here we are told both P → Q and Q → P hold:

  • P → Q: knowing P fixes Q.

  • Q → P: knowing Q fixes P.

Since each of P and Q determines the other, they reciprocally (mutually) determine one another. This bidirectional determination is exactly a mutual functional dependency; P and Q are equivalent attribute sets.

Contrast with the other dependency types

  • Partial dependency: a non-prime attribute depends on only PART of a composite key — a one-way dependency on a key fragment, with no reverse arrow.

  • Full functional dependency: a non-prime attribute depends on the WHOLE composite key (not any proper subset) — again strictly one-directional, about a composite key.

  • Transitive dependency: an indirect chain X → Y and Y → Z that yields X → Z through an intermediate attribute — a one-way chain, not a pair of attributes that each directly determine the other.

  • Multivalued dependency: written X →→ Y, it concerns a SET of values associated with X (a different, non-functional kind of dependency, used for 4NF), not a single-valued determination in both directions.

Only one type captures determination in both directions: a mutual functional dependency.

optionFeedback.html: Partial dependency describes a non-prime attribute relying on only a fragment of a composite key. That is a single-direction relationship tied to part of a key, so it does not match a setting where each attribute determines the other.

Full functional dependency means an attribute depends on the entire composite key rather than a proper subset of it. It is still a one-way dependency about a composite key, so it does not capture the reverse arrow that is also present here.

Transitive dependency describes an indirect chain: X → Y and Y → Z give X → Z through an intermediate attribute. It is a one-directional chain rather than a pair of attributes that each directly determine the other, so it does not fit two attributes linked by arrows in both directions.

Multivalued dependency (X →→ Y) deals with a set of independent values linked to one attribute and is the basis of 4NF. It is not a single-valued determination, so it does not describe two attributes each fixing the other.

Both P → Q and Q → P hold, so each attribute uniquely fixes the other — a reciprocal, two-way determination. That bidirectional functional determination is precisely what a mutual functional dependency means, and it makes P and Q equivalent attribute sets.

title: Consider relation R(ABCDEF) with the FD set The number of
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Consider a relation R(ABCDEF) with the FD set F = {A → B, B → C, C → D, D → E}. The number of super keys of R is:
solution:
Answer: 16

  • Compute the closure of A: A → B, B → C, C → D, D → E, so A+ = {A, B, C, D, E}.

  • A alone does not determine F, so A is not a key. Adding F yields (A, F)+ = {A, B, C, D, E, F}, so {A, F} is a key.

  • Check minimality: removing A or F from {A, F} loses attributes, so {A, F} is a minimal (and the only) candidate key.

  • Count superkeys: there are 6 attributes total and the candidate key has size 2, so 4 attributes remain. Each of those 4 can be included or not in a superkey containing {A, F}, giving 2^4 = 16 superkeys.

Therefore, the number of superkeys of R is 16.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. A alone determines B, C, D, and E (A → B → C → D → E) but not F, so A is not a key. The only candidate key is {A, F}. There are 4 other attributes (B, C, D, E) that may be present or absent in a superkey containing {A, F}, giving 2^4 = 16 superkeys. Therefore 8 is not correct.

Incorrect. The candidate key is {A, F}: A determines B, C, D, E but not F, so A must be paired with F to get all attributes. With 4 remaining attributes (B, C, D, E) that can be included or excluded independently, the number of superkeys is 2^4 = 16, not 6.

Correct. A determines B, C, D, and E via the chain of FDs, so A alone lacks F. Adding F gives {A, F}+ = {A, B, C, D, E, F}, so {A, F} is a candidate key. It is minimal, so every superkey must contain {A, F}. The remaining four attributes (B, C, D, E) can be chosen or not, yielding 2^4 = 16 superkeys.

Incorrect. There is a valid numeric answer: 16. Because A → B → C → D → E, combining A with F gives a candidate key {A, F}. The four remaining attributes can be included or excluded independently, so there are 2^4 = 16 superkeys. "None of these" is therefore not correct.

title: For relational schema R(A, consider the following Functional Dependencies (FDs):
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
For a relational schema R(A, B, C, D, E, F) consider the following Functional Dependencies (FDs):

A ➡ B

C ➡ DF

AC ➡ E

D ➡ F

Determine the candidate key from the given Functional Dependencies (FDs).
solution:
A set of attributes K is a superkey of R if its closure K+ — found by repeatedly applying the given functional dependencies — contains every attribute of R. K is a candidate key if it is additionally minimal, meaning no proper subset of K is already a superkey. Any attribute that never appears on the right-hand side of any FD must belong to every candidate key, because no other attribute can ever derive it.

  1. Scan the right-hand side of every given FD (A → B, C → DF, AC → E, D → F): B, D, E and F each appear as some FD's right-hand side, but A and C never do.

  2. Since A and C never appear on any right-hand side, both must belong to every candidate key, so start by testing the closure of {A, C}.

  3. Apply A → B: B is added, giving {A, B, C}.

  4. Apply C → DF: D and F are added, giving {A, B, C, D, F}.

  5. Apply AC → E: E is added, giving {A, B, C, D, E, F}, which is every attribute of R.

  6. Because (AC)+ = R, the set {A, C} is a superkey.

  • Test A alone: only A → B applies, so A+ = {A, B}, which does not reach R — A alone is not a superkey.

  • Test C alone: only C → DF applies (D → F adds nothing new), so C+ = {C, D, F}, which also does not reach R — C alone is not a superkey either.

  • Since neither proper subset of {A, C} is a superkey, {A, C} is minimal, and since A and C must appear in every candidate key, it is the only candidate key of R.

The candidate key of R is AC.

optionFeedback.html: Applying the given dependencies to {A, B, C}: A → B reproduces B, C → DF yields D and F, and the rule that A and C together yield E then adds E, so the closure of {A, B, C} works out to {A, B, C, D, E, F}.

Applying the given dependencies to {A, C, D}: C → DF reproduces D and yields F, A → B yields B, and the rule that A and C together yield E then adds E, so the closure of {A, C, D} works out to {A, B, C, D, E, F}.
Applying the given dependencies to {A, C}: A → B yields B, C → DF yields D and F, and the rule that A and C together yield E then adds E, so the closure of {A, C} works out to {A, B, C, D, E, F}.
Applying the given dependencies to {A, B}: A → B reproduces B, while C → DF and the rule needing A and C together cannot fire without C, so the closure of {A, B} works out to {A, B}.

title: Consider the relation and following functional dependencies: R(id,name,date,rollno,class) FD: {id→name,
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Consider the relation R(id, name, date, rollno, class) and the functional-dependency set F = {id → name; {rollno, id} → {class, date}; class → date; class → id; name → id; name → rollno}. Which of the following is a canonical (minimal) cover of F?

options.html: {id → name, rollno → class, class → date, class → id, name → id, name → rollno}

solution:
Concept

A canonical cover must be equivalent to the original functional-dependency set.

Every dependency has one attribute on its right-hand side, no left-hand side contains an extraneous attribute, and no dependency is redundant.

Application

  1. Split {rollno, id} → {class, date} into {rollno, id} → class and {rollno, id} → date.

  2. Compute the closure of {id}: id → name and name → rollno give rollno; with id and rollno, the original dependencies give class and date. Thus rollno is extraneous in both composite left-hand sides, yielding id → class and id → date.

  3. Remove id → date because id → class followed by class → date already implies it. The remaining dependencies are id → name, id → class, class → date, class → id, name → id, and name → rollno.

Cross-check and contrast

The reduced set implies every original dependency. Conversely, removing any dependency from it loses part of the original closure.

  • The offered set containing {rollno, id} → class retains an extraneous determinant attribute.

  • The offered set containing {rollno, id} → {class, date} keeps a non-singleton right-hand side and does not list name → id.

  • The offered set containing rollno,→{class, date} has a malformed determinant and does not list class → id.

  • The offered four-dependency set does not contain a dependency that derives class or date.

Result: the canonical cover is {id → name, id → class, class → date, class → id, name → id, name → rollno}. None of the supplied options equals this set.

optionFeedback.html: This displayed set has six dependencies. Its left-hand sides are id, {rollno, id}, class, class, name, and name; each right-hand side has one attribute.
This displayed set has five dependencies. Its left-hand sides are id, {rollno, id}, class, class, and name; one right-hand side groups {class, date}.

This displayed set has six dependencies. It is incorrect because it improperly identifies 'id' as an extraneous attribute on the left-hand side of {rollno, id} → class. In the original set, the closure of 'rollno' is just {rollno}. Because 'rollno' cannot determine 'class' on its own, dropping 'id' changes the meaning of the dependencies, making this set not equivalent to the original set F.
This displayed set has four dependencies. Its left-hand-side sequence is id, class, name, and name; each right-hand side has one attribute.

title: Consider the relation R(A, satisfies the following FDs: B→A D→A
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the relation R(A, B, D) that satisfies the following FDs:
B→A
D→A
AB→D
What is the canonical cover for the FD set?
solution:
Concept: A canonical (minimal) cover of a set of functional dependencies F is an equivalent set Fc in which every dependency has a single attribute on its right-hand side, no dependency has an extraneous left-hand-side attribute, and no dependency is itself implied by the others. Two closure tests build it: to check if a left-hand-side attribute is extraneous, compute the closure of the remaining left-hand-side attribute(s) under the COMPLETE original F — if that closure already contains the right-hand-side attribute, the dropped attribute was extraneous. To check if an entire dependency X→Y is redundant, compute the closure of X using every OTHER dependency in the set (excluding X→Y itself) — if that closure already contains Y, the dependency is redundant.

Application: Apply both tests to F = {B→A, D→A, AB→D}.

  1. Every right-hand side (A, A, D) is already a single attribute, so this requirement is already met.

  2. Extraneous-attribute test on AB→D: compute B+ using the complete original F, not a reduced set. Applying B→A gives B+ = {A, B}. Since AB ⊆ {A, B}, applying AB→D adds D, giving B+ = {A, B, D}. Because D is already reachable from B alone, A is extraneous in AB→D, and the dependency can be replaced by B→D.

  3. This is exactly the step the reported concern is about: B→A does not replace AB→D — both B→A and AB→D are applied together, from the original F, purely to compute B's closure. That closure containing D is what licenses dropping A from the left-hand side; AB→D itself is never discarded until this closure test justifies it.

  4. The working set is now F' = {B→A, D→A, B→D}. Redundancy test on B→A: compute B+ using only the other two dependencies, {D→A, B→D}. Applying B→D gives {B, D}; applying D→A then gives {A, B, D}. A is reachable without using B→A, so B→A is redundant and is removed.

  5. Redundancy test on D→A: compute D+ using only the remaining dependency, {B→D}. No dependency has D on its left-hand side, so D+ stays {D} — A is not reachable, so D→A is NOT redundant and must stay.

  6. Redundancy test on B→D: compute B+ using only {D→A}. No dependency has B on its left-hand side, so B+ stays {B} — D is not reachable, so B→D is NOT redundant and must stay.

Cross-check: The redundancy tests above already guarantee equivalence — the only dependency removed, B→A, was shown to be implied by the two that were kept, and each retained dependency was shown to be necessary, so no information was lost. As a spot check, B's closure under the reduced set — apply B→D to get {B, D}, then D→A to get {A, B, D} — matches B+ computed under the original F in step 2.

Canonical cover: {B→D, D→A}

optionFeedback.html: This is where a student lands after reducing the composite dependency's left-hand side and treating that single step as the complete canonical-cover procedure. The full procedure pairs that reduction with a separate redundancy-elimination pass over the dependencies.
This is where a student lands after carrying out both parts of the procedure — reducing the composite dependency's left-hand side and then running the redundancy-elimination pass over what remains.

This is where a student lands after deciding that an original single-attribute dependency must be preserved unchanged, and reducing only the composite dependency. The procedure applies its tests uniformly and treats no dependency as protected from removal.

This is where a student lands after assuming a composite left-hand side can never be simplified, and concluding on that basis that the set cannot be reduced. Whether it can be is settled by running the extraneous-attribute test on that composite dependency.
