Justification: split A → BC into A → B and A → C; AB → C is implied by B → C and is redundant; A → C is implied by A → B and B → C and is redundant. The remaining minimal set is A → B and B → C.

title: Is candidate key of iff, must be superkey of relation
subject: Data Base Management System
subtopic: Super Key, Candidate Key & Primary Key
text:
X is a candidate key of relation R if and only if:

(I) X is a superkey of R.

(II) No proper subset of X is a superkey of R.
solution:
Concept

A superkey is an attribute set that functionally determines every attribute of a relation. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: it has the superkey property, but none of its proper subsets has that property.

Thus candidate-key status requires both sufficiency for identifying tuples and minimality of the identifying attribute set.

Application

Statement (I) supplies the superkey requirement. Statement (II) supplies the minimality requirement. Together they exactly express the definition of a candidate key.

Contrast

  • (I) alone allows a nonminimal superkey, such as {A, B} when A → B.

  • (II) alone can hold for a set that does not determine all attributes.

  • (I) OR (II) permits either one of those incomplete cases.

  • (I) AND (II) requires both the superkey and minimality properties.

Result

Therefore, the required combination is (I) AND (II).

optionFeedback.html: In R(A, B) with A → B and X = {A, B}, statement (I) is true because X determines A and B; the proper subset {A} also determines A and B.
In R(A, B) with no nontrivial functional dependency and X = {A}, statement (II) is true because a proper subset—the empty set—is not a superkey; X determines A but not B.
In R(A, B) with A → B and X = {A, B}, statement (I) is true because X determines A and B, while statement (II) is false because {A} also determines A and B; the OR expression is true for this state.
In R(A, B) with A → B and X = {A}, statement (I) is true because X determines A and B, and statement (II) is true because the empty set does not; the AND expression is true for this state.

title: How many maximum superkeys possible if R(A1,A2,…,A10) has attributes?
subject: Data Base Management System
subtopic: Super Key, Candidate Key & Primary Key
text: What is the maximum number of superkeys possible if R(A1, A2, …, A10) has 10 attributes?
solution:
Concept: A superkey of a relation is any subset of its attributes that functionally determines every attribute of a tuple — no two tuples can agree on the values of that subset. A candidate key is a minimal superkey (removing any attribute from it breaks that guarantee). Because every superset of a superkey is itself a superkey, the total count of superkeys depends entirely on which attributes form the relation's minimal keys.

Application:

  1. To maximise the number of superkeys for a relation with n attributes, make the “contains at least one key” condition as easy as possible to satisfy — this happens when every single attribute is, on its own, a candidate key.

  2. When each of the n attributes individually determines the whole tuple, any non-empty subset of the attribute set already contains at least one such key, so every non-empty subset qualifies as a superkey.

  3. R(A1, A2, …, A10) has n = 10 attributes, so its attribute set has 210 = 1024 subsets in total (including the empty set).

  4. The empty set can never be a superkey — it determines nothing about any tuple — so it is excluded: 210 − 1 = 1024 − 1 = 1023.

  5. Hence the maximum possible number of superkeys for this relation is 1023.

Cross-check:

Test the reasoning on a smaller relation: for n = 2 attributes (A, B), if both A and B are individually keys, the non-empty subsets {A}, {B} and {A, B} are all superkeys — 3 of them, matching 22 − 1 = 3. Scaling the same logic to n = 10 gives 210 − 1 = 1023, confirming the result. This is different from the case where exactly one specific attribute is the sole candidate key — there, only the subsets that contain that particular attribute are superkeys, giving 2(n−1) = 29 = 512, which is a smaller count, not the maximum.

Answer: 1023

title: Maximum number of superkeys for the relation schema R(X,Y,Z,W) with
subject: Data Base Management System
subtopic: Super Key, Candidate Key & Primary Key
text: Maximum number of superkeys for the relation schema R(X,Y,Z,W) with X and Y as keys is
solution:
To find the maximum number of superkeys for relation schema R(X,Y,Z,W) where X and Y are keys, note that a superkey must include at least one key. Since X and Y are keys, any superset of X or Y is a superkey.

The total number of subsets of the attributes is 2^4 = 16, since there are 4 attributes (X, Y, Z, W).

Subsets that do not include X or Y are not superkeys. These are subsets of {Z, W}, which has 2^2 = 4 subsets.

Therefore, the number of superkeys is total subsets minus non-superkey subsets: 16 - 4 = 12.

title: Candidate keys containing attribute A under the given functional dependencies
subject: Data Base Management System
subtopic: Super Key, Candidate Key & Primary Key
text: Consider a relation R(A, B, C, D, E) with FDs AC -> B, BD -> C, CE -> D, DA -> E, and EB -> A. Find the number of candidate keys that contain attribute A.
solution:
Concept

A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes whose closure is all of R. The phrase “contain attribute A” refers to membership of A in the key itself, not merely to A appearing in the key’s closure; every candidate key has closure ABCDE.

  • ACE⁺ = ABCDE: AC → B supplies B, and CE → D supplies D.

For each set above, no proper subset determines all five attributes, so all three are candidate keys. BCE and BDE are also candidate keys of the relation, but neither contains A and therefore neither is counted.

Therefore, the number of candidate keys that contain attribute A is 3.

title: Which of the following attributes can be considered as composite,
subject: Data Base Management System
subtopic: Super Key, Candidate Key & Primary Key
text: Which of the following attributes can be considered as composite, single-valued and key attribute?
solution:
Concept

Three independent properties of an entity attribute are being tested together:

  • Composite: an attribute that can be split into smaller meaningful sub-parts (for example, Address into street / city / PIN).

  • Single-valued: an attribute that holds exactly one value per entity (the opposite of multi-valued).

  • Key: an attribute whose value is unique, so it can identify one entity unambiguously.

The answer must satisfy all three properties at the same time, so the safest method is to start from the strictest, least-common property and eliminate.

Apply the strictest test first: the key requirement

Uniqueness is the property the fewest attributes have, so test it first. Among the choices, only an enrollment number is guaranteed unique per student, so it is the only possible key. Age, date of birth and gender all repeat across different students, so none of them can be a key, and each is therefore eliminated regardless of its other properties.

Confirm the remaining properties

Each student has exactly one enrollment number, so it is single-valued. By convention institutions encode structure inside it, for example [Year]-[Stream]-[RollNo], so it can be decomposed into meaningful sub-parts and is treated as composite. It therefore satisfies all three requirements, while the eliminated options fail on the key requirement.

Why the close distractor still fails

  • Date of birth is the strongest trap: it is genuinely composite (day / month / year) and single-valued, but two students can share a birth date, so it is not a key and cannot be the answer.

  • Age is single-valued but atomic (not composite) and not unique; it is also usually derived from date of birth.

  • Gender is a simple, single-valued attribute that is neither composite nor unique.

Result: an enrollment number is the only attribute here that is simultaneously composite, single-valued and a key.

optionFeedback.html: Age is single-valued but it is atomic, so it is not composite, and many students can share the same age, so it cannot serve as a key. It is also usually derived from date of birth rather than stored directly.

Date of birth is genuinely composite (day, month, year) and single-valued, so it is tempting; however, it fails the key requirement, because two or more students can have the same birth date and so it cannot uniquely identify an entity.
Gender is a simple, single-valued attribute. It cannot be broken into sub-parts, so it is not composite, and it repeats across many students, so it cannot act as a key.

An enrollment number is unique to each student (key), holds one value per student (single-valued), and encodes structured sub-parts such as [Year]-[Stream]-[RollNo] (composite), so it meets all three criteria together.

title: Which of the following statements regarding Super Key and Primary
subject: Data Base Management System
subtopic: Super Key, Candidate Key & Primary Key
text: Which of the following statements regarding Super Key and Primary Key is incorrect?

options.html: Every primary key is a super key.
A super key may contain additional attributes not required for unique identification.
A table can have multiple super keys.
Every super key is selected as the primary key of a table.
A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table

solution:
Concept

A super key is any set of one or more attributes that uniquely identifies every row (tuple) in a relation. A candidate key is a minimal super key (no attribute can be removed without losing uniqueness). The primary key is the ONE candidate key that the database designer chooses to be the row identifier for the table. So the hierarchy is: super keys (broadest) contain candidate keys, and exactly one candidate key is promoted to primary key.

Applying it to the statements

The question asks for the statement that is FALSE. The false statement claims that every super key is selected as the primary key of a table. That cannot be true: a table typically has many super keys, but only one of them is designated as the primary key. Selection happens once, on a single candidate key; the remaining super keys stay just super keys (some are alternate/candidate keys, others carry redundant extra attributes).

Why the others are true

  • Every primary key is a super key: the primary key uniquely identifies each row, which is exactly the defining property of a super key, so it is a super key by definition.

  • A super key may contain additional attributes not required for unique identification: this is precisely why a super key need not be minimal; remove the redundant attributes and it becomes a candidate key.

  • A table can have multiple super keys: any super key plus any extra attributes is still a super key, so the count of super keys can be large.

  • A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table: this is the basic definition of a primary key.

Result

The statement "Every super key is selected as the primary key of a table" is the incorrect one, because only a single chosen candidate key becomes the primary key, not every super key.

optionFeedback.html: As a matter of definition, this statement holds: a primary key uniquely identifies each row, and unique identification is exactly what makes a set of attributes a super key. So a primary key satisfies the super-key property automatically.

This statement holds: a super key need not be minimal, so it can include attributes beyond those strictly needed for uniqueness. Removing the redundant attributes from such a super key produces a candidate key.
This statement holds: appending any extra attribute to an existing super key yields another super key, so a single table can contain many distinct super keys.

This statement does not hold: a table usually has several super keys, yet only a single candidate key is designated as the primary key. The remaining super keys are never promoted, so the claim that every super key becomes the primary key contradicts how key designation works.
This statement holds: uniquely identifying each record is the basic definition of a primary key, so it is a correct description of what a primary key does.

title: Let be relation schema with the following dependencies EC Which
subject: Data Base Management System
subtopic: Super Key, Candidate Key & Primary Key
text: Let R ={A, B, C, D, E, F} be a relation schema with the following dependencies C → F, E → A, EC → D, A → B Which of the following is a key for R ?
solution:
Solution: Find the candidate key(s) by computing attribute closures.

Compute the closure of EC:

  • Start with {E, C}.

  • E → A, so add A. Now have {E, C, A}.

  • C → F, so add F. Now have {E, C, A, F}.

  • A → B, so add B. Now have {A, B, C, E, F}.

  • EC → D (we already have E and C), so add D. Now have {A, B, C, D, E, F}.

Since EC+ = {A, B, C, D, E, F}, EC determines all attributes and is therefore a key.

Check minimality:

  • E+ = {E, A, B} (from E → A and A → B) — missing C, D, F, so E alone is not a key.

  • C+ = {C, F} (from C → F) — missing A, B, D, E, so C alone is not a key.

Thus EC is minimal and is a candidate key.

Briefly check the other choices:

  • CD+: start {C, D}; C → F gives F, so CD+ = {C, D, F}. Cannot derive A, B, or E, so CD is not a key.

  • AE+: start {A, E}; E → A and A → B give {A, B, E}. Cannot derive C, D, or F, so AE is not a key.

  • AC+: start {A, C}; C → F and A → B give {A, B, C, F}. Cannot derive E or D, so AC is not a key.

Final answer: EC is a candidate key for R.

optionFeedback.html: CD is not a key. Compute the closure: starting with C and D, C → F gives F, so CD+ = {C, D, F}. None of the other dependencies allow you to derive A, B, or E from these, so CD does not determine all attributes.

EC is a candidate key. Compute the closure: start with E,C. E → A gives A; C → F gives F; A → B gives B; and EC → D gives D. So EC+ = {A, B, C, D, E, F}, which is all attributes. Neither E alone nor C alone gives all attributes, so EC is minimal and thus a candidate key.

AE is not a key. Compute the closure: starting with A and E, E → A adds nothing new, and A → B gives B, so AE+ = {A, E, B}. There is no way to derive C, D, or F from these, so AE does not determine all attributes.

AC is not a key. Compute the closure: starting with A and C, C → F gives F and A → B gives B, so AC+ = {A, C, B, F}. Without E you cannot use EC → D, and there is no rule to get E, so AC does not determine D or E and therefore is not a key.

title: Referential Integrity constraint is related to which of the following:
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Referential Integrity constraint is related to which of the following:
solution:
Answer: Referential integrity is enforced using foreign keys.

Explanation: Referential integrity ensures that relationships between tables remain consistent by controlling the values stored in a foreign key column.

  • A foreign key in a child table must match an existing primary or candidate key value in the referenced parent table, or be NULL if the foreign key allows nulls.

  • This prevents orphan records and maintains consistency across related tables.

  • Example: If Orders.customer_id is a foreign key referencing Customers.id, every non-null Orders.customer_id value must exist in Customers.id.

title: Field in table can be taken as foreign key if
subject: Data Base Management System
text: A field in a table can be taken as a foreign key if

options.html: It is present in all other tables
Is a primary key in some other table
Is not present in any other table

solution:
Concept

A foreign key is a field (or set of fields) in one table whose values are constrained to match an existing key in another (referenced) table. The column it points to in that other table must be a key that uniquely identifies each row — in standard relational design this is the primary key of the referenced table. This referential link is what lets a foreign key value act as a reliable pointer to exactly one row elsewhere.

Application

A field qualifies as a foreign key precisely when its values reference the primary key of some other table. The defining property is not anything about the field's own table; it is the relationship that the field's values point to the primary key column of a different table, guaranteeing every foreign key value corresponds to an existing parent row.

Why the other choices fail

  • “Has unique values” describes a candidate/primary key within the table itself, not a reference to another table; a foreign key column may legitimately contain duplicate values (many child rows can point to the same parent).

  • “Is present in all other tables” is not required — a foreign key relates to exactly one referenced table, not to every table in the schema.

  • “Is not present in any other table” contradicts the very idea of a reference: a foreign key exists only because its values are shared with the key of another table.

optionFeedback.html: Whether the same field name happens to appear in other tables is not something any database constraint declares or enforces — it is purely incidental naming, unlike the formally declared properties that determine a field's role. A schema can reuse a column name across many tables with no significance attached to it at all.

Having unique values is a property confined to the field's own table — it is what characterizes a candidate or primary key there. It says nothing about any link to a different table, so satisfying it alone does not make a field a foreign key.

Referring to the primary key of another table is exactly what creates the referential link: each value here must match an existing key in that other table, so it reliably points to one parent row. This is the property that makes the field a foreign key.

Whether a field's name happens to appear nowhere else in the schema is, likewise, not something any database constraint declares or enforces — it is purely incidental naming, unlike the formally declared properties that determine a field's role. A field can be uniquely named in the schema with no significance attached to that fact at all.

title: When foreign key constraint is enforced in relational database, which
subject: Data Base Management System
text: When a foreign key constraint is enforced in a relational database, which condition must normally be satisfied while inserting a non-NULL value into the foreign key column?

options.html: The value can be inserted without checking the referenced table.
The value must match an existing value in the referenced primary key or unique key column.
A new primary key value is automatically generated in the parent table.
The foreign key checks only uniqueness of the inserted value.
The foreign key column must always contain NULL values.

solution:
A foreign key (FK) enforces referential integrity between a child table and a parent (referenced) table. The rule is: every non-NULL value placed in the foreign key column must already exist as a value in the referenced primary key (or unique/candidate key) column of the parent table.

This prevents "orphan" rows that point to a parent record that does not exist. So when you insert a non-NULL FK value, the database first checks the referenced table; if no matching parent value is found, the INSERT is rejected with a foreign-key-violation error. (A NULL is allowed and bypasses this check, but the question specifically concerns a non-NULL value.)

Therefore the condition that must be satisfied is: the inserted value must match an existing value in the referenced primary/unique key column. The correct option is "The value must match an existing value in the referenced primary key or unique key column."

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. A foreign key exists precisely so that the database does validate the inserted value against the referenced (parent) table. Skipping that check would allow orphan rows, which is exactly what the constraint is designed to prevent.

Correct. Referential integrity requires that any non-NULL value in the foreign key column already exist as a value in the referenced primary key (or unique/candidate key) column of the parent table; otherwise the INSERT is rejected.
Incorrect. A foreign key never creates or auto-generates a row in the parent table. The parent value must already be present; the FK only references it, it does not insert it.

Incorrect. A foreign key does not enforce uniqueness on the child column; the same FK value may repeat across many child rows (a many-to-one link). What it checks is existence of the value in the parent table, not uniqueness in the child.
Incorrect. A foreign key column is not required to be NULL. NULL is merely permitted (it means "no reference"); the column normally holds real, non-NULL values that point to existing parent rows.

title: In DBMS, which referential integrity action of foreign key constraint
subject: Data Base Management System
text: In DBMS, which referential integrity action of a foreign key constraint automatically deletes related child records when the corresponding parent record is deleted?
solution:
Correct answer: Cascade.

In a relational DBMS, a FOREIGN KEY constraint can specify a referential action that defines what happens to the dependent (child) rows when the referenced (parent) row is deleted or updated. The ON DELETE CASCADE action automatically removes all matching child rows whenever the corresponding parent row is deleted, keeping referential integrity intact without leaving orphan rows.

Example: CREATE TABLE orders ( ... customer_id INT REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE CASCADE ); — deleting a customer then also deletes that customer's orders automatically.

The other choices are not the deletion-propagating referential action: Restrict is a referential action, but it BLOCKS the parent deletion when child rows exist (it does not delete them); Commit, Rollback and Savepoint are transaction-control (TCL) concepts, not foreign-key referential actions at all.

optionFeedback.html: Restrict (or NO ACTION) is a genuine referential action, but it does the opposite of what is asked: when child rows exist, it rejects/blocks the deletion of the parent row rather than removing the children. So no automatic deletion of child records occurs.
Commit is a transaction-control (TCL) command that permanently saves the work done in the current transaction. It has nothing to do with foreign-key referential actions or with deleting child rows.

Rollback is a transaction-control (TCL) command that undoes the changes of the current transaction back to the last commit or savepoint. It is not a foreign-key referential action and does not delete dependent rows.

Correct. ON DELETE CASCADE is the referential action that propagates a parent-row deletion to its children: when the referenced parent row is deleted, every matching child (dependent) row is automatically deleted too, preventing orphan rows and preserving referential integrity.

A Savepoint marks an intermediate point within a transaction so you can later roll back part of it. It is a transaction-control feature, not a foreign-key referential action, and it does not delete child records.

title: Which of the following statements is true regarding Foreign Key
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following statements is true regarding a Foreign Key in a relational database?

options.html: A foreign key uniquely identifies every record in a table.
A foreign key is primarily used to sort records in ascending order.
A foreign key establishes a relationship between two tables using referenced values.
A foreign key must always contain only unique values.
A foreign key cannot contain duplicate or NULL values.

solution:
Concept

A foreign key is a column (or set of columns) in one table whose values must match the values of a candidate key (usually the primary key) in another — the referenced or parent — table. Its defining role is to enforce referential integrity: it ties rows in a child table to existing rows in a parent table, thereby modelling a relationship between the two tables.

Applying it here

The statement that a foreign key “establishes a relationship between two tables using referenced values” captures exactly this definition: the foreign-key column points at values that already exist in the referenced table, creating and constraining the link between the two relations. That is the purpose for which foreign keys exist.

Why the other statements fail

  • “Uniquely identifies every record” — that is the job of a primary key, not a foreign key; a foreign-key value commonly repeats across many child rows.

  • “Used to sort records in ascending order” — ordering is done with ORDER BY (and assisted by indexes); a foreign key imposes no ordering on rows.

  • “Must always contain only unique values” — uniqueness is a property of primary/unique keys; the same foreign-key value may appear in many rows (e.g. many orders referencing one customer).

  • “Cannot contain duplicate or NULL values” — a foreign key may both repeat and, unless declared NOT NULL, hold NULL to represent “no related row.”

Result

A foreign key establishes a relationship between two tables using referenced values — it is the mechanism of referential integrity, not of identity, ordering, or uniqueness.

optionFeedback.html: Uniquely identifying every record in a table is the role of the primary key. A foreign-key column is not required to be unique, so describing it as a per-row unique identifier misreads its purpose.
Sorting records into ascending order is handled by an ORDER BY clause (with help from indexes). A foreign key imposes no ordering on the data, so tying it to ascending sort is a misconception.

A foreign-key column holds values that must already exist as a key in a referenced (parent) table; that referencing is what links rows in the two tables and lets the database enforce referential integrity between them — the very purpose for which foreign keys are defined.

“Always only unique values” describes a primary or unique key constraint. The same foreign-key value can legitimately appear in many rows — for example many child rows referencing one parent — so mandatory uniqueness does not apply here.
A foreign key may repeat across rows, and unless its column is declared NOT NULL it may also hold NULL to mean “no related row.” Ruling out all duplicates and NULLs overstates the constraint.

title: Match the following with respect to RDBMS \(\begin{array}{clcl} \text{(a)} \text{Entity
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Match the following with respect to RDBMS :

\(\begin{array}{clcl} \text{(a)} & \text{Entity integrity} & \text{(i)} & \text{enforces some specific business rule that do not} \\ &&& \text{fall into entity or domain} \\ \text{(b)} & \text{Domain integrity} & \text{(ii)} & \text{Rows can’t be deleted which are used by} \\ &&& \text{other records} \\ \text{(c)} & \text{Referential integrity} & \text{(iii)} & \text{enforces valid entries for a column} \\ \text{(d)} & \text{Userdefined integrity} & \text{(iv)} & \text{No duplicate rows in a table} \end{array}\)

Code :
solution:
Correct matching and brief explanations:

  • Entity integrity → No duplicate rows in a table. Ensures each row can be uniquely identified (primary key).

  • Domain integrity → Enforces valid entries for a column. Controls data type, permissible values, and value ranges for attributes.

  • Referential integrity → Rows can’t be deleted which are used by other records. Maintains consistency of foreign key relationships between tables.

  • User-defined integrity → Enforces some specific business rules that do not fall into entity or domain constraints. Used for application-specific or organization-specific constraints.

So the correct mapping is: (a) Entity integrity → No duplicate rows; (b) Domain integrity → Enforces valid entries for a column; (c) Referential integrity → Rows referenced by other records cannot be deleted; (d) User-defined integrity → Enforces specific business rules.

optionFeedback.html: This mapping is incorrect. Entity integrity does not mean enforcing valid entries for a column; it ensures uniqueness of rows via the primary key (no duplicate rows). Domain integrity enforces valid column values. Referential integrity controls relationships between tables (for example, preventing deletion of rows that are referenced). User-defined integrity enforces specific business rules. The correct pairings are: Entity integrity → No duplicate rows; Domain integrity → Enforces valid entries for a column; Referential integrity → Rows used by other records cannot be deleted; User-defined integrity → Enforces specific business rules.

Correct. Entity integrity ensures each row can be uniquely identified (no duplicate rows) via keys. Domain integrity enforces valid values and types for a column. Referential integrity maintains consistency between related tables (for example, preventing deletion of a row referenced by others). User-defined integrity covers additional business rules that are not captured by entity or domain constraints.

This mapping is incorrect. Domain integrity was paired with preventing deletions of referenced rows, which is actually a referential integrity concern. Referential integrity was paired with enforcing valid column entries, which belongs to domain integrity. The correct mapping is: Domain integrity → Enforces valid entries for a column; Referential integrity → Rows referenced by other records cannot be deleted. Entity integrity and user-defined integrity are also mismatched here.

This mapping is incorrect. Entity integrity was paired with preventing deletion of referenced rows, but entity integrity actually ensures uniqueness of rows (no duplicate rows). Referential integrity is the rule that prevents deleting rows used by other records. Domain integrity (valid column values) and user-defined integrity (business-specific rules) should be matched accordingly.

title: What is the primary role of referential integrity constraints in

text: What is the primary role of referential integrity constraints in a relational database system?

options.html: To verify that values in a foreign key correspond to valid entries in the referenced primary key
To stop repeated values from being inserted into a column

optionFeedback.html: Correct. This is the exact definition and primary role of a referential integrity constraint.
This option describes a unique constraint, not referential integrity. Check if the question asks about relationships between tables or single-column rules.

title: How does properly implemented foreign key constraint contribute to the
subject: Data Base Management System
text: How does a properly implemented foreign key constraint contribute to the consistency property in a database transaction?

options.html: By ensuring that all inserted rows are committed immediately
By ensuring that a referenced record exists in the parent table
By automatically removing orphan records during insertion
By allowing duplicate values in the referencing column

solution: A foreign key enforces referential integrity, which directly supports the Consistency (C) property of ACID transactions. It guarantees that a child table cannot reference a non-existent value in the parent table. If a transaction attempts to insert an invalid reference or delete a parent record that still has active child records, the database engine automatically rejects the transaction, preventing data corruption and keeping the system in a valid state.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Immediate commitment is related to the Durability (D) and Isolation (I) properties of a transaction managed by transaction logs and commit protocols, not foreign key constraints.

Correct. By validating that every foreign key value points to a valid primary key in the parent table, the database prevents "dangling pointers" or orphan references, preserving structural consistency.

Incorrect. Inserting data into a child table does not delete records. While properties like ON DELETE CASCADE can remove child records when a parent is deleted, foreign keys reject invalid child rows during insertion rather than removing them.

Incorrect. While foreign key columns can contain duplicate values by default (unless paired with a unique constraint), allowing duplicates does not actively contribute to maintaining transactional consistency.

optionFeedback.html: Whether the same field name happens to appear in other tables is not something any database constraint declares or enforces — it is purely incidental naming, unlike the formally declared properties that determine a field's role. A schema can reuse a column name across many tables with no significance attached to it at all.

Having unique values is a property confined to the field's own table — it is what characterizes a candidate or primary key there. It says nothing about any link to a different table, so satisfying it alone does not make a field a foreign key.

Referring to the primary key of another table is exactly what creates the referential link: each value here must match an existing key in that other table, so it reliably points to one parent row. This is the property that makes the field a foreign key.

Whether a field's name happens to appear nowhere else in the schema is, likewise, not something any database constraint declares or enforces — it is purely incidental naming, unlike the formally declared properties that determine a field's role. A field can be uniquely named in the schema with no significance attached to that fact at all.

title: Employee salary should not be greater than Rs. This is

solution:
Concept

An integrity constraint is a rule attached to a relation that every stored row must satisfy, so the database can never hold data that violates the rule. A domain (CHECK) constraint is the integrity-constraint variety that restricts the permitted values of a column to those meeting a stated condition.

Application

"Employee salary should not be greater than Rs. 12,000" places a condition on the values allowed in the salary column. In SQL this is written as a CHECK constraint, for example CHECK (salary <= 12000). Because it limits the legal values of a single attribute, it is a domain constraint, which is one kind of integrity constraint. So the rule classifies as an integrity constraint.

Contrast

  • Referential constraint: governs a relationship between two tables via a foreign key (a value in one table must exist as a key in another); the salary rule involves no second table, so it does not apply.

  • Over-defined constraint: not a recognised category of database constraint; it has no defined meaning in the relational model.

  • Feasible constraint: not a database-constraint term either; "feasibility" belongs to optimisation, not to DBMS integrity rules.

Therefore the salary rule is an integrity constraint.

"Over-defined constraint" is not a category in the relational model; database constraints are classified as domain, key, entity-integrity and referential-integrity, with no such named type.

title: What is the goal of normalization in database design?
subject: Data Base Management System
text: What is the goal of normalization in database design?
solution:
Concept

Database normalization is the systematic decomposition of a relational schema into smaller tables guided by functional dependencies (1NF -> 2NF -> 3NF -> BCNF). Its governing design objective, as stated in relational database theory, is to eliminate insertion, deletion, and update anomalies that occur when a single fact is stored redundantly across multiple rows — not merely to shrink storage size or speed up queries.

Application

Applying that principle here: storing a fact once and referencing it via a key removes the possibility that inserting a new record forces an unrelated fact to be entered, that deleting a record erases a fact that should have survived, or that updating a fact requires touching several rows to keep the data consistent. Reducing redundancy is the mechanism decomposition uses, but avoiding these three named anomalies is the design goal that mechanism serves.

Contrasting the other options

  • 'To increase data redundancy' runs opposite to what normalization does: functional-dependency decomposition is used to shrink the number of stored copies of a fact, not increase them.

  • 'To optimize query performance' names a possible side effect, not the design objective: a normalized schema is usually split into more tables, which typically requires more joins per query — organizations often denormalize deliberately afterward to regain query speed.

  • 'All of these' would require every listed statement to hold at once; since the query-performance statement does not hold as a general design objective, the combined claim fails.

So the option that matches relational database theory's stated purpose of normalization is reducing data anomalies — insertion, deletion, and update anomalies — through functional-dependency-driven decomposition.

optionFeedback.html: Data redundancy refers to how many times a single fact is physically stored across a schema's rows and tables. The number of stored copies for a given schema is shaped mainly by how far its tables have been decomposed according to functional dependencies (1NF through BCNF), along with the data itself.

Data anomalies — insertion, deletion, and update anomalies — refer to how many other rows must be revisited to keep a duplicated determinant-dependent fact consistent when one copy of it changes. How many such duplicated facts remain in a schema is shaped mainly by how far its tables have been decomposed according to functional dependencies, along with the data itself.

Query performance refers to how many joins, index lookups, and table scans a query requires to return its result. How many joins a given query needs is shaped mainly by how many tables a schema is split into, along with which specific relations and attributes that query accesses.

'All of these' refers to the joint claim that redundancy count, anomaly count, and join count all change together as a schema is decomposed. Whether those three move together for a given design is shaped by how its functional dependencies and query patterns interact, not by a fixed rule.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q156
subject: Data Base Management System
text: The process of eliminating redundancy in a database is called
solution:
Concept

Database normalization is the systematic process of organizing a relational database's tables and columns according to a series of formal rules (the normal forms: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF), using functional-dependency analysis to guide how tables are decomposed. The goal is to keep each fact stored in only one place -- removing repeating groups and reducing redundant (duplicate) data, which lowers the risk of insertion, update, and deletion anomalies.

Application to this question

The question asks for the name of the process whose goal is specifically to eliminate redundancy in a database. Normalization is directed at exactly this: it decomposes tables using functional-dependency analysis and applies the normal-form rules so that each piece of information is intended to appear only once, directly matching what the stem describes.

Why the other options do not fit

  • Replication: creates and maintains additional copies of the same data across multiple servers or nodes (for availability and read scaling) -- this increases the number of copies of data, the opposite of eliminating redundancy.

  • Virtualization: abstracts physical database server hardware and resources into one or more logical (virtual) instances for resource management and consolidation -- it does not change how data is structured within a schema.

  • Minimization: is a data-governance and privacy principle about limiting how much personal data is collected and retained, not a formal schema-design technique for restructuring tables.

Therefore, the process of eliminating redundancy in a database is Normalization.

optionFeedback.html: Replication is the process of creating and continuously synchronizing duplicate copies of the same data across multiple database servers or nodes, typically to improve availability, fault tolerance, and read performance.

Virtualization is the abstraction of physical database server hardware and resources (compute, storage, memory) into one or more logical instances, allowing multiple virtual database environments to run on shared physical infrastructure.

Normalization is the process of organizing a database's tables and columns according to the normal-form rules (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF), using functional-dependency analysis between attributes to guide how a table is decomposed into smaller, related tables.

Data minimization is a data-governance and privacy principle that limits the volume and retention period of personal data collected by a system, commonly required under regulatory frameworks such as GDPR.

Therefore, the best offered answer is “Remove redundancy,” understood as reducing avoidable redundancy.

title: Which one of the following is true?
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the relation R(A, B, C, D, E, P, G) with the following functional dependencies:
AB → CD, DE → P, C → E, P → C, B → G
Which one of the following is true?

options.html: R is in 3NF, but not in BCNF

solution:
Concept

Second Normal Form (2NF) requires that the relation is in 1NF and that no non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on only a part of any candidate key. A non-prime attribute is one that belongs to no candidate key. A partial dependency occurs when a non-prime attribute is determined by a proper subset of a candidate key. The normal forms are nested: a relation must clear 2NF before it can be considered for 3NF, and 3NF before BCNF, so a 2NF violation rules out all higher forms.

Application to this relation

Step 1 - Find the candidate key. Attributes A and B never appear on the right-hand side of any FD, so they must belong to every candidate key. Compute the closure of {A, B}:

  1. Start: {A, B}.

  2. Apply AB → CD to add C and D, giving {A, B, C, D}.

  3. Apply C → E to add E, giving {A, B, C, D, E}.

  4. Apply DE → P to add P, giving {A, B, C, D, E, P}.

  5. Apply B → G to add G, giving {A, B, C, D, E, P, G}.

The closure {A, B}+ equals all seven attributes, and neither A nor B alone closes to the whole relation, so {A, B} is the unique, minimal candidate key. The prime attributes are A and B; the non-prime attributes are C, D, E, P, and G.

Step 2 - Test for a partial dependency. The proper subsets of the key {A, B} are {A} and {B}. The dependency B → G uses only {B}, a proper subset of the key, to determine G, and G is non-prime. That is exactly a partial dependency of a non-prime attribute on part of the candidate key.

Cross-check and contrast

Because a partial dependency exists, the relation fails 2NF. Since the normal forms are nested, failing 2NF automatically means it is neither in 3NF nor in BCNF, so the strongest correct statement is that the relation is not in 2NF. The remaining FDs (AB → CD, DE → P, C → E, P → C) do not repair this: the single FD B → G is sufficient to break 2NF.

optionFeedback.html: This claims R already satisfies BCNF, the strongest normalization tier. But the candidate key is {A, B}, and B → G lets the proper subset {B} determine the non-prime attribute G — a dependency that must be cleared before any higher tier is even reachable.

This claims R clears the boundary into 3NF while still falling short of BCNF. But the same dependency B → G ties the non-prime attribute G to {B} alone, a proper subset of the candidate key {A, B} — a gap that must be resolved before that 3NF-versus-BCNF boundary is even relevant.

This claims R clears the lower normalization tier and only falls short at the 3NF boundary. But the dependency B → G ties the non-prime attribute G to {B} alone, a proper subset of the candidate key {A, B} — that gap belongs to the lower tier itself, so the 3NF comparison never becomes relevant.

This claims R fails at the 2NF boundary itself. The candidate key {A, B} has proper subset {B}, and B → G ties the non-prime attribute G to that subset alone — exactly the gap that keeps R from clearing 2NF.

title: Which of the following normal forms deals with ensuring that

The fundamental requirement of Second Normal Form (2NF) is the elimination of partial dependencies.

  • What it means: A partial dependency occurs when a non-key attribute depends on only a part of a composite primary key, rather than the entire key.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q157
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which normal form removes partial dependency ?
solution:
Concept: In relational database normalization, each higher normal form removes one specific class of dependency. Second Normal Form (2NF) requires a relation to already satisfy 1NF, and additionally requires that every non-prime attribute be fully functionally dependent on the whole of every candidate key -- not on just part of a composite key. A non-prime attribute depending on only part of a composite candidate key is called a partial dependency, and eliminating it is exactly what the 1NF-to-2NF transformation does.

Application: A partial dependency can only arise when a candidate key is composite (made of more than one attribute); with a single-attribute key, every non-prime attribute is automatically dependent on the whole key. Converting a 1NF relation to 2NF means decomposing it so that any attribute depending on only part of the composite key is moved into its own relation keyed on that part, leaving every remaining non-prime attribute dependent on the whole key -- this decomposition is precisely what removes the partial dependency.

Cross-check (contrast with the other normal forms):

  • 1NF only requires that every column hold a single atomic value and that there be no repeating groups; it does not analyze functional dependency between the key and non-key attributes at all, so it has no mechanism to remove partial dependency.

  • 3NF builds on 2NF by removing transitive dependency -- the case where a non-prime attribute depends on another non-prime attribute rather than directly on the key -- which is a different dependency class from partial dependency.

  • BCNF strengthens 3NF by requiring every determinant of a functional dependency in the relation to be a superkey (a candidate key or a superset of one), which addresses anomalies from overlapping candidate keys rather than partial dependency specifically.

Since partial dependency is defined as a non-prime attribute depending on only part (not all) of a composite candidate key, and only the 2NF definition explicitly targets and removes this dependency, the normal form that removes partial dependency is 2NF.

optionFeedback.html: 1NF (First Normal Form) is defined by requiring every column in a relation to hold a single atomic (indivisible) value, with no repeating groups or multi-valued fields within a row; it addresses the structure of attribute values themselves, not the functional-dependency relationship between the key and other attributes.

2NF (Second Normal Form) is defined by requiring every non-prime attribute in a relation to be fully functionally dependent on the whole of each candidate key -- so no non-prime attribute may be determined by only part of a composite key.

3NF (Third Normal Form) is defined by requiring that no non-prime attribute be transitively dependent on a candidate key -- that is, no non-prime attribute may be determined through another non-prime attribute rather than directly by the key.

BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form) is defined by requiring that every determinant of a functional dependency in the relation be a superkey (a candidate key or a superset of one), which eliminates anomalies arising from overlapping candidate keys.

  • 1NF removes repeating groups/non-atomic values.

  • 2NF (1NF + no partial functional dependency of any non-prime attribute on a proper subset of a candidate key) removes partial dependencies.

  • 3NF (2NF + for every functional dependency X -> A that holds, either X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute) removes transitive dependencies.

  • BCNF strengthens 3NF by requiring every determinant of a functional dependency to be a superkey.

  • 4NF (BCNF + every non-trivial multivalued dependency has a superkey as its determinant) removes multivalued-dependency anomalies.

Application

The blank in the stem asks for the normal form whose defining elimination criterion is exactly "no partial functional dependency." That criterion is, by definition, the boundary between 1NF and 2NF: a relation already in 1NF is promoted to 2NF precisely by removing every partial functional dependency of a non-prime attribute on a proper subset of a candidate key. So the blank is filled by 2NF.

Contrast

The other three normal forms are defined by a different elimination criterion, so none of them is a valid fit for this blank:

  • 3NF's defining criterion is that every functional dependency X -> A must have X as a superkey or A as a prime attribute, eliminating transitive dependencies of a non-prime attribute through a non-superkey determinant, not partial dependencies.

  • BCNF's defining criterion is that every determinant of any functional dependency must be a superkey — a condition about determinants, not about partial dependency on part of a key.

  • 4NF's defining criterion is that every non-trivial multivalued dependency must have a superkey as its determinant, an entirely different (and stricter, later-stage) condition than partial functional dependency.

Note that 3NF, BCNF, and 4NF each additionally require the relation to already be free of partial dependencies (since they are progressively stronger than 2NF), but none of them is defined by that condition — 2NF is the unique form whose defining, distinguishing criterion is "no partial functional dependency."

2NF is defined as: the relation is in 1NF, and additionally every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on each candidate key, i.e., no non-prime attribute has a partial functional dependency on a proper subset of a candidate key.

4NF is defined as: the relation is in BCNF, and additionally for every non-trivial multivalued dependency X ->-> Y that holds in the relation, X must be a superkey (i.e., every multivalued-dependency determinant is a superkey).

title: Let R(A,B,C,D,E,P,G) be relational schema in which the following FDs
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Let R(A, B, C, D, E, P, G) be a relational schema in which the following functional dependencies are known to hold:

  • AB → CD

  • DE → P

  • C → E

  • P → C

  • B → G

The relation schema R is ______.

options.html: In third normal form, but not in Boyce-Codd normal form
In second normal form, but not in third normal form

solution:
A relation is in Second Normal Form (2NF) when it is already in 1NF and, in addition, every non-prime attribute (one that belongs to no candidate key) is fully functionally dependent on each candidate key as a whole — with no non-prime attribute depending on only a proper subset of a key. Such a subset-only dependency is called a partial dependency, and its presence is exactly what disqualifies a relation from 2NF. Testing this requires first finding every candidate key via attribute-closure computation, then checking whether any proper subset of a key closes (directly via a given FD, or indirectly through the closure) to include a non-prime attribute.

  1. List the FDs: AB → CD, DE → P, C → E, P → C, B → G, over the seven attributes A, B, C, D, E, P, G.

  2. Neither A nor B ever appears on the right-hand side of any FD (the right-hand sides across all five FDs are C, D, P, E, G) — so no combination of the remaining attributes can ever derive A or B on its own; every candidate key of R must therefore contain both A and B.

  3. Compute the closure of {A, B}: AB → CD adds C and D, giving {A,B,C,D}; B → G adds G, giving {A,B,C,D,G}; C → E adds E, giving {A,B,C,D,E,G}; DE → P adds P, giving {A,B,C,D,E,G,P} — every attribute of R.

  4. Since every candidate key must already contain A and B (step 2), and {A,B} alone closes to the full attribute set (step 3), AB is R's unique, minimal candidate key. A and B are therefore the only prime attributes; C, D, E, P, G are all non-prime.

  5. Test every FD's left-hand side against the key AB: B → G has left side B, a proper subset of AB, and right side G, a non-prime attribute — this is a partial dependency of a non-prime attribute on part of the key.

A partial dependency is sufficient by itself to fail 2NF, and since the normal forms nest as BCNF ⊆ 3NF ⊆ 2NF (every BCNF relation is in 3NF, and every 3NF relation is in 2NF), failing 2NF automatically rules out 3NF and BCNF as well. Independently, C → E and P → C confirm the same conclusion from another angle: C and P are non-superkey determinants of non-prime attributes (E and C respectively), so the relation would fail BCNF and 3NF even without considering B → G — but it is specifically the B → G partial dependency that pushes R below 2NF.

Hence R is not in 2NF.

optionFeedback.html: This treats every functional dependency in the list as if its left-hand side were automatically a superkey of R. Checking each one shows that isn't true: B → G, C → E, and P → C each have a single-attribute determinant that is not itself a superkey of R (B individually reaches only {B, G}; C and P individually reach only a handful of attributes, never all seven) — so BCNF's requirement, that every determinant of a non-trivial dependency must be a superkey, is broken multiple times over.

This assumes that once a determinant fails the superkey test, the weaker 3NF condition (which permits X → A when A is a prime attribute) rescues the relation. It doesn't here: take C → E — E is not part of any candidate key of R, so the prime-attribute exception 3NF offers does not apply, and this dependency alone breaks 3NF, not merely BCNF.

Selecting this means assuming the relation comfortably clears 2NF and only runs into trouble at a higher normal form. That assumption is unearned: spotting a candidate key and confirming the full key determines the remaining attributes does not, on its own, establish 2NF. Since the 2NF condition itself was never actually tested here, treating it as satisfied and blaming the failure solely on 3NF is not justified by the reasoning given.

R's attributes never fully close under any single attribute — only the pair AB does: applying AB → CD, then B → G, then C → E, then DE → P in sequence reaches every attribute of R, and neither A nor B alone gets there, so AB is R's only candidate key. Within that key, B by itself already determines G via B → G, even though G is not part of any candidate key and B is only a proper subset of AB.

title: Consider relation (ABCDE) with the following dependencies AC How many
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider a relation R (ABCDE) with the following dependencies

A ⟶ B

C ⟶ D

AC ⟶ E

D ⟶ C

How many tables will be formed, if we decompose the relation R into 3NF?
solution:
Given Relation:
R(A, B, C, D, E)

Functional Dependencies:
1. A → B
2. C → D
3. AC → E
4. D → C

Step 1: Find Candidate Keys

Since A never appears on the RHS of any FD, it must be present in every candidate key.

Check closure of AC:

(AC)+ = {A, C}
A → B ⇒ {A, B, C}
C → D ⇒ {A, B, C, D}
AC → E ⇒ {A, B, C, D, E}

Hence, AC is a Candidate Key.

Check closure of AD:

(AD)+ = {A, D}
A → B ⇒ {A, B, D}
D → C ⇒ {A, B, C, D}
AC → E ⇒ {A, B, C, D, E}

Hence, AD is also a Candidate Key.

Candidate Keys = {AC, AD}

Prime Attributes = A, C, D
Non-Prime Attributes = B, E

Step 2: Check 3NF Conditions

A functional dependency X → Y satisfies 3NF if:
1. X is a superkey, OR
2. Y is a prime attribute.

Checking each FD:

A → B
- A is not a superkey.
- B is a non-prime attribute.
⇒ Violates 3NF.

C → D
- C is not a superkey.
- D is a prime attribute.
⇒ Satisfies 3NF.

AC → E
- AC is a candidate key (superkey).
⇒ Satisfies 3NF.

D → C
- D is not a superkey.
- C is a prime attribute.
⇒ Satisfies 3NF.

Step 3: 3NF Synthesis

Create relations for the functional dependencies:

R1(A, B)     from A → B

R2(C, D)     from C → D and D → C

R3(A, C, E)  from AC → E

Now check whether any relation contains a candidate key of the original relation.

R3(A, C, E) contains candidate key AC.

Therefore, no additional relation is required.

Final Decomposition:

R1(A, B)
R2(C, D)
R3(A, C, E)

Total Number of Tables = 3

Answer: 3 (Option A)

optionFeedback.html: Correct Answer. The 3NF decomposition results in three relations: T1(A,B), T2(C,D), and T3(A,C,E). T3 contains the candidate key AC, so no extra relation is needed.

Incorrect. The original relation is not in 3NF because A → B violates 3NF conditions. Hence decomposition is required.
Incorrect. An additional table is not needed because T3(A,C,E) already contains the candidate key AC, ensuring a lossless and dependency-preserving decomposition.

options.html: Merge all attributes into a single table

solution:
To satisfy Third Normal Form (3NF), the single table must be decomposed into Employees(EmpID, Name, Dept) and Departments(Dept, DeptPhone). The original table violates 3NF because it contains a transitive functional dependency (EmpID → Dept → DeptPhone) , where the non-prime attribute DeptPhone depends on EmpID via another non-prime attribute, Dept. The first table, Employees, retains the candidate key EmpID along with its direct attributes (Name and Dept). The second table, Departments, extracts the violating dependency so that Dept becomes its primary key to cleanly map DeptPhone. This specific decomposition ensures a lossless join and preserves all functional dependencies, allowing the original schema to be perfectly reconstructed using Dept as a foreign key connection.

solution:
A relation is in second normal form (2NF) only when every non-prime attribute is fully dependent on each candidate key as a whole, with no non-prime attribute depending on just part of a composite key (a partial dependency). Third normal form (3NF) additionally forbids transitive dependencies among non-prime attributes, and Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) strengthens this further by requiring every determinant, the left side of any functional dependency, to be a superkey.

For the relation R(E, D, A, B), only the dependencies whose attributes lie inside this relation matter.

  1. The dependencies B→C, F→G, F→H, and (E, F)→1 involve attributes outside R and are not relevant; only A→B, D→E, and E→D apply.

  2. Compute A+: using A→B, A+ = {A, B}, which is not all four attributes, so A alone is not a key.

  3. Compute (A, D)+: using A→B and D→E, (A, D)+ = {A, B, D, E} - every attribute - so AD is a superkey, and removing either A or D breaks the closure, making AD a minimal candidate key.

  4. Compute (A, E)+: using A→B and E→D, (A, E)+ = {A, B, D, E} as well, so AE is also a minimal candidate key.

  5. The candidate keys are therefore {A, D} and {A, E}; A, D, and E are prime attributes, and B is the only non-prime attribute.

  6. A→B is a partial dependency: A is a proper subset of both candidate keys, yet it determines the non-prime attribute B on its own, which violates the 2NF condition.

Because 2NF is a precondition for both 3NF and BCNF, a relation that fails 2NF automatically fails 3NF and BCNF too. This is confirmed independently: A is a determinant (of A→B) but A+ is not equal to {A, B, D, E}, so A is not a superkey, which directly breaks the BCNF requirement as well.

Since R(E, D, A, B) satisfies none of 2NF, 3NF, or BCNF, the correct choice is none of the above.

optionFeedback.html: Second normal form (2NF) requires every non-prime attribute to be fully functionally dependent on each candidate key as a whole; a non-prime attribute that depends on a proper subset of a composite key, rather than the whole key, creates a partial dependency, which 2NF disallows.
Third normal form (3NF) is 2NF together with the absence of transitive dependencies: a non-prime attribute must depend directly on a candidate key, not indirectly through another non-prime attribute.

Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) requires every determinant in the relation - the left-hand side of any functional dependency - to be a superkey, meaning its attribute closure covers every attribute of the relation; this is a stricter condition than 3NF.

This option applies when a relation is not even in 2NF, the weakest of 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF - since 3NF and BCNF each build on 2NF as a precondition, a relation that is not in 2NF cannot be in 3NF or BCNF either.

title: Relation has eight attributes ABCDEFGH. Fields of contain only atomic
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Relation R has eight attributes ABCDEFGH. Fields of R contain only atomic values.

F = {CH → G, A → BC, B → CFH, E → A, F → EG} is a set of functional dependencies (FDs) so that F⁺ is exactly the set of FDs that hold for R.

The relation R is:
solution:
Concept

Normal forms are defined relative to the candidate keys of a relation. An attribute is prime if it belongs to some candidate key, otherwise non-prime. 2NF forbids a partial dependency: no non-prime attribute may depend on a proper subset of any candidate key. So the test is: find every candidate key, label prime vs non-prime attributes, then check whether any non-prime attribute is determined by part of a key.

Finding the candidate keys

An attribute that never appears on the right-hand side of any FD cannot be produced by any closure, so it can never be derived from other attributes and must therefore appear in every candidate key. Here D appears on no right-hand side (and on no left-hand side either), so every candidate key must contain D.

Compute attribute closures (each step adds attributes forced by an FD whose left side is already included):

  1. (AD)⁺: A → BC adds B, C; B → CFH adds F, H; F → EG adds E, G. With D this gives all eight attributes → AD is a key.

  2. (BD)⁺: B → CFH → then F → EG → then E → A; with D this closes to all eight → BD is a key.

  3. (ED)⁺: E → A → then A → BC, B → CFH, F → EG; with D closes to all eight → ED is a key.

  4. (FD)⁺: F → EG → then E → A → A → BC, B → CFH; with D closes to all eight → FD is a key.

Candidate keys: AD, BD, ED, FD. Prime attributes (appear in some key): A, B, D, E, F. Non-prime attributes: C, G, H.

Applying the 2NF test

Take the FD A → BC. A is a proper subset of the candidate key AD, and C is a non-prime attribute. So a non-prime attribute (C) depends on part of a key (A). This is exactly a partial dependency, which 2NF prohibits.

Because atomic values are given, R is in 1NF; but the partial dependency breaks 2NF, so R is in 1NF and not in 2NF.

Cross-check

If a relation fails 2NF it cannot satisfy any stronger form, so 3NF and BCNF are automatically ruled out. A second witness of the partial dependency is B → CFH: B is part of key BD and C, F, H reach non-prime C as well, confirming the violation independently.

optionFeedback.html: Atomic field values establish the first normal form, and the next condition is then tested against the candidate keys AD, BD, ED, FD with the prime attributes A, B, D, E, F and non-prime C, G, H. Working those conditions in order, the relation settles at exactly this level rather than any higher form; the worked solution carries the full step-by-step derivation.

This level is chosen by a solver who focuses on the transitive-dependency boundary that separates the two highest non-trivial forms, while skipping the earlier conditions. Derive the candidate keys AD, BD, ED, FD, mark which attributes are prime and which are non-prime, and test every condition in order from the lowest upward; doing so does not land the relation here.

This level is chosen by a solver who jumps to the boundary between the two strongest forms, assuming the lower conditions were already cleared. Derive the candidate keys AD, BD, ED, FD, mark prime versus non-prime attributes, and evaluate every condition in order from the lowest upward; doing so does not land the relation here.

This level is chosen by a solver who checks only the strongest condition, that every non-trivial determinant be a superkey. Determinants such as A and B are not superkeys, and the lower conditions must each be tested in order against the candidate keys AD, BD, ED, FD; doing so does not land the relation here.

solution:
CONCEPT: A relation is in BCNF only when every non-trivial functional dependency X→Y has X as a superkey. A decomposition preserves a functional dependency when that dependency can still be logically derived — via attribute closure — using only the functional dependencies that hold inside the decomposed relations, without needing to join them back together. The standard BCNF-decomposition algorithm always produces a lossless-join set of BCNF relations, but it does NOT guarantee that every original dependency survives this way.

APPLICATION: check each functional dependency set for its key(s), its BCNF violation (if any), the BCNF decomposition it forces, and whether that decomposition still preserves every original dependency.

Yes — A→B sits inside (A, B) and B→C sits inside (B, C)

No — AB→C needs A, B, C together, which no single component has

CROSS-CHECK: verify the lost dependency independently by computing the closure of AB using only the functional dependencies that hold inside the decomposed relations (A, C) and (B, C).

  • Inside (A, C), only C→A holds; inside (B, C), no non-trivial dependency holds. So the only dependency available after decomposition is C→A.

  • Closure of AB under {C→A} alone is just {A, B} — C→A cannot fire because C is not yet known, so C can never be added, and AB→C can never be reconstructed from the pieces.

  • This confirms AB→C is genuinely lost by the decomposition, not merely awkward to see — the two decomposed relations must be rejoined to verify it.

Therefore, among the three functional-dependency sets, AB→C, C→A is the only one that does not admit a decomposition that is simultaneously lossless, in BCNF, and dependency-preserving.

optionFeedback.html: For A→B, B→C, the only key is A (A determines B, and B determines C, so A determines everything). Splitting on B→C gives (B, C) and (A, B); both pieces are in BCNF, and both original dependencies live inside a single component each, so this set does have a dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition.

For A→B, B→C, C→A, the dependencies form a cycle, so A, B, and C are each individually a candidate key. Every dependency already has a superkey on its left side, meaning the relation is already in BCNF and trivially preserves every dependency without any decomposition.

For AB→C, C→A, the candidate keys are AB and BC (both close to all of A, B, C), so AB→C does not violate BCNF. But C→A does violate BCNF, because C alone is not a superkey. The only BCNF-safe split is on C→A into (A, C) and (B, C); AB→C needs A, B, and C together to be enforced, but no single decomposed relation holds all three attributes, so AB→C cannot be checked without rejoining the pieces — the decomposition loses that dependency.

Checking each of the three dependency sets shows exactly one of them cannot be decomposed into BCNF while keeping every original dependency intact, so a qualifying case does exist among the given sets.

Assume that no two faculty members within a single department have the same name, that each faculty member has only one office, and that each office belongs to exactly one department (so office determines dept). 3NF refers to Third Normal Form and BCNF refers to Boyce-Codd Normal Form.

Then Faculty is:
solution:
Concept. A relation is in 3NF if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → A, at least one holds: X is a superkey, OR A is a prime attribute (part of some candidate key). A relation is in BCNF, a strictly stronger form, only if the left-hand side X of every non-trivial dependency is a superkey — the prime-attribute escape clause of 3NF is removed.

Application to this relation.

  1. Derive the functional dependencies. Names are unique within a department, so (facName, dept) determines a faculty row: (facName, dept) → office, rank, dateHired. From the data each office sits in exactly one department (A101→Art, M201→Math, C101→CSC, …), giving office → dept.

  2. Find the candidate keys. (facName, dept) determines every attribute, so it is a candidate key. Because office → dept, the set (facName, office) also determines dept and hence all attributes, so it is a candidate key too. Prime attributes are therefore facName, dept and office.

  3. Test BCNF. Take office → dept. The determinant office is not a superkey, because one office is shared by several faculty (C101 is used by both Mohan and Tanuja), so office cannot fix facName, rank or dateHired. A non-superkey determinant violates BCNF.

  4. Test 3NF. For the same office → dept, apply the prime-attribute escape: the right-hand side dept is a prime attribute (it is part of the candidate key (facName, dept)). 3NF permits this dependency, and no other dependency breaks the rule, so 3NF holds.

Common pitfall. It can look like office alone determines everything (office → facName, rank, dateHired) once office → dept is established, but the data does not license that: office C101 is shared by two different faculty rows — (Mohan, Professor, 1980) and (Tanuja, Instructor, 2001) — same office, yet different facName, rank and dateHired. So office fixes only dept, never the rest; it is the sole non-superkey determinant, among the relation's stated dependencies, that separates 3NF (which tolerates it here) from BCNF (which does not).

Cross-check. BCNF ⊂ 3NF always, so a relation can be in 3NF yet fail BCNF, but never the reverse. Here the single offending dependency among those stated, office → dept, fails BCNF (non-superkey determinant) but passes 3NF (prime right-hand side) — exactly the gap between the two forms.

Result: the relation is in 3NF but not in BCNF.

optionFeedback.html: This membership pair would require a dependency that violates the weaker test while every determinant passes the stricter superkey test.
This membership pair would require a non-superkey determinant whose dependent attribute is prime.
This membership pair would require every non-trivial dependency to have a superkey determinant.
This membership pair would require a non-superkey determinant whose dependent attribute is non-prime.

title: If table has only one candidate key which of the
subject: Data Base Management System
text: If a table R has only one candidate key, which of the following statements must necessarily be true?

options.html: R is in 3NF and also in BCNF
R is in 2NF but not in BCNF

solution:
Normal forms nest strictly: BCNF is inside 3NF, which is inside 2NF, which is inside 1NF. 2NF forbids a non-prime attribute from having a partial dependency on any candidate key (only possible when that key is composite). 3NF additionally forbids a transitive dependency - for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> A, either X must be a superkey or A must be a prime attribute. BCNF tightens this further: for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> A, X alone must be a superkey. None of these definitions depends on HOW MANY candidate keys a relation has - they depend only on the functional dependencies among its attributes.

  1. Single, non-composite key with no other dependency: R(A, B) with sole candidate key A and only the dependency A -> B. A composite key is required for a partial dependency, so this R cannot violate 2NF; and since the only determinant, A, is already a superkey, R also satisfies BCNF (hence 3NF). This single-key relation sits in BCNF.

  2. Single, non-composite key with a transitive dependency: R(A, B, C) with sole candidate key A and the dependencies A -> B, B -> C. Because the key is not composite, 2NF still cannot be violated here. But B -> C is transitive: B is not a superkey and C is not a prime attribute, so this R fails 3NF and therefore fails BCNF too, while still satisfying 2NF.

  3. Composite sole key with a partial dependency: R(A, B, C) with sole candidate key {A, B} and the dependency A -> C. Here C, a non-prime attribute, depends on just A - a proper subset of the composite key - which is exactly a partial dependency. This R fails 2NF itself, and therefore 3NF and BCNF as well.

  • R is in 3NF and also in BCNF - true for the first relation above, but false for the second and third, so it cannot hold for every relation with one candidate key.

  • R is in 2NF but not in BCNF - matches the second relation above, but the first stays inside BCNF (so ‘not in BCNF’ fails) and the third fails 2NF itself (so ‘in 2NF’ fails); it does not hold for every such relation either.

  • R is not in 3NF - matches the second and third relations above, but the first relation is in 3NF (and BCNF); again not a universal statement.

Because a relation with exactly one candidate key can land in BCNF, in 2NF-but-not-BCNF, or even outside 2NF depending only on its functional dependencies, no single one of the three specific claims holds for every such relation - the correct choice is that none of the given statements is universally true.

optionFeedback.html: Having exactly one candidate key does not by itself rule out a transitive dependency among the non-key attributes. If the sole key is a single non-composite attribute A with A -> B and B -> C, the relation violates 3NF (and therefore BCNF) even though there is only one candidate key - a single key never guarantees the strongest normal forms hold.

This assumes a single candidate key rules out a partial dependency, but that lone key can itself be composite. If the only candidate key is {A, B} and a non-prime attribute depends on just A (a proper subset of the key), the relation already fails 2NF - so it is not even in 2NF, let alone in the specific ‘2NF-but-not-BCNF’ shape claimed here.

This overgeneralises a case where a stray dependency breaks a higher normal form onto every relation with one candidate key. Take a sole key A with only the dependency A -> B and no other attribute dependencies: every non-trivial dependency here has the candidate key as its determinant, so this relation actually satisfies BCNF (and hence 3NF too). A single candidate key alone does not force 3NF to fail.

Whether a relation lands in BCNF, in 2NF-but-not-BCNF, or fails even 2NF depends entirely on the functional dependencies among its attributes, not on how many candidate keys it has. Relations with exactly one candidate key exist in each of these categories - a single-attribute key with only its own dependency stays inside BCNF; a transitive dependency under a non-composite key breaks 3NF/BCNF while keeping 2NF; a partial dependency under a composite sole key breaks 2NF itself. So no fixed claim about 2NF, 3NF, or BCNF can hold for every relation with one candidate key.

title: Consider the relation R(A,B,C,D,E,F,G) with given functional dependencies: FD={A→D, AF→C,

solution:

Check for partial dependencies:

  • A → D: A is a proper subset of the candidate key {A, E}, and D is a non-prime attribute. This is a partial dependency.

Conclusion: The relation is in 1NF but fails 2NF due to the partial dependency A → D; therefore the highest normal form of the relation is 1NF.

Incorrect. The relation is not in 2NF because there is a partial dependency: A (a proper subset of the candidate key {A, E}) → D (a non-prime attribute). That violates the definition of 2NF.

Incorrect. A relation must satisfy 2NF before it can be in 3NF. Here A→D is a partial dependency on part of the candidate key {A, E}, so the relation is not even in 2NF and therefore cannot be in 3NF.
Incorrect. BCNF requires every determinant to be a candidate key. The dependency A→D violates earlier normal forms (A is not a candidate key but determines D), so the relation cannot satisfy BCNF.

title: In database normalization, what problem does 4NF (Fourth Normal Form)
subject: Data Base Management System
text: In database normalization, what problem does 4NF (Fourth Normal Form) address ?
solution: Fourth Normal Form (4NF) is designed to eliminate redundancy caused by multi-valued dependencies. A relation is in 4NF if it is already in Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) and has no non-trivial multi-valued dependencies. A multi-valued dependency occurs when one attribute determines multiple independent values of another attribute, leading to data duplication. For example, if a course has multiple instructors and multiple textbooks independently, storing them in one table creates unnecessary combinations. By decomposing the table to separate these independent multi-valued facts, 4NF ensures data integrity and reduces anomalies. Partial dependencies (Option A) are addressed in Second Normal Form (2NF), while transitive dependencies (Option B) are handled in Third Normal Form (3NF). Join dependencies (Option D) relate to Fifth Normal Form (5NF), not 4NF. Therefore, the correct answer is Option C.

text: If D = {R1, R2} is a decomposition of R, and F is the set of functional dependencies on R, then which of the following ensures that the decomposition D is lossless (nonadditive)?
solution:
Concept

For a binary decomposition of R into R1 and R2, the join is lossless with respect to F exactly when the common attributes functionally determine all attributes of at least one fragment.

Equivalently, (R1 ∩ R2) → R1 or (R1 ∩ R2) → R2 must belong to F+.

Application

Let X = R1 ∩ R2 and Y = R1 − R2. Then R1 = X ∪ Y.

  1. The condition X → Y states that the common attributes determine the attributes unique to R1.

  2. Reflexivity gives X → X. Applying the union rule to X → X and X → Y gives X → X ∪ Y, that is, X → R1.

  3. Conversely, X → R1 gives X → Y by decomposition because Y is a subset of R1. Thus X → Y and X → R1 are equivalent conditions here.

  4. The non-membership statement supplies no such dependency, while (R1 ∪ R2) → (R1 − R2) is the trivial dependency R → Y and does not test what the common attributes determine.

Cross-check

Starting from either equivalent condition and applying Armstrong’s axioms derives the other. Therefore both ((R1 ∩ R2) → (R1 − R2)) ∈ F+ and ((R1 ∩ R2) → R1) ∈ F+ ensure a lossless decomposition.
