It is not dependency preserving because the functional dependencies between B and C (B -> C and C -> B) are not contained in either R1(A,C) or R2(A,B) and cannot be inferred from the projected dependencies.

This choice is incorrect. The decomposition is not lossy — it is lossless because A is common and A -> B holds, satisfying the lossless-join test. While dependency preservation fails (the B–C dependencies are lost), the decomposition is not lossy.

title: Consider relation R(A,B,C,D,E,F,G) with set of functional dependencies: F={AD→BF, CD→EGC,
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider a relation R(A,B,C,D,E,F,G) with a set of functional dependencies:

F={AD→BF, CD→EGC, BD→F, E→D, F→C, D→F}

The relation R is decomposed into the following two relations after finding the minimal cover for the above set of functional dependencies: R1(A,B,C,D,E), R2(A,D,F,G)

Use the functional dependencies in the minimal cover to determine the nature of this decomposition and find the correct statement below:

options.html: Decomposition is lossy and not dependency preserving
Decomposition is lossless and not dependency preserving

solution:
Check lossless join:

Common attributes between R1(A,B,C,D,E) and R2(A,D,F,G): {A, D}.

  • Compute closure of {A, D}:

    From AD → B,F add B and F.

    From F → C add C.

    With C and D, CD → E,G adds E and G.

    Thus AD+ = {A, B, C, D, E, F, G} (all attributes). Therefore AD is a key and the decomposition is lossless.

Check dependency preservation:

  • Relevant minimal set of dependencies (after splitting right-hand sides and removing redundant FDs): AD → B, D → F, F → C, CD → E, CD → G, E → D.

  • Project these onto R1(A,B,C,D,E): AD → B, CD → E, E → D (F → C and D → F are not inside R1).

  • Project these onto R2(A,D,F,G): D → F (AD → B, CD → E, etc. are not inside R2).

  • Union of projected dependencies contains AD → B and D → F, so AD → B,F can be derived. However, F → C is not present in the union: computing F+ under the union gives only {F} (no rule with LHS F), so C cannot be derived.

  • Therefore the dependency F → C is not preserved by the decomposition.

Final conclusion:

The decomposition is lossless (AD is a key) but not dependency preserving (F → C cannot be enforced from the projected dependencies).

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The decomposition is lossless because the common attributes {A, D} form a key for the original relation (AD+ yields all attributes), but it is not dependency preserving: the dependency F→C cannot be enforced from the projections alone because F and C are split across the two relations.

Incorrect. The decomposition is not lossy — it is lossless because AD is a key (AD+ produces all attributes). Also, dependency preservation does fail, so the second part is correct but the first part is wrong.
Incorrect. The decomposition is lossless (AD is a key), so it is not lossy. It is true that dependency preservation fails, but classifying the decomposition as lossy is wrong.

Correct. AD is a key for the full relation (compute AD+ to see it determines A,B,C,D,E,F,G), so the join is lossless. However, dependency preservation fails because the dependency F→C cannot be obtained from the set of dependencies that lie entirely inside the two decomposed relations.

However, the decomposition is not lossy: the common attribute d is a key for the (d,b,c) relation (d determines b and c), so the join is lossless.

title: Which one of the following statements about normal forms is
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which one of the following statements about normal forms is FALSE?

options.html: It is always possible to achieve a lossless and dependency-preserving decomposition into 3NF.
Achieving a lossless and dependency-preserving decomposition into BCNF is always guaranteed.
Every relation with exactly two attributes satisfies BCNF.

solution:
Answer: The statement "Achieving a lossless and dependency-preserving decomposition into BCNF is always guaranteed." is false.

  • BCNF imposes stricter conditions compared to 3NF. This is true: BCNF requires every non-trivial functional dependency to have a superkey on the left-hand side, which is stronger than 3NF.

  • It is always possible to achieve a lossless and dependency-preserving decomposition into 3NF. This is true: the 3NF synthesis algorithm produces a decomposition that is lossless and preserves the original functional dependencies.

  • Achieving a lossless and dependency-preserving decomposition into BCNF is always guaranteed. This is false: although you can always decompose to BCNF while keeping the decomposition lossless, dependency preservation is not guaranteed. For example, with attributes A, B, C and functional dependencies A -> B and B -> C, a BCNF decomposition can separate attributes so that the transitive dependency A -> C is not preserved directly in any single decomposed relation.

  • Every relation with exactly two attributes satisfies BCNF. This is true: in a two-attribute relation, any non-trivial dependency makes the determinant a key (or there are no non-trivial dependencies), so the BCNF condition holds.

Summary: The false statement is the claim that BCNF decomposition always preserves dependencies. Lossless BCNF decompositions are possible, but they may not preserve all functional dependencies, whereas 3NF has algorithms that ensure both losslessness and dependency preservation.

optionFeedback.html: This statement is true. BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form) requires that for every non-trivial functional dependency, the left-hand side is a superkey. That is a stricter requirement than Third Normal Form (3NF), so every BCNF relation is in 3NF but not every 3NF relation is in BCNF.

This statement is true. There is a standard synthesis algorithm that produces a decomposition into 3NF that is both lossless (preserves joins) and dependency-preserving (all original FDs can be checked on the decomposed relations).

This statement is false. While you can always decompose a relation into BCNF in a way that is lossless, that decomposition does not always preserve all functional dependencies. For example, with attributes A, B, C and FDs A -> B and B -> C, a BCNF decomposition may separate attributes so that the original dependency A -> C is no longer directly preserved.

This statement is true. For a relation with exactly two attributes, any non-trivial functional dependency must make one attribute determine the other, so the determinant is a key (or there are no non-trivial dependencies). Either way, the BCNF condition holds for two-attribute relations.

title: You are given the following set of functional dependencies for
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
You are given the following set of functional dependencies for a relation R(A,B,C,D,E,F),

F = {AB → C, DC → AE, E → F }.

i. Is this relation in BCNF?

ii. Is the decomposition (A,B,C,D) (B,C,D,E,F) a dependency preserving decomposition?
solution:
Given relation R(A, B, C, D, E, F) with functional dependencies: AB → C, DC → AE, E → F.

Part i: Is R in BCNF?

BCNF requires that for every FD X → Y, X is a superkey. Check the closures:

  1. AB → C: AB+ = {A, B, C}. Cannot derive D, E, or F, so AB is not a superkey.

  2. DC → AE: From DC → AE and E → F, DC+ = {D, C, A, E, F}. B is not obtained, so DC is not a superkey.

  3. E → F: E+ = {E, F}, which is not all attributes, so E is not a superkey.

Because none of the FD left-hand sides are superkeys, R is not in BCNF.

Part ii: Is the decomposition (A,B,C,D) and (B,C,D,E,F) dependency preserving?

Check where each original FD appears in the decomposed relations:

  • AB → C: All attributes A, B, C are in relation (A,B,C,D), so this FD is preserved in that relation.

  • DC → AE: This FD splits across the decomposed relations: DC → A is preserved in (A,B,C,D) and DC → E is preserved in (B,C,D,E,F). Together they preserve DC → AE.

  • E → F: Both attributes E and F appear in (B,C,D,E,F), so E → F is preserved there.

Since every original functional dependency is present in one of the decomposed relations (or can be reconstructed from FDs present in the components), the decomposition is dependency preserving.

Final Answer: i: No (R is not in BCNF). ii: Yes (the decomposition is dependency preserving).

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The relation is not in BCNF. Compute closures: AB+ = {A, B, C} (cannot derive D, E, F), DC+ = {D, C, A, E, F} (missing B), and E+ = {E, F}. None of the determinants are superkeys, so BCNF does not hold. The decomposition given is dependency preserving, so answering both parts Yes is wrong.

Incorrect. The relation is not in BCNF because AB, DC, and E are not superkeys (see closures above). The decomposition is dependency preserving: AB→C is present in the (A,B,C,D) relation; DC→A is in (A,B,C,D) and DC→E and E→F are in (B,C,D,E,F). So the decomposition does preserve the original FDs.

Partially correct: the relation is not in BCNF. However, the decomposition is dependency preserving, so the second part is incorrect. All original FDs are preserved because AB→C appears in the (A,B,C,D) relation, DC→A appears in (A,B,C,D) and DC→E appears in (B,C,D,E,F), and E→F appears in (B,C,D,E,F).

Correct. R is not in BCNF because none of the given left-hand sides are superkeys: AB+ = {A,B,C}, DC+ = {D,C,A,E,F} (missing B), and E+ = {E,F}. The decomposition into (A,B,C,D) and (B,C,D,E,F) is dependency preserving because AB→C is in the first relation, DC→A is in the first relation, DC→E and E→F are in the second relation — together these preserve DC→AE and all original FDs.

title: Consider relation R(P,Q,R,S,T) with the following functional dependencies: FD: {P→QT,
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider a relation R(P,Q,R,S,T) with the following functional dependencies:
FD: {P→QT, RS→Q, T→S, S→P}
Which of the following is true for decomposition of R into R1:(P,Q,S),R2:(R,S,T) :
solution:
🔹 To determine if the decomposition of R(P,Q,R,S,T) into R1(P,Q,S) and R2(R,S,T) is Lossless and/or Dependency Preserving, we must evaluate both properties systematically.

1. Lossless Join Property Test

A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if and only if the intersection of their attributes functionally determines all attributes of at least one of the relations:

$$(R_1 \cap R_2) \rightarrow R_1 \quad \text{or} \quad (R_1 \cap R_2) \rightarrow R_2$$

  1. Find the intersection:

    $$R_1 \cap R_2 = \{P, Q, S\} \cap \{R, S, T\} = \{S\}$$

  2. Compute the attribute closure of the intersection under the original FDs (S+):

    • Start with S+ = {S}

    • Using S -> P, we get S+ = {P, S}

    • Using P -> QT, we get S+ = {P, Q, S, T}

    • Using T -> S (no new attributes)

    • Result: S+ = {P, Q, S, T}

  3. Check containment:

    • Is R1 ⊆ S+? {P, Q, S} ⊆ {P, Q, S, T} -> Yes!

    • Is R2 ⊆ S+? {R, S, T} ⊄ {P, Q, S, T} (Missing R)

Since (R1 ∩ R2) -> R1, the decomposition is Lossless.

2. Dependency Preservation Test

A decomposition is dependency preserving if the union of the closures of FDs projected onto each individual relation contains all original FDs: (F1 ∪ F2)+ = F+.

Let's find the projected functional dependencies for R1 and R2:

FDs for R1(P,Q,S):

Compute closures using original FDs to find valid dependencies restricted only to {P, Q, S}:

  • P+ = {P, Q, S, T} ∩ {P, Q, S} = {P, Q, S} => {P -> QS}

  • S+ = {P, Q, S, T} ∩ {P, Q, S} = {P, Q, S} => {S -> PQ}

  • Q+ = {Q}

FDs for R2(R,S,T):

Compute closures restricted only to {R, S, T}:

  • T+ = {T, S} ∩ {R, S, T} = {S, T} => {T-> S}

  • S+ = {P, Q, S, T}∩ {R, S, T} = {S, T} => {S -> T}

  • (RS)+ = {P, Q, R, S, T} ∩ {R, S, T} = {R, S, T} => {RS -> T}

Check original FDs against (F1 ∪ F2):

  • T -> S: Preserved directly in F2.

  • S -> P: Preserved directly in F1.

  • P -> QT: P -> Q is in F1. To see if P -> T is preserved, compute P+ under (F1 ∪ F2):

    $$P^+ = \{P\} \xrightarrow{P \rightarrow QS} \{P, Q, S\} \xrightarrow{S \rightarrow T} \{P, Q, S, T\}$$

    Since T is in the closure, P -> QT is preserved.

  • RS -> Q: Compute (RS)+ under (F1 ∪ F2):

    $$({RS})^+ = \{R, S\} \xrightarrow{S \rightarrow PQ} \{P, Q, R, S\}$$

    Since Q is in the closure, RS -> Q is preserved.

All original functional dependencies are preserved, so the decomposition is Dependency Preserving.

Conclusion

The decomposition is both Lossless and Dependency Preserving.

optionFeedback.html:
Lossless: The common attribute between R1 and R2 is S. Its closure is S+ = {P, Q, S, T}, which contains all attributes of R1. Since the intersection forms a superkey for at least one of the relations, no data or valid relationships are lost during a join operation.

Dependency Preserving: All original functional dependencies ({P ->QT, RS -> Q, T-> S, S-> P}) can be reconstructed through the valid dependencies present inside the individual schemas of R1 and R2.

This option incorrectly claims that the decomposition is lossy. A decomposition is only lossy if the intersection of the two schemas fails to functionally determine either R1 or R2 completely. Because S -> R1 holds true, the join is guaranteed to be lossless.

This option correctly identifies the lossless nature but incorrectly concludes that dependencies are lost. It is easy to mistake RS-> Q as lost because the attributes are split (R, S are in R2 while Q is in R1). However, tracking the closure under the decomposed FDs reveals (RS)+ = {P, Q, R, S}, meaning the dependency is still implicitly enforced and thus preserved.
Since Option 1 perfectly characterizes the mathematical properties of this relational decomposition, this choice is invalid.

title: Given relation R(A,B,C) with FDs set {A->B, B->C, C->B} Lossless
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Given a relation R(A, B, C) with the set of functional dependencies F = {A -> B, B -> C, C -> B}.

(i) A lossless-join decomposition of R is always possible.

(ii) A dependency-preserving decomposition of R is always possible.

Assume every decomposition considered includes all the attributes of R, and "always possible" means at least one such decomposition exists (not that every decomposition has the stated property).
solution:
Concept: A lossless-join decomposition of a relation R is a split into fragments whose natural join reconstructs R exactly; a dependency-preserving decomposition is one whose fragments' projected functional dependencies, taken together, imply every dependency in the original set F. For a binary split R1, R2 (with R1 union R2 = R), the standard lossless-join test says the split is lossless exactly when the shared attributes R1 intersect R2 functionally determine R1 or determine R2. Two general theorems govern existence: a lossless-join decomposition of R always exists for any relation schema and any FD set (the BCNF decomposition algorithm is guaranteed, by construction, to always split off a lossless fragment at each step); a dependency-preserving decomposition of R also always exists for any relation schema and FD set (the 3NF synthesis algorithm constructs one) -- even though a decomposition that is simultaneously lossless, dependency-preserving, and in BCNF is not always achievable together.

Application:

  1. Compute the closure of A under F = {A -> B, B -> C, C -> B}: starting from {A}, A -> B adds B giving {A, B}; then B -> C adds C, giving A+ = {A, B, C} = R. So A is a (minimal) candidate key of R.

  2. Split R into R1(A, B) and R2(B, C). Check the lossless-join test on the shared attributes: R1 ∩ R2 = {B}, and B -> C holds, so B functionally determines {B, C} = R2. The test (R1 ∩ R2) -> R2 is satisfied, so this split is lossless.

  3. Project F onto each fragment: R1(A, B) retains A -> B; R2(B, C) retains both B -> C and C -> B. Together these projected dependencies reconstruct all three original dependencies, so this same split is also dependency-preserving.

  4. So a single split, R1(A, B) and R2(B, C), is simultaneously lossless and dependency-preserving -- demonstrating that a decomposition with each property exists.

Cross-check: Try a different split, R1(A, B) and R2(A, C). Here R1 ∩ R2 = {A}; since A is a key, A functionally determines all of R (hence both R1 and R2), so this split is also lossless by the same test. But projecting F onto it keeps only A -> B and A -> C; the dependencies B -> C and C -> B are lost, so this split is lossless but not dependency-preserving. A third split, R1(A, B) and R2(C) (no shared attribute at all), fails the lossless test outright: the empty intersection determines nothing, so joining the fragments back can produce spurious rows. None of this contradicts either statement: the statements ask whether a decomposition with each property EXISTS, not whether every decomposition has it -- the R1(A, B)/R2(B, C) split above already exhibits one with both properties at once.

Result: Since a decomposition of R exists that is both lossless and dependency-preserving, both (i) and (ii) are true.

optionFeedback.html: Splitting R into R1(A, B) and R2(B, C) gives a shared attribute set {B}; since B -> C holds, B functionally determines {B, C} = R2, so this split satisfies the lossless-join test. The same split also keeps A -> B on one side and both B -> C and C -> B on the other, so it preserves every original dependency too. A decomposition achieving each property therefore exists, making both statements true.

This treats dependency-preservation as unattainable for R, but that is not the case. A general theorem guarantees that a dependency-preserving decomposition always exists for any relation and FD set (via 3NF synthesis), and it can be confirmed directly here too by finding a split whose projected dependencies still combine to give back A -> B, B -> C, and C -> B. So dependency-preservation is achievable, not only losslessness.

This treats losslessness as unattainable for R, but the standard lossless-join test only needs the fragments' shared attributes to functionally determine one of the fragments -- and since A -> B and B -> C together give A+ = {A, B, C}, a split whose shared attribute(s) determine the rest of R will satisfy that test. So losslessness is achievable too, not only dependency-preservation.

This reasons from a worst-case or arbitrary split, for example one with no shared attribute, or one that separates B from C, where information or a dependency is indeed lost. But the statements only ask whether some suitable split achieves each property, not whether every split does. A carefully chosen split of R achieves both properties at once, so neither statement is false.

title: Consider relation R(A,B,C,D,E,F) with the following functional dependencies: FD’s {A→C,
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider a relation R(A, B, C, D, E, F) with the following functional dependencies:

FDs = {A → C, BD → F, EF → A, D → B}

What is the minimum number of relations required to decompose R into 3NF while keeping the decomposition lossless and dependency-preserving?
solution:
Concept — 3NF synthesis algorithm:

To decompose a relation into 3NF, take a minimal cover of its functional dependencies (FDs) and create one relation schema per distinct left-hand side, grouping together every FD that shares it. Because each original FD now lives inside some relation, dependency preservation holds by construction. If none of these grouped relations contains a full candidate key of the original relation, the algorithm adds exactly one extra relation whose schema equals a candidate key — this single addition is what makes the overall join lossless.

Concept — candidate key via attribute closure:

A candidate key is a minimal attribute set K whose closure K+ (computed by repeatedly applying the FDs) equals every attribute of the relation, while no proper subset of K reaches all attributes. Any attribute that never appears on the right-hand side of any FD must belong to every candidate key, since nothing else can ever produce it.

Application to this relation:

  1. List the attributes that never appear on a right-hand side: scanning A → C, BD → F, EF → A, D → B, only D and E never occur on any right-hand side, so D and E must belong to every candidate key.

  2. Compute the closure {D, E}+ : start with {D, E}. D → B adds B, giving {B, D, E}. BD → F adds F (both B and D are present), giving {B, D, E, F}. EF → A adds A, giving {A, B, D, E, F}. A → C adds C, giving all six attributes {A, B, C, D, E, F}. Since {D, E}+ is everything and neither D nor E alone reaches all six attributes, (D, E) is a candidate key.

  3. Reduce to a minimal cover before grouping: test whether B is extraneous in BD → F by checking D+ against the whole FD set. D → B gives {B, D}; with B and D both present, BD → F now applies and adds F, giving D+ = {B, D, F}. Since F is already reachable from D alone, B is extraneous — BD → F collapses to D → F. The FDs D → B and D → F now share the same left-hand side D, so a minimal cover is {A → C, D → B, D → F, EF → A}.

  4. Group the minimal-cover FDs by left-hand side to build the synthesized relations: R1(A, C) for A → C; R2(D, B, F) for D → B and D → F; R3(E, F, A) for EF → A.

  5. Check whether any of these three relations already contains the full candidate key (D, E): R1 has neither D nor E, R2 has D but not E, and R3 has E but not D. No relation contains both, so the algorithm adds one more relation, R4(D, E), to guarantee the lossless join.

  6. Count the relations produced: R1, R2, R3 and R4 — four relations in total.

Cross-check — why three relations are never enough here:

None of R1(A, C), R2(D, B, F), R3(E, F, A) contains the full candidate key (D, E): R1 has neither D nor E, R2 has D but not E, and R3 has E but not D. So the ONLY way a three-relation decomposition could still be lossless is by merging two of these three into one relation whose schema finally contains both D and E — and since only R2 carries D and only R3 carries E, R2 and R3 are the only pair whose merge can possibly supply the complete key; merging R1 with either R2 or R3 still leaves the key incomplete; and merging all three collapses to R itself, which retains every original violation. So R2 ∪ R3, on schema (A, B, D, E, F), is the only candidate worth testing. The FDs still holding on it are D → B, D → F and EF → A, and its own candidate key is again (D, E) (same closure computation, just without C). Test D → B against this merged relation: D alone closes to {B, D, F} — not a superkey, since A and E are missing — and B is not part of the merged relation’s candidate key (D, E), so B is not a prime attribute either. D → B therefore violates 3NF inside the merged relation (the same failure recurs for D → F), so this merge is illegal — and it was the only merge that could have worked. Four relations — one holding the standalone candidate key (D, E) plus one per grouped FD — is therefore both necessary and sufficient.

Result: minimum number of relations required = 4.

II. Dependency preserving
solution:
Step 1: Find the candidate key: Attributes that do not appear on the right-hand side of any FD are A and D, so any key must include A and D. Compute closure: AD+ contains A; from A → B add B; from B → C add C; therefore AD+ = ABCD. Hence AD is a candidate key (and the only one).

Step 2: Identify BCNF violations: Both A → B and B → C have left sides that are not superkeys of R, so they violate BCNF and we must decompose.

  1. Decompose using B → C: produce relation BC and relation ABD.

  2. In ABD, A → B still violates BCNF (A is not a key for ABD), so decompose ABD into AB and AD.

  3. Final BCNF relations: BC, AB, and AD.

Dependency preservation: Both original FDs are preserved in the decomposition: A → B is preserved within AB, and B → C is preserved within BC.

Lossless decomposition: One of the resulting relations (AD) contains the candidate key of the original relation. Because a decomposition that includes a relation containing a candidate key is lossless, the decomposition is lossless.

Conclusion: The BCNF decomposition of R yields relations BC, AB, and AD, which is both lossless and dependency preserving. Therefore both statements are true.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The decomposition into BCNF for this relation is not only lossless — it also preserves the given functional dependencies. After decomposition the final relations include AB (which preserves A → B) and BC (which preserves B → C), and the relation AD contains the candidate key, so the decomposition is lossless as well.

Incorrect. The decomposition is lossless and also dependency preserving. The final BCNF decomposition yields relations AB, BC, and AD. A → B is preserved in AB and B → C is preserved in BC; AD contains the candidate key, ensuring losslessness.

Correct. A and D do not appear on any right-hand side, so AD is the candidate key. Decompose on B → C to get BC and ABD; then decompose ABD on A → B to get AB and AD. Final BCNF relations are BC, AB, and AD. Both functional dependencies are preserved (A → B in AB, B → C in BC), and the relation AD is a candidate key so the decomposition is lossless.

Incorrect. Both statements are true for the BCNF decomposition of this relation. The decomposition can be carried out to produce relations BC, AB, and AD; this preserves both A → B and B → C and is lossless because AD is a candidate key.

title: How many minimum relations are required for the following Relation
subject: Data Base Management System
text: How many minimum relations are required for the following Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) with FD {A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A} to convert into BCNF without violation of lossless and dependency preserving decomposition _________.
solution:
Original FDs: A→BC, B→D, CD→E, E→A.
BCNF decomposition (dependency‑preserving & lossless):
1. R1(ABC) for A→BC
2. R2(BD) for B→D
3. R3(CDE) for CD→E
4. R4(EA) for E→A
Why not merge R1 and R4 → R(ABCE)?
Projected FDs in ABCE: A→BC, E→A (⇒ E→ABC).
Check BCNF: every FD’s LHS must be a superkey.
For A→BC, A is NOT a superkey of ABCE (A⁺ = {A,B,C} ≠ ABCE).
Hence ABCE violates BCNF.
BD and CDE are BCNF (B and CD are keys in their relations).
The 4-relation set preserves all FDs and is lossless; the 3-relation set (BD, ABCE, CDE) is not BCNF.
Final: Minimum relations for BCNF, lossless, dependency‑preserving = 4.

optionFeedback.html: One relation (keeping the original R) is not sufficient. In the original schema several functional dependencies have left-hand sides that are not superkeys (for example B→D and A→BC in the full relation), so the original relation is not in BCNF. Therefore a single-relation design cannot satisfy BCNF while also preserving all given dependencies and remaining lossless.

Two relations cannot both be in BCNF and also preserve all of the given dependencies while ensuring a lossless decomposition. Any two-relation split would force at least one relation to contain a dependency whose left-hand side is not a superkey in that relation (for example A→BC or B→D), causing a BCNF violation or losing dependency preservation.

Three relations still does not work. A natural 3-way attempt is R1(ABC), R2(BD), R3(CDE) merged into a 3-relation set like BD, ABCE, CDE by merging ABC and EA. However ABCE violates BCNF because A→BC holds in ABCE while A is not a superkey there (A+ in ABCE = {A,B,C} ≠ {A,B,C,E}). Thus a 3-relation decomposition fails BCNF.

Four relations is correct. Decompose into R1(ABC) for A→BC, R2(BD) for B→D, R3(CDE) for CD→E, and R4(EA) for E→A. In each relation the left-hand side of the defining FD is a key (A is key in ABC, B is key in BD, CD is key in CDE, E is key in EA), so each relation is in BCNF. All original FDs are preserved in these relations, and the decomposition is lossless.

title: Consider schema R(A, and following functional dependencies. Then decomposition of
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider a schema R(A, B, C, D) with the following functional dependencies:

  • A → B

  • B → C

  • C → D

  • D → B

The decomposition of R into R1(A, B), R2(B, C) and R3(B, D) is __________ .

options.html: Not dependency preserving and not lossless join.

solution:
Concept

A binary decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless iff the common attributes (R1 ∩ R2) form a superkey of at least one of R1 or R2 — i.e. (R1 ∩ R2) → R1 or (R1 ∩ R2) → R2. A decomposition is dependency-preserving iff the union of the FDs projected onto each subrelation has the same closure as the original FD set F, so every original FD is implied by the projections.

Set-up

First note the cycle B → C → D → B. Hence B, C and D are mutually equivalent: B⁺ = C⁺ = D⁺ = {B, C, D}. So each of B, C, D determines the other two. (A is determined by nothing, since no FD has A on its right side.)

Lossless-join check

  1. R1(A, B) ⋈ R2(B, C): common attribute is B. In R2, B → C holds, so B is a key of R2. The intersection determines a whole subrelation, so this join is lossless and yields R12(A, B, C).

  2. R12(A, B, C) ⋈ R3(B, D): common attribute is B. Since B⁺ = {B, C, D} ⊇ {B, D}, we have B → D, so B is a key of R3(B, D). Again the intersection is a key, so this join is lossless and reconstructs R(A, B, C, D).

Both binary joins are lossless, so the overall decomposition is lossless.

Dependency-preservation check

Project the FDs onto each subrelation and take the union F′:

  • R1(A, B) gives A → B.

  • R2(B, C) gives B → C and (since C⁺ ⊇ {B}) C → B.

  • R3(B, D) gives B → D and (since D → B) D → B.

Now recover every original FD from F′:

  • A → B : present directly (from R1).

  • B → C : present directly (from R2).

  • C → D : not stored directly, but F′ has C → B (R2) and B → D (R3); by transitivity C → B → D gives C → D.

  • D → B : present directly (from R3).

Every original FD is implied by F′, so the decomposition is dependency-preserving.

Conclusion

The decomposition is both lossless-join and dependency-preserving.

Cross-check (the key idea behind the lossless rule)

The reason losslessness holds here is exactly the rule that the shared attribute must be a key (superkey) in at least one of the two relations being joined. Because the cycle makes B equivalent to C and D, B acts as a key in both R2 and R3, so neither join introduces spurious tuples.

optionFeedback.html: Both properties are settled by the same observation: the cyclic dependencies among B, C and D make them mutually equivalent, so the shared attribute behaves as a key wherever these relations are joined, and the projected dependencies chain together to account for every original dependency. This is why this combined outcome is the one the FDs support.

Reaching this pairing means you accepted the join behaviour but judged dependency preservation separately and concluded against it. Preservation is decided by comparing the closure of the union of the projected dependencies with the closure of the original set — not by whether each dependency sits inside one subrelation. Redo that closure comparison carefully before fixing either half.

Reaching this pairing means you judged dependency preservation one way but decided the reconstruction would lose information. The lossless test for each pairwise join is purely about whether the shared attribute is a superkey of one of the two relations being joined, which you settle by computing that attribute's closure under the given FDs. Recompute that closure before fixing either half.

Reaching this pairing means both properties were ruled out together. Each property has its own independent test and must be evaluated separately rather than dismissed in one stroke; the cyclic dependencies in this set make the closures behave in a way that is easy to underestimate. Evaluate each property on its own terms before settling on a combined verdict.

title: In relational database, which one of the following is CORRECT:
subject: Data Base Management System
text: In a relational database, which one of the following is CORRECT:

options.html: A relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF.
If all attributes of a relation are prime attributes then the relation is in BCNF.
Every relation has at least one non-prime attribute.

solution:
Answer: A relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF.

Reasoning (proof):

  • Let the relation have exactly two attributes, A and B. Any non-trivial functional dependency must be either A -> B, B -> A, or have the whole set {A, B} on the left.

  • If A -> B holds, then A determines both attributes (A -> A is trivial), so A is a key (a superkey). The same argument applies if B -> A holds. If the left side is {A, B}, it is already a superkey.

  • Therefore every non-trivial FD has a superkey on the left, so the relation satisfies BCNF.

Why the other statements are false (brief counterexamples):

  • Statement: If all attributes are prime then the relation is in BCNF. Counterexample: R(A, B, C) with A -> B and B -> A (A and B determine each other) and no FD involving C. Candidate keys are {A, C} and {B, C}, so every attribute is prime, but A -> B violates BCNF because A is not a superkey.

  • Statement: Every relation has at least one non-prime attribute. Counterexample: R(A, B) with A -> B and B -> A. Candidate keys are {A} and {B}, so both attributes are prime and there is no non-prime attribute.

  • Statement: BCNF decomposition preserves functional dependencies. Counterexample: R(A, B, C) with FDs AB -> C and C -> B. Decomposing to (B, C) and (A, C) preserves C -> B but AB -> C is not preserved in any single decomposed relation; it can only be recovered by joining, so dependency preservation fails.

Summary: The two-attribute case forces any non-trivial FD to have a superkey on its left, so such relations are always BCNF. Other statements are false as shown by the counterexamples above.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. In a relation with exactly two attributes {A, B}, any non-trivial functional dependency must be either A -> B or B -> A (or both). If A -> B holds then A determines both attributes so A is a key (a superkey); similarly for B -> A. Thus every non-trivial dependency has a superkey on the left, so the relation satisfies BCNF.

Incorrect. All attributes being prime (each attribute belongs to some candidate key) does not guarantee BCNF. Counterexample: R(A, B, C) with dependencies A -> B and B -> A and no dependency involving C. Candidate keys are {A, C} and {B, C}, so every attribute is prime, but A -> B has a left side that is not a superkey, violating BCNF.

Incorrect. A relation can have all attributes prime (so no non-prime attribute exists). Counterexample: R(A, B) with A -> B and B -> A. Candidate keys are {A} and {B}, so every attribute is prime and there is no non-prime attribute.

Incorrect. BCNF decomposition guarantees a lossless-join decomposition but does not always preserve all functional dependencies. Counterexample: R(A, B, C) with FDs AB -> C and C -> B. Decomposing to relations (B, C) and (A, C) preserves C -> B but AB -> C is not preserved as a dependency in any single decomposed relation (it can only be recovered by joining), so dependency preservation fails.

title: Consider block(with spanned organization) that can hold exactly either record(1
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider a file with spanned organization in which a block can hold exactly 16 records (1 record = 32 bytes). The file uses a multilevel sparse primary index: the first level stores one search-key and data-block-pointer entry per data block, and each upper-level internal node has B-tree order 20 (that is, at most 20 pointers).
Find the total number of blocks needed for a file containing 10,000 records, where X is the number of blocks needed to store the file and Y is the total number of blocks across all levels of the primary index. The search key is 8 bytes and a block pointer is 6 bytes. Then X + Y = _________
solution:
Concept — Multilevel sparse primary index: a sparse primary index stores one key–block-pointer entry per data block. If that first index level occupies more than one block, an upper index level points to those blocks; the process stops when the upper level fits in one root block. Therefore, total index storage is the sum of blocks at every level.

  1. Block size: 16 × 32 = 512 bytes, so the block size is 512 bytes.

  2. Data-file blocks: 10,000 ÷ 16 = 625 blocks exactly, so X = 625.

  3. First index level: The sparse primary index has 625 entries. Each entry uses 8 + 6 = 14 bytes, so one index block holds floor(512 ÷ 14) = 36 entries. Hence the first level needs ceil(625 ÷ 36) = 18 blocks.

  4. Root level: An upper internal node can store 20 pointers. Since 18 ≤ 20, one root block points to all 18 first-level blocks, and no further level is needed.

  5. Result: Y = 18 + 1 = 19, so X + Y = 625 + 19 = 644.

  • Capacity check: 18 × 36 = 648 entries, while 17 × 36 = 612; therefore exactly 18 first-level blocks are required.

  • B-tree versus B+ tree: This calculation does not assume a B+ tree leaf layout. The first level consists of ordinary sparse primary-index blocks sized from the 8-byte key and 6-byte data-block pointer; only the upper internal level uses the supplied B-tree order of 20.

  • Terminology check: Primary describes what is indexed—the file’s ordering key with one sparse entry per data block. Making that primary index multilevel changes its storage hierarchy, not its classification.

Final answer: X + Y = 644.

title: Block can hold records or key pointers. database contains records
subject: Data Base Management System
text: A block can hold either 4 data records or 8 key pointers. A database file contains 48 records. If a dense index is built on this file, what is the total number of blocks required to store both the data file and the index?
solution:
Concept: In a dense index, the index stores exactly one entry (a key plus a pointer to the record) for every record in the data file - the number of index entries always equals the number of records. So the total space needed to store an indexed file = blocks needed for the data records + blocks needed for the index entries.

  1. Data blocks: each block holds 4 records, and there are 48 records, so data blocks needed = 48 / 4 = 12.

  2. Dense index entries: one entry per record, so there are 48 key pointers to store.

  3. Index blocks: each block holds 8 key pointers, so index blocks needed = 48 / 8 = 6.

  4. Total blocks required = data blocks + index blocks = 12 + 6 = 18.

Cross-check: 48 divides evenly by both 4 and 8, so neither count needs rounding up for a partial block. The index blocks already contain the pointers themselves, so no separate block is needed just to hold addresses.

title: Consider disk with block size bytes and block pointer of
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Consider a disk with block size = 1024 bytes and block pointer of 8 bytes and record pointer of 8 bytes. The file has 25,000 student records. Every record is of fixed length of 100 bytes. The key (Roll No) size is of 2 bytes. The file is not ordered by the key file (Roll No) and wants to construct a secondary index on RollNo. Then which of the following statements is/are true when we apply multi-level Indexing on above file?

options.html: Number of blocks in the 2nd level Index is 4.
Number of blocks in the 2nd level Index is 1.
To access a record average number of block access is 5.
To access a record average number of block access is 4.

solution:
Given: block size = 1024 bytes; block pointer = 8 bytes; record pointer = 8 bytes; key size = 2 bytes; number of records = 25,000; record size = 100 bytes.

Index entry size (key + pointer) = 2 + 8 = 10 bytes. Use the pointer size that applies to this secondary index (8 bytes), so each index entry is 10 bytes.

Entries per index block = floor(1024 / 10) = 102 entries per block.

  • Total index entries (dense index) = 25,000 (one entry per record).

  • First-level index blocks = ceil(25,000 / 102) = 246 blocks (102 * 245 = 24,990, so an additional block is needed for the remaining 10 entries).

  • Second-level index blocks = ceil(246 / 102) = 3 blocks.

  • Third-level index blocks = ceil(3 / 102) = 1 block.

Number of index levels above the data = 3 (first, second, third).

Average number of block accesses to retrieve a record = number of index levels + 1 (to access the data block) = 3 + 1 = 4

Summary: second-level index requires 3 blocks, and average block accesses to fetch a record using the multilevel index = 4.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Each index entry is 10 bytes (2-byte key + 8-byte pointer), so an index block holds floor(1024/10) = 102 entries. First-level index blocks = ceil(25000/102) = 246. Second-level blocks = ceil(246/102) = 3, not 4.
Incorrect. With 102 entries per index block, the first-level index needs 246 blocks. The second-level index therefore needs ceil(246/102) = 3 blocks, not 1.
Incorrect. There are 3 index levels above the data (first, second, third), so the total average block accesses = number of index levels + 1 (to read the data block) = 3 + 1 = 4, not 5.

Correct. Index entry size = 2 + 8 = 10 bytes, entries per index block = floor(1024/10) = 102. First-level blocks = ceil(25000/102) = 246, second-level = ceil(246/102) = 3, third-level = ceil(3/102) = 1. So there are 3 index levels; accesses = 3 + 1 = 4 block accesses.

title: Embedded pointer provides
subject: Data Base Management System
text: An embedded pointer provides:
solution:
Concept

A database access path is a structural route used to locate records. A pointer stored inside a data record creates a link that can be followed in addition to the file’s main organization.

This differs from a key, which identifies a record or entity, and from an index, which is a separate lookup structure.

Application

Because the pointer is embedded in one record and links to another record, it supplies an additional route for reaching related data. That role is a secondary access path.

Contrast

  • A physical record key identifies a record through storage-related location information; it is not the link stored inside another record.

  • An inverted index is a separate structure that maps terms or attribute values to lists of matching records.

  • A primary key is a logical uniqueness constraint used to identify each row or entity.

Result

Therefore, an embedded pointer provides a secondary access path.

optionFeedback.html: This mechanism traverses a stored record-to-record link: lookup begins at the current record and continues at the linked record.
This identifier encodes or corresponds to storage-location information so the storage manager can address a record directly.
This lookup structure maps terms or attribute values to postings that list the matching records.
This schema constraint uses designated field values to identify rows and enforce distinct identifiers.

title: Embedded pointer provides
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Embedded pointer provides
solution: An embedded pointer is a mechanism used in database file organization, specifically within secondary indexes. It allows the system to locate data records without relying solely on the primary key. By storing pointers directly within the index structure, it creates a secondary access path, enabling efficient retrieval of records based on non-primary key attributes.

optionFeedback.html: Embedded pointers are utilized within secondary indexing to support efficient record retrieval.
Embedded pointers are associated with indexing mechanisms rather than defining the physical record key.
Inverted indexes map search terms to documents, which is different from how embedded pointers function in database file structures.
A prime key serves as the primary identifier for records, distinct from the role of embedded pointers in file organization.

title: The physical location of record determined by formula that transforms

text: The physical location of a record determined by a formula that transforms a file key into a record location is
solution: The physical location of a record determined by a formula that transforms a file key into a record location is known as hashing. In this method, a hash function calculates the direct address of the record based on its key value, allowing for efficient retrieval without searching through other records.

optionFeedback.html: A hashed file uses a hash function to calculate the physical address directly from the key.
B-Tree files use tree structures for ordered access, not direct formula-based address calculation.
Indexed files use a separate index structure to locate records, rather than calculating the physical location directly from the key using a formula.
Sequential files store records in order, requiring sequential access or searching, not direct calculation of location from the key.

title: Consider table that describes the customers Customers(custid, name, gender, rating)
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider a table that describes the customers : 

Customers(custid, name, gender, rating)

The rating value is an integer in the range 1 to 5 and only two values (male and female) are recorded for gender. Consider the query “how many male customers have a rating of 5”? The best indexing mechanism appropriate for the query is
solution: The query filters on 'gender' and 'rating'. Both columns have very low cardinality (2 distinct values for gender, 5 for rating). Bitmap indexes are specifically designed for columns with low cardinality and equality conditions. They allow efficient combination of multiple filters using bitwise operations. Therefore, a bitmap index is the most appropriate mechanism for this specific query pattern.

optionFeedback.html: Linear hashing is optimized for single-key equality searches. It does not efficiently support combining multiple low-cardinality filter conditions.
Extendible hashing is designed for dynamic data distribution. It is less efficient than other structures for filtering on multiple low-cardinality attributes.
B+ Trees are versatile but less space-efficient than bitmap indexes for columns with very few distinct values.
This indexing method uses bitmaps to represent data presence, enabling fast bitwise operations for filtering low-cardinality columns.

title: Which of the following is dense index?
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following is dense index?
solution: In database management systems, indexes are classified by their density. A primary index is typically sparse, containing entries only for the first record of each data block. In contrast, a secondary index is dense because it requires an entry for every distinct search key value to locate records scattered throughout the file. Therefore, a secondary index is classified as a dense index.

optionFeedback.html: Primary indexes are typically sparse, containing entries only for the first record of each block.
Clustered indexes organize data physically but are not the standard definition for a dense index in this context.
A secondary index is considered a dense index because it contains an entry for every search key value, allowing direct access to records regardless of their physical location.

title: Consider an employee file consisting of records with each record

text: Consider an employee file consisting of 35000 records with each record of size 75 bytes stored on a disk of block size 512 bytes. Suppose that the file is ordered by ordering key field Eid and primary index is built on Eid. Size of Eid and block pointer is 9 bytes and 6 bytes respectively. title: Which of the following statement is/are correct regarding sequential file
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding sequential file organization?

I. The entire file must be read for insertion of a new record and deletion of a record.

II. On average, half of the records in the file must be processed to find the location of a record.
solution:
Concept

An ordered sequential file keeps records in search-key order. A successful search without an index proceeds sequentially, while insertions and deletions are normally handled by merging or rewriting the ordered file so that the key sequence is preserved.

These costs follow from maintaining physical order: lookup scans records in sequence, and a structural update must reproduce the ordered output rather than place a record arbitrarily.

Application

  1. For Statement I, a new record or deletion is incorporated during a rewrite or merge of the ordered file; the existing file is read through to produce the updated ordered file.

  2. For Statement II, a successful linear search can stop anywhere from the first record to the last, so its average work is about n/2 record examinations.

  3. Therefore Statement I and Statement II both describe the classical ordered sequential-file model.

Cross-check and contrast

  • “Only I” omits the average half-file cost of a successful sequential search.

  • “Only II” omits the batch rewrite or merge needed to preserve key order during insertion or deletion.

  • “Neither I nor II” treats both characteristic costs as absent.

Result: Both I and II.

optionFeedback.html: The update side assumes that a key-ordered file is rebuilt by merging records; the lookup side assumes that an index supplies each record address.
The update side assumes that new records can be appended without preserving key order; the lookup side assumes that records are inspected one by one.
The update side assumes that a key-ordered file is rebuilt by merging records; the lookup side assumes that records are inspected one by one.
The update side assumes that new records can be appended without preserving key order; the lookup side assumes that an index supplies each record address.

title: What is the purpose of the "INDEX" in SQL?
subject: Data Base Management System
text: What is the purpose of the "INDEX" in SQL?

options.html: To specify the default value for a column
To uniquely identify each row in a table
To define a relationship between two table

solution:
Answer: To speed up data retrieval

Explanation: Indexes improve the speed of data retrieval operations by creating a data structure (commonly a B-tree or hash) that allows the database to locate rows without scanning the entire table.

  • How it works: An index stores selected column values with pointers to table rows so lookups on those columns are much faster.

  • Common types: B-tree (general-purpose range and equality queries), hash (equality lookups), bitmap (low-cardinality columns).

  • Trade-offs: Indexes speed reads but add storage overhead and make inserts/updates/deletes slower because the index must be updated.

  • Uniqueness: A unique index enforces uniqueness for a column or set of columns, but a non-unique index only improves lookup performance and does not guarantee unique rows.

  • When to use: Index columns frequently used in WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY, or GROUP BY clauses; avoid indexing columns with very low selectivity or very small tables where full scans are cheap.

optionFeedback.html: This describes a column default value, which is set with a DEFAULT constraint (e.g., DEFAULT 0). An INDEX does not set default values for columns.
Uniquely identifying rows is usually the job of a primary key or a UNIQUE constraint. A unique index can enforce uniqueness, but a regular index does not inherently guarantee that each row is unique.

Correct — indexes speed up data retrieval by maintaining a data structure (such as a B-tree or hash) that lets the database find rows faster than scanning the whole table. Keep in mind indexes add storage overhead and can slow inserts/updates/deletes because the index must be maintained.

Defining relationships between tables is done with foreign keys, not indexes. Foreign key constraints enforce referential integrity; indexes may be used to speed joins on the foreign key column but do not define the relationship by themselves.

title: Calculate the order of leaf(p leaf and non leaf(p) nodes
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
In a B+ tree, the order of a node is the maximum number of entries (search keys) it can hold within one disk block. Using the parameters below, calculate the order of a leaf node (pleaf) and of a non-leaf / internal node (p). A leaf node stores (search key + record pointer) entries; an internal node stores search keys with their separating block pointers.

  • Search key field = 12 bytes

  • Record pointer = 10 bytes

  • Block pointer = 8 bytes

  • Block size = 1 KB = 1024 bytes
solution:
Concept

In a B+ tree the order of a node is fixed by requiring one node to fit inside a single disk block. The two node types store different things: a leaf node holds data entries, each = (search key + record pointer), plus one trailing block pointer that chains to the next leaf; a non-leaf / internal node holds only search keys and block pointers (no record pointers, because data lives only in the leaves). So you size each node by adding up the bytes of what it actually stores and keeping the total within the block size.

Application

Given: search key = 12 B, record pointer = 10 B, block pointer = 8 B, block size = 1024 B.

Leaf node order (pleaf): each entry = key + record pointer = 12 + 10 = 22 B, and a leaf keeps one extra block pointer (8 B) to link to its sibling:

  1. pleaf x 22 + 8 ≤ 1024

  2. pleaf x 22 ≤ 1016

  3. pleaf ≤ 1016 / 22 = 46.18

  4. Take the floor: pleaf = 46.

Non-leaf (internal) node order (p): here p is the number of search keys; a node holding p keys needs (p + 1) block pointers to separate its children, and the official sizing keeps this within one block:

  1. 12 x p + 8 x (p + 1) ≤ 1024

  2. 12p + 8p + 8 ≤ 1024

  3. 20p ≤ 1016

  4. p ≤ 1016 / 20 = 50.8

  5. Take the floor: p = 50.

Cross-check / contrast

Confirm each count is the largest that still fits one 1024-byte block:

  • pleaf = 46: 46 x 22 = 1012 B (+8 B sibling link = 1020 B ≤ 1024); 47 entries would need 1034 B — overflow.

  • p = 50: with 50 search keys and 51 block pointers, 50 x 12 + 51 x 8 = 600 + 408 = 1008 B ≤ 1024; 51 keys (with 52 pointers) would need 1028 B — overflow.

  • Sanity check on the asymmetry: a leaf entry (22 B) is heavier than an internal-node key slot (12 B paired with an 8 B pointer), so the leaf holds fewer entries than the internal node — any answer that swaps the two values fails this check.

Result: pleaf = 46 and p = 50.

text: Consider below statements – (I) Each non-leaf node in B⁺ tree has between ⌈n/2⌉ and n children, where n is fixed for a particular tree. (II) The search key of a clustering index is always primary key. (III) Secondary indices must be dense. (IV) In a dense index, an index entry appears for only some of the search-key values. Which of the above statements are true?
solution:
In a B⁺ tree of order n, every non-leaf node must have between ⌈n/2⌉ and n children so the tree stays height-balanced. An index is dense when it stores one index entry for every distinct search-key value in the file, and sparse when it stores entries for only some of those values; a sparse index is possible only when the file is physically sorted on that key. A clustering index is the index built on the attribute that fixes this physical ordering — that attribute need not be the primary key — while a secondary index is built on an attribute that does not fix the physical order, so it can never skip entries and must always be dense.

  1. Statement (I): a non-leaf B⁺-tree node's child count is bounded between ⌈n/2⌉ and n by the standard node-fanout rule, so statement (I) is true.

  2. Statement (II): a clustering index's search key is whichever attribute fixes the file's physical order, and that attribute is not required to be the primary key, so statement (II) is false.

  3. Statement (III): a secondary index cannot rely on the file being sorted by its own key, so it must carry an entry for every search-key value — matching the dense-index requirement — so statement (III) is true.

  4. Statement (IV): carrying an entry for only some of the search-key values is the definition of a sparse index, not a dense one, so statement (IV) is false.

Cross-check: among the four offered pairs, only 'I and III' pairs two true statements — 'I and IV' and 'I and II' each pair a true statement with a false one, and 'II and III' pairs a false statement with a true one — so 'I and III' is the only internally consistent pair.

Therefore, statements (I) and (III) are true, and the correct option is 'I and III'.

Statement II concerns the search key of a clustering index, which is defined as the attribute that fixes the file's physical ordering — it need not be the primary key. Statement III concerns secondary indices: since a secondary key never fixes the file's physical order, the index cannot skip entries and must carry one for every search-key value.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q61
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which operation benefits most dramatically from the linked leaf nodes in a B+ tree?
solution:
In a B+ tree, every actual data record (or record pointer) is stored only at the leaf level; internal nodes hold only separator or routing keys, which may repeat leaf keys but exist purely to guide the search downward. The leaf nodes are additionally chained together in a sequential linked list, separate from this internal index structure. This leaf-level linked list is what lets a program move from one leaf to the very next leaf directly, without re-descending from the root through the internal nodes.

  1. A successor lookup needs the entry that comes immediately after a given key in sorted order.

  2. Once the leaf holding the given key is known, the next entry can be read directly: it is either the following entry within the same leaf, or, if the given key is the last entry in its leaf, the first entry of the adjacent leaf reached through the leaf's linked-list pointer.

  3. This turns a "move to the next key" step into a single pointer hop (O(1) amortized), rather than needing to re-locate that position by searching again from the root of the tree.

  4. By contrast, exact key search always performs a fresh root-to-leaf descent guided by separator keys, and never uses the leaf-to-leaf pointers to complete the search. Parent node splitting, an internal node dividing on insertion overflow, is handled purely through the internal-node hierarchy and does not rely on the leaf-level links at all. Structural rebalancing after a deletion, redistributing entries between sibling leaves or merging two leaves, may need to update the surviving neighboring leaf's linked-list pointer as routine bookkeeping when a leaf is removed via a merge, but its own cost comes from the redistribution or merge logic itself, not from walking the leaf chain; it gains no traversal speed-up from the linked list the way a successor lookup does.

This matches the standard justification for choosing B+ trees over plain B-trees for range or sequential access: a plain B-tree has no leaf-level linked list, so without maintaining extra parent or path information, moving from one key to the next typically means re-locating that position through the internal-node structure rather than following a direct pointer. Successor and range-style traversal are the operations whose own per-step cost is most directly reduced by following that leaf-linked list; the other three operations either do not use it at all or only perform incidental pointer bookkeeping on it, rather than gaining a genuine per-step speed benefit from it.

Therefore, the operation that benefits most dramatically from the linked leaf nodes in a B+ tree is successor lookup.

optionFeedback.html: An exact key search determines whether a specific target key exists in the collection and, if so, locates the single record associated with it; it requires resolving exactly one key value using the ordering already encoded in the index.

A successor lookup determines the key value that comes immediately after a given key in the overall sorted ordering of stored keys; it requires resolving exactly one key value adjacent to the given key, without needing any keys further away in that ordering.

Parent node splitting occurs when an internal node accumulates more entries than its maximum branching factor allows during insertion; the node's entries are divided between two new nodes, and a median key is promoted to that node's own parent.

Structural rebalancing after a deletion occurs when a node's entry count falls below the minimum required for that node type; entries are then redistributed between sibling nodes, or two siblings are merged, to restore the minimum-occupancy invariant.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q77
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following best explains why B+ trees typically have smaller height than B-trees?

options.html: B+ trees use hashing internally to compress keys
Internal nodes store only keys, allowing higher fan-out
Leaf nodes are stored sequentially on disk

solution:
Concept

For a fixed-size disk page/node, the height of a B-tree or B+ tree is governed by its fan-out (the maximum number of children per node): height is approximately log base fan-out of N, for N keys. A B-tree keeps a data pointer/record alongside every key in every node (leaf and internal), while a B+ tree keeps data pointers only in leaf nodes - internal nodes store just keys and child pointers. Removing the data payload from internal-node entries lets more entries fit into the same fixed-size page, directly raising the fan-out of internal nodes.

Application

  1. Assume one disk page can hold a fixed amount of space, say 100 units.

  2. In a B-tree, each internal-node entry needs room for a key plus a child pointer plus a data/record pointer, so fewer entries fit per page - say 10 entries, giving fan-out approximately 11.

  3. In a B+ tree, each internal-node entry needs room only for a key plus a child pointer (no data pointer), so roughly twice as many entries fit per page - say 20 entries, giving fan-out approximately 21.

  4. For N = 1,000,000 keys, a B-tree with fan-out 11 needs about log base 11 of 1,000,000, approximately 5.8, i.e. 6 levels, while a B+ tree with fan-out 21 needs about log base 21 of 1,000,000, approximately 4.6, i.e. 5 levels.

  5. The B+ tree therefore reaches every key in one fewer disk-page access on average - a direct consequence of its internal nodes carrying only keys.

Cross-check

The general height formula for any multiway search tree is height approximately log base fan-out of N; since fan-out is the only variable that changed in this comparison (both structures index the same N keys), a strictly larger fan-out must produce a strictly smaller or equal height. This confirms that internal nodes storing only keys - and thereby allowing a higher fan-out - is the mechanism behind a B+ tree's smaller height, and is consistent with why B+ trees, not B-trees, are the standard choice for filesystem and database indexes, where minimizing disk-page reads per lookup matters most.

optionFeedback.html: Hashing-based indexes (such as hash tables) achieve average O(1) lookup by mapping a key directly to a bucket via a hash function, but they do not preserve key order and cannot support efficient range scans. B-trees and B+ trees are both ordered, comparison-based multiway search structures - they route a search by comparing key values at each node, not by hashing.

In a B+ tree, internal (non-leaf) nodes hold key values paired with child pointers that route a search to the correct subtree, while a full data pointer or record is attached to a key only at the leaf level. A B-tree, by contrast, attaches a data pointer to a key in every node it appears in, leaf or internal.

Physical sequential placement of leaf nodes on disk is one way a file-organization scheme could arrange stored blocks for fast sequential reads. A B+ tree, however, typically maintains leaf ordering through explicit next-leaf pointers stored inside each leaf node, a logical linkage that does not require the leaves' underlying disk blocks to be physically contiguous.

Whether duplicate key values are permitted is an implementation-level policy (a duplicate value can be stored as a separate entry or attached to a shared entry with a list of records), and both B-tree and B+ tree implementations that choose to support duplicates apply that same policy consistently across their nodes.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q126
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following ensures minimal disk accesses in B-tree searches ?
solution:
Concept: A B-tree is a self-balancing, disk-oriented multiway search tree. Because a random disk read is far slower than any CPU work, B-tree design is optimized to minimize the NUMBER OF DISK BLOCKS READ during a search, which equals the tree's height. Search cost is O(log_t n), where t (the minimum degree, i.e. the fan-out/order) controls how many keys and children each node holds.

Each B-tree node is allocated a maximum capacity (a maximum number of keys and child pointers) chosen to match the size of one disk block — this maximum capacity is the LARGE FAN-OUT (high order). Because a single disk read can therefore examine many keys at once, height stays low: even in the worst case, where every node holds only the guaranteed minimum share of that capacity, the tree's height still grows merely logarithmically, with a large base tied to the order. This bounded, shallow height directly translates into very few disk accesses per search — which is exactly why a large fan-out (order) is the design property that ensures minimal disk accesses, regardless of how full any individual node happens to be.

  • Root splitting is a maintenance step performed during insertion when a node overflows its capacity, so it keeps the tree balanced at write time — it is not itself a property that reduces disk accesses during a search.

  • Variable-sized nodes are not how B-trees are built: nodes follow a fixed order/degree bound matched one-to-one with a disk block; letting node size vary unpredictably would break that mapping to disk blocks.

  • Minimum height for a fixed number of keys is the smallest possible number of levels, achievable when every node is packed to its maximum capacity at every level. A B-tree does not guarantee this: it only guarantees that each non-root node stays at least half full, so a valid but under-filled B-tree can need more levels than that theoretical minimum. Its height is still bounded and grows logarithmically because of the order, but bounded-and-logarithmic is not the same guarantee as strictly minimal — the actual design lever is the large fan-out (order), not an independent 'minimum height' property.

So the design choice engineers actually make — a large fan-out (order) — is what ensures minimal disk accesses in B-tree searches.

optionFeedback.html: Root splitting is a restructuring operation performed during insertion when a node exceeds its key capacity: the node's median key moves up to form a new root, and the tree's height increases by one level.

Large fan-out (order) is the maximum number of child pointers a single B-tree node is allowed to hold at any level of the tree; the node's maximum key count is one less than this child-pointer maximum.

Variable-sized nodes describes a node-organization scheme in which each node's allocated maximum capacity is set independently for that node, so different nodes within the same tree structure can be built to different maximum capacities.
Minimum height for a fixed number of keys is the fewest possible levels a tree structure can have, a count that is reached only when every node at every level is packed to its full key capacity.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q160
subject: Data Base Management System
text: In a B+ tree, actual data is stored in
solution:
In a hierarchical index, nodes generally serve one of two purposes: guiding a search toward the right location, or holding the actual payload the search is looking for. A well-designed index keeps these two jobs on separate tiers — the guiding nodes stay lightweight (holding only keys and pointers) so more of them fit in a disk block, which increases fan-out and keeps the tree shallow; the payload is confined to one dedicated tier so the rest of the tree never has to carry that extra weight.

Tracing a search through a B+ tree shows exactly where that payload tier sits:

  1. The search starts at the root, which compares the search key against its separator keys to choose the correct child pointer — a purely guiding step.

  2. It then descends through zero or more internal nodes, each of which again uses separator keys, not payload, to pick the next child pointer downward.

  3. The search ends only when it reaches a leaf node; that is the dedicated payload tier described above, so the leaf holds the key together with the actual record or a pointer to the record on disk.

  4. Every leaf node is additionally linked to its neighboring leaves through sibling pointers, so once a leaf is reached, a range of records can be scanned in sequence without walking back up the tree.

This is exactly what distinguishes a B+ tree from a plain B-tree: a B-tree may keep data records inside internal nodes as well, whereas a B+ tree deliberately confines all data to the leaf level so every internal node stays small (keys and pointers only, no payload), improving fan-out and reducing tree height. Since the root and internal nodes are defined purely as guiding structures, and 'parent node' is only a relative name for any node that has children (root or internal), none of these levels is where actual data resides in a B+ tree — the leaf level is the sole data-holding tier, exactly the dedicated payload tier the opening principle described. (This routing/payload split describes any tree with more than one level; in the degenerate case of a single-node tree, that lone node acts as both root and leaf together.)

optionFeedback.html: The root has no node above it in the tree; every search begins there, before any child pointer is followed.
An internal node sits strictly below at least one other node in the tree and strictly above at least one further node.
A leaf node has no child nodes of its own, regardless of how large the tree grows.

A parent node is any node that has one or more child pointers into the level directly beneath it; whether a given node counts as a parent is relative to which level is being considered, not a fixed position in the tree.

Suppose a B+ tree is used for indexing a database file. Consider the following information:

size of the search key field= 10 bytes, block size = 1024 bytes, size of the record pointer= 9 bytes, size of the block pointer= 8 bytes.

Let K be the order of internal node and L be the order of leaf node of B+ tree, then (K, L)=______.
solution:
Compute leaf node order L (maximum number of key-record pairs in a leaf):

  • Usable bytes in a leaf = block size - pointer to next leaf = 1024 - 8 = 1016.

  • Bytes per leaf entry = key size + record pointer size = 10 + 9 = 19.

  • Leaf order L = floor(1016 / 19) = 53.

Compute internal node order K (maximum number of block pointers in an internal node):

  • If m is the number of block pointers, the node stores m pointers (8 bytes each) and m - 1 keys (10 bytes each).

  • Space constraint: 8m + 10(m - 1) ≤ 1024 ⇒ 18m ≤ 1034 ⇒ m ≤ 57.44.

  • Maximum integer m = 57, so K = 57.

Final answer: (K, L) = (57, 53).

optionFeedback.html: Correct. For a leaf, usable bytes = block size - pointer to next leaf = 1024 - 8 = 1016. Each leaf entry uses key + record pointer = 10 + 9 = 19 bytes, so leaf order L = floor(1016 / 19) = 53. For an internal node, if m is the number of block pointers then the node uses m * 8 bytes for pointers and (m - 1) * 10 bytes for keys, so 8m + 10(m - 1) ≤ 1024 ⇒ 18m ≤ 1034 ⇒ m ≤ 57.44, hence maximum pointers K = 57. Therefore (K, L) = (57, 53).

Incorrect. The leaf order 52 is wrong because the correct leaf capacity is floor((1024 - 8) / (10 + 9)) = floor(1016 / 19) = 53. The internal order 50 is smaller than the actual maximum: solving 8m + 10(m - 1) ≤ 1024 gives m ≤ 57.44, so the maximum pointer count is 57 (not 50).

Incorrect. Both numbers are too large for the given block size. The leaf value 64 exceeds capacity because floor((1024 - 8) / (10 + 9)) = 53, not 64. The internal value 60 is invalid because 8*60 + 10*59 = 1070 bytes, which exceeds the 1024-byte block size, so the maximum pointer count is 57.

Incorrect. Both values are too small. The leaf order should be 53 (computed as floor((1024 - 8) / (10 + 9)) = 53) and the internal maximum pointer count is 57 (from 8m + 10(m - 1) ≤ 1024 ⇒ m ≤ 57.44).

title: The order of leaf node in tree is the maximum
subject: Data Base Management System
text: The order of a leaf node in a B+ tree is the maximum number of (value, data record pointer) pairs it can hold. Given that the block size is 1K bytes, data record pointer is 7 bytes long, the value field is 9 bytes long and a block pointer is 6 bytes long, what is the order of the leaf node ?
solution:
Key insight: a B+ tree leaf node stores (value, data record pointer) pairs plus one extra block pointer that chains it to the next leaf. So its order — the maximum number of pairs it can hold — is order = floor((block size − block pointer size) / (value size + record pointer size)).

  1. Pair size = value field + data record pointer = 9 + 7 = 16 bytes.

  2. Usable bytes in the leaf block = block size − block pointer = 1024 − 6 = 1018 bytes.

  3. Order = floor(1018 / 16) = floor(63.625) = 63.

Cross-check: 63 pairs plus the leaf's 6-byte block pointer use 63 × 16 + 6 = 1014 bytes, leaving 1024 − 1014 = 10 bytes spare in the 1024-byte block — so 63 pairs fit. One more pair (64) would alone need 64 × 16 = 1024 bytes, already the entire block, leaving no room for the 6-byte block pointer, so 64 pairs do not fit. This confirms 63 is the maximum.

Therefore the maximum number of (value, data record pointer) pairs a leaf can hold — the order of the leaf node — is 63.

optionFeedback.html: Reserving 6 bytes for the leaf's block pointer leaves 1024 − 6 = 1018 usable bytes. Each (value, data record pointer) pair uses 9 + 7 = 16 bytes, and floor(1018 / 16) = 63 — the largest number of pairs that fits within the leaf block.
64 pairs alone would need 64 × 16 = 1024 bytes, which already consumes the entire block before any space is set aside for the leaf's 6-byte block pointer, so 64 pairs cannot fit.
67 pairs would need 67 × 16 = 1072 bytes, well beyond the 1018 bytes left in the block once the 6-byte block pointer is reserved, so 67 pairs cannot fit.
68 pairs would need 68 × 16 = 1088 bytes, far more than the 1018 bytes available after reserving the leaf's 6-byte block pointer, so 68 pairs cannot fit.

title: Match the following: List-1 List-2 Relational Algebra Procedural Query Language
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Match the following:

List-2

II) Relational Calculus

solution:
Concept: Relational query languages are classified as procedural or non-procedural — a procedural language (Relational Algebra) specifies both the result and the exact sequence of operations to obtain it, while a non-procedural/declarative language (Relational Calculus) specifies only the desired result. Separately, in ER modelling, Generalization is the bottom-up process of combining several lower-level entity sets that share common attributes into one higher-level entity set, while Specialization is the reverse, top-down process of dividing a higher-level entity set into distinct lower-level subsets based on distinguishing features.

List-1 item

List-2 match

Why

I) Relational Algebra

Q) Procedural Query Language

It performs operations (select, project, join, etc.) in a defined sequence to retrieve data.

II) Relational Calculus

P) Non-Procedural Query Language

It states the desired result through a formula, without specifying the sequence of operations.

III) Generalization

S) Bottom-Up Approach

It starts from several specific entity sets and generalizes upward into one higher-level set.

IV) Specialization

R) Top-Down Approach

It starts from one general entity set and specializes downward into distinguishing subsets.

Cross-check against the other options:

  • I-Q, II-P, III-R, IV-S reverses only the ER-model pairing — it assigns Generalization to the top-down direction and Specialization to the bottom-up direction, which is backwards.

  • I-P, II-Q, III-S, IV-R reverses only the query-language pairing — it assigns Relational Algebra to non-procedural and Relational Calculus to procedural, which is backwards.

  • I-P, II-Q, III-R, IV-S reverses both pairings at once.

Thus the correct matching is I-Q, II-P, III-S, IV-R.
