This mapping is correct on all four pairs: Relational Algebra is procedural (it specifies both the result and the sequence of operations), Relational Calculus is non-procedural (it specifies only the desired result), Generalization is the bottom-up approach (combining specific entity sets into one general set), and Specialization is the top-down approach (dividing a general entity set into specific subsets).

Your Generalization/Specialization pairing is right, but the Relational Algebra/Relational Calculus pairing is swapped — recheck which query language specifies the exact retrieval steps and which one does not.

Both pairings here are swapped: the query-language classification (Relational Algebra vs. Relational Calculus) and the ER-model hierarchy direction (Generalization vs. Specialization) are each assigned the opposite of what they should be. Recheck both concepts before re-attempting.

title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - June 2009 - source row 18
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
(i) DML includes a query language based on both relational algebra and tuple calculus

(ii) DML includes a query language based on tuple calculus

(iii) DML includes a query language based on relational algebra

(iv) DML includes a query language based on none of the relational algebra and tuple calculus

Which one is correct ?
solution:
In relational database theory, a query language for retrieving data can be procedural or non-procedural. Relational algebra is procedural: it specifies both the desired result and an explicit sequence of operations (selection, projection, join, and so on) to obtain it. Relational calculus is non-procedural (declarative); in its tuple-calculus form it specifies only the desired result through a predicate over tuple variables, leaving the retrieval steps unspecified. Codd's theorem establishes that relational algebra and the safe (domain-independent) tuple relational calculus are equivalent in expressive power (relational completeness).

DML's query language is defined on both foundations together, not implementation detail but textbook grounding. A declarative DML statement, such as SQL's SELECT with a WHERE condition, is a predicate over the desired tuples, which is precisely the tuple-relational-calculus formulation. The same query can equally be written as a sequence of relational-algebra operations, such as selection, projection, and join, that produces the identical result. Because both formulations exist for the same query language and Codd's theorem shows they are equivalent in expressive power, DML's query language is correctly described as based on both relational algebra and tuple calculus, which is exactly what statement (i) says.

  • Statement (ii) keeps only the tuple-calculus half and drops the relational-algebra formulation that the same query language is equally defined by under Codd's equivalence, so it is an incomplete description of DML's basis.

  • Statement (iii) keeps only the relational-algebra half and drops the tuple-calculus formulation that the same query language is equally defined by under Codd's equivalence, so it too is an incomplete description.

  • Statement (iv) denies both foundations, which contradicts the well-established dual algebra-and-calculus basis of relational query languages.

Because DML's query language genuinely combines both formal foundations rather than only one, statement (i), DML includes a query language based on both relational algebra and tuple calculus, is the correct statement.

optionFeedback.html: This statement asserts that DML's query language draws on both relational algebra and tuple calculus at once -- the procedural and non-procedural formal foundations of relational query languages.
This statement restricts DML's query-language basis to tuple calculus alone, covering only the non-procedural, predicate-based branch of relational query theory.
This statement restricts DML's query-language basis to relational algebra alone, covering only the procedural, operation-sequence branch of relational query theory.
This statement asserts that DML's query language draws on neither relational algebra nor tuple calculus, excluding both formal foundations of relational query languages.

title: Which operation is used to extract specified columns from table?
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which operation is used to extract specified columns from a table?
solution:
Concept

Relational algebra uses operators to transform relations. Projection is a unary operator, written π, that returns selected attributes of a relation; under set semantics, duplicate result tuples are removed.

Application

The task is to retain only specified columns from one table. That is the role of projection, represented here by the value Project.

Contrast

  • Join combines compatible tuples from two input relations according to a condition.

  • Extract is an informal data-retrieval verb, not the conventional relational-algebra operator name.

  • Substitute describes replacing a value or expression, not a standard relational-algebra operator for this task.

Cross-check

For example, applying πname, department(Employee) produces a relation containing only the name and department attributes. Thus the required operation is Project.

optionFeedback.html: This formal unary relational-algebra operator has the signature πA(R), with one relation and an attribute-list operand.
This formal binary relational-algebra operator has the signature R ⋈θ S, with two relations and a predicate operand.
This general retrieval verb has no defined relational-algebra operator signature or fixed relation/attribute operands.
This replacement action has no defined relational-algebra operator signature; its operands are a value or expression and a replacement.

title: Map the following statements to True or False respectively. Count
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Map the following statements to True (T) or False (F), respectively.

  • S1: COUNT includes NULL values when it is applied to an attribute of a table.

  • S2: AVG includes NULL values in its calculation.

  • S3: The projection operation of relational algebra is equivalent to the SELECT clause of SQL.
solution:
CONCEPT

SQL aggregate functions applied to an expression ignore NULL inputs. COUNT(expression) counts non-NULL results, while AVG(expression) averages only the non-NULL results.

In relational algebra, projection chooses attributes, or columns, from a relation. The SELECT list in SQL performs the corresponding column-selection role.

APPLICATION

  1. For S1, COUNT(attribute) does not count rows in which that attribute is NULL. Therefore S1 is False.

  2. For S2, AVG(attribute) omits NULL values from both the sum and the number of values used as the divisor. Therefore S2 is False.

  3. For S3, relational-algebra projection selects attributes, and the SQL SELECT list selects the output columns. Therefore S3 is True. Relational algebra uses set semantics; SQL may require SELECT DISTINCT when duplicate elimination is material.

CROSS-CHECK AND CONTRAST

For attribute values 10, NULL, and 20, COUNT(attribute) is 2 and AVG(attribute) is 15. A query such as SELECT attribute FROM R returns that chosen column, matching the column-selection role of projection.

  • TFF assigns True to S1 even though COUNT(attribute) excludes NULL values; it also assigns False to the projection comparison.

  • TFT assigns True to S1 even though COUNT(attribute) excludes NULL values.

  • TTF assigns True to both NULL-aggregation statements and False to the projection comparison.

Hence the truth-value sequence is FFT.

optionFeedback.html: FFT represents S1 as False, S2 as False, and S3 as True.
TFF represents S1 as True, S2 as False, and S3 as False.
TFT represents S1 as True, S2 as False, and S3 as True.
TTF represents S1 as True, S2 as True, and S3 as False.

title: What does the following relational algebra expression do? σSalary (Employee)

options.html: Finds only the Salary values from Employee where Salary is greater than 35000
Finds all the tuples in Employee where the Salary is greater than 35000
Finds all the Salaries in Employee where the number of values is greater than 35000

solution:
The expression σ Salary > 35000 (Employee) is a selection operation. Selection filters rows/tuples from a relation based on a condition. Here, it returns all tuples of Employee for which Salary > 35000.

It does not project only the Salary attribute; projection would use π, not σ. Therefore, the correct answer is Option C.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. This omits the selection condition. σ Salary > 35000 does not return all Employee tuples; it returns only rows where Salary is greater than 35000.
Incorrect. This describes projection of only the Salary attribute. The σ operator performs selection, so it returns complete tuples/rows, not only Salary values.
Correct. σ is the selection operator. It filters Employee rows where Salary > 35000 and returns all attributes of those matching tuples.
Incorrect. The expression does not count values and does not return only salaries. It filters Employee tuples by the condition Salary > 35000.

title: Consider the following instance of relation District District Name Population
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following instance of a relation District –

Which district names will be returned by the following relational algebra expression?
πₙₐₘₑ (σₙₐₘₑ≠"AJ" (District)) − [πₙₐₘₑ (σₚₒₚᵤₗₐₜᵢₒₙ>5 (District)) ∩ πₙₐₘₑ (σₙₐₘₑ="AJ" (District))]
solution:
Concept: Selection σₙₐₘₑ(R) keeps only the tuples of relation R that satisfy the predicate; projection πₙₐₘₑ(R) then extracts just that attribute from the surviving tuples (duplicates removed). For two such projected sets, intersection (∩) keeps tuples common to both, and set difference (A − B) keeps the tuples of A that are absent from B.

  1. Left operand: πₙₐₘₑ (σₙₐₘₑ≠"AJ" (District)) — σₙₐₘₑ≠"AJ" keeps every row whose name is not "AJ". From District {JA:10, AJ:50, MM:5}, this is {JA, MM}. πₙₐₘₑ of this is {JA, MM}.

  2. First factor of the bracket: πₙₐₘₑ (σₚₒₚᵤₗₐₜᵢₒₙ>5 (District)) — σₚₒₚᵤₗₐₜᵢₒₙ>5 keeps every row with population greater than 5. Both JA (10) and AJ (50) satisfy this; MM (5) does not, since 5 is not strictly greater than 5. So the selection is {JA, AJ}, and πₙₐₘₑ gives {JA, AJ}.

  3. Second factor of the bracket: πₙₐₘₑ (σₙₐₘₑ="AJ" (District)) — σₙₐₘₑ="AJ" keeps only the row named "AJ", i.e. {AJ}. πₙₐₘₑ gives {AJ}.

  4. Intersect the two projected sets: {JA, AJ} ∩ {AJ} = {AJ}.

  5. Subtract from the left operand: {JA, MM} − {AJ}. Since "AJ" is not an element of {JA, MM}, removing it changes nothing, leaving {JA, MM}.

Cross-check: πₙₐₘₑ (σₙₐₘₑ="AJ" (District)) can never contain any name other than "AJ", so the bracket’s intersection is always a subset of {AJ} — at most {AJ}, never more, regardless of any population value. The left operand πₙₐₘₑ (σₙₐₘₑ≠"AJ" (District)) excludes "AJ" by construction. Subtracting a set that is at most {AJ} from a set that never contains "AJ" removes nothing, so the expression evaluates to {JA, MM} as long as AJ exists in District — independent of the exact population figures. Final result: {JA, MM}.

optionFeedback.html: JA (population 10) satisfies name≠"AJ" and population>5 but does not satisfy name="AJ"; MM (population 5) satisfies name≠"AJ" but does not satisfy population>5 or name="AJ".
JA (population 10) satisfies name≠"AJ" and population>5 but does not satisfy name="AJ".
JA (population 10) satisfies name≠"AJ" and population>5 but does not satisfy name="AJ"; AJ (population 50) satisfies population>5 and name="AJ" but does not satisfy name≠"AJ".
AJ (population 50) satisfies population>5 and name="AJ" but does not satisfy name≠"AJ".
This records that no option was chosen for the item; it does not evaluate name≠"AJ", population>5, or name="AJ" over any District tuple.

title: Which of the following is/are true: a1,a1,a2,a3,a4….an(σA(R)) a1,a1,a2,a3,a4….an(R)) a1,a1,a2,a3,a4….an(R⋂S) a1,a1,a2,a3,a4….an(R-(R-S))
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Which of the following is/are true:
S1 : Π a1,a1,a2,a3,a4….an(σA(R)) ≡ σA(Π a1,a1,a2,a3,a4….an(R))
S2: Π a1,a1,a2,a3,a4….an(R⋂S) ≡ Π a1,a1,a2,a3,a4….an(R-(R-S))
solution:
Answer: only S2 is true.

  • S1 (Π ... (σ_A(R)) ≡ σ_A(Π ... (R))) is false in general.

    Reason: A selection uses attributes referenced in the predicate A. If the projection on the right-hand side removes one or more of those attributes, the selection cannot be applied after projection (or would yield a different result). Therefore the two sides need not be equivalent.

    Counterexample: Let R(a,b) = {(1,10),(2,20)} and A be the condition a = 1. Let the projection be π_b. Then π_b(σ_{a=1}(R)) = {10}. But σ_{a=1}(π_b(R)) cannot select on a because a was removed by the projection, so the results differ.

  • S2 (Π ... (R ⋂ S) ≡ Π ... (R - (R - S))) is true.

    Reason: This follows from the set identity R ∩ S = R - (R - S). For any tuple t,

    1. If t ∈ R ∩ S, then t ∈ R and t ∈ S, so t ∉ (R - S), hence t ∈ R - (R - S).

    2. If t ∈ R - (R - S), then t ∈ R and t ∉ (R - S). The latter means it is not the case that t ∈ R and t ∉ S, so t ∈ S. Thus t ∈ R ∩ S.

    Since the two relations are equal, projecting the same list of attributes from each yields identical results: Π(...)(R ∩ S) = Π(...)(R - (R - S)).

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Statement S1 is not generally true: selection and projection do not commute because projection can remove attributes needed by the selection predicate. Example: let R(a,b) = {(1,10),(2,20)} and let the selection condition be a = 1. Then π_b(σ_{a=1}(R)) = {10}. But σ_{a=1}(π_b(R)) cannot be evaluated (or would yield no rows) because attribute a was removed by the projection, so the two sides are not equivalent.

Incorrect. Statement S1 is false for the reason above: projection can drop attributes needed by the selection. Statement S2 is true because R ∩ S is equal to R - (R - S), so projecting either expression yields the same result.

Correct. Statement S2 is true because of the set identity R ∩ S = R - (R - S). Projecting either side of that identity produces the same result. Statement S1 is not generally true because projection can remove attributes required to evaluate the selection predicate.

Incorrect. 'None of the above' is not correct because Statement S2 is true (R ∩ S = R - (R - S) so their projections are equal). Statement S1 is false because projection can eliminate attributes needed for the selection.

title: Consider the instances of relational schema: SID (students) SID student.SID=enrolled.SID

text:
Consider the instances of relational schema:

ΠSID (students) - ΠSID (σstudent.SID=enrolled.SID Λ enrolled.CID=course.CID Λ age≥22(student x enrolled x course)
Which of the following is true:

options.html: return the SID of all student who enrolled some subject and age is greater than 22
return the SID of some student who enrolled all subjects and age is less than 22
return the SID of all student who doesn’t enrolled any subject or age is less than 22
return the SID of all student who doesn’t enrolled any subject and age is less than 22

solution:
Given expression: π SID (students) − π SID (σ student.SID = enrolled.SID ∧ enrolled.CID = course.CID ∧ age ≥ 22 (student × enrolled × course))

  • First part: π SID (students) returns the SID of every student in the students relation.

  • Second part: σ student.SID = enrolled.SID ∧ enrolled.CID = course.CID ∧ age ≥ 22 (student × enrolled × course) finds tuples where a student is matched to an enrolled course and the student’s age is at least 22. Projecting SID from that selection gives SIDs of students who are enrolled in at least one course and have age ≥ 22.

  • Set difference: Subtracting the second set from all student SIDs yields the SIDs of students who are not in the set of enrolled-and-age≥22 students.

optionFeedback.html: This describes students who are enrolled in some subject and whose age is greater than 22. The inner projected set in the expression indeed finds students who are enrolled and satisfy an age condition, but the full expression subtracts that set from the set of all students. So this option describes the set being removed, not the final result, and is therefore incorrect.

This claims students who enrolled in all subjects and whose age is less than 22. The expression does not require a student to be enrolled in every course (universal enrollment); it only identifies students enrolled in at least one course. Thus this description is incorrect.

Correct. The expression takes all student SIDs and removes the SIDs of students who are enrolled in at least one course and whose age is at least 22. The remaining SIDs are students who either have not enrolled in any course or whose age is less than 22.

This says students who have not enrolled in any subject and whose age is less than 22 (an AND). The actual expression returns students who either have not enrolled in any subject OR have age less than 22. Using AND here is too restrictive, so this option is incorrect.

solution: To find tuples that are in one relation but not in another, we need an operation that returns elements exclusive to the first relation. Let’s analyze each operation: Cartesian Product: Combines every tuple from the first relation with every tuple from the second. It produces all possible pairs, not tuples exclusive to one relation. Explanation:

  • Interpretation: Let relation A have attributes X ∪ Y and relation B have attributes Y. The division A ÷ B returns the distinct X-values that are paired with every tuple of B.

  • Requirement for a result value: For a single X-value to appear in A ÷ B, there must be a tuple in A for that X-value combined with every one of the n tuples of B. In other words, each result value needs at least n tuples in A.

  • Maximum count: Given m total tuples in A, the maximum number of distinct X-values that can each have at least n associated tuples is the number of complete groups of size n that can be formed from m tuples, which is floor(m/n).

  • Why other expressions are wrong: m counts all tuples (not grouped by X-values), m - n is not meaningful for the grouping requirement and can be negative, and ceiling(m/n) can overcount when m is not divisible by n because partial groups do not produce valid result values.

title: An example of fourth generation programming language is

solution:
CONCEPT: Programming languages are classified into "generations" by how much they abstract away the machine. First- and second-generation languages (machine code, assembly) and third-generation languages (3GLs, e.g. procedural languages) all require the programmer to spell out HOW to compute a result, step by step. A fourth-generation language (4GL) instead lets the user state WHAT result is wanted — the underlying engine figures out how to produce it. 4GLs are typically domain-specific (report generation, GUI building, database querying) rather than general-purpose.

APPLICATION: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the textbook example of a 4GL: a query like "SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 90" declares WHAT rows are wanted; the database engine decides HOW to fetch them (index choice, join order, etc.). Because SQL is declarative and domain-specific to data retrieval/manipulation rather than a general imperative language, some learners feel it "isn't really programming" — that's a fair intuition, but it is exactly the property (declarative, what-not-how) that puts SQL in the fourth-generation bracket in CS/DBMS curricula, which is the classification this question is testing.

  • C: a compiled, procedural language from the 1970s — the programmer writes explicit step-by-step instructions (loops, pointers, memory management), the defining trait of a third-generation language.

  • COBOL: also procedural and imperative, built in the 1960s for business data processing — same third-generation, how-to-compute style as C.

  • MERCURY: a logic/functional language where a programmer states relationships and constraints for the system to solve — this declarative, knowledge-based style is generally placed a tier ABOVE fourth-generation, in the fifth-generation (AI/logic) bracket.

  • SQL: declarative and domain-specific to data queries — matches the fourth-generation definition applied above.

optionFeedback.html: C is a compiled, procedural language from the 1970s: the programmer must spell out every computational step explicitly — loops, pointers, manual memory management. This step-by-step, imperative style is the classic hallmark of a third-generation language (3GL).

MERCURY is a logic/functional language: the programmer declares relationships and constraints, and the system resolves them via inference rather than following a written sequence of steps. This knowledge-based, inference-driven style is generally classified as a fifth-generation language (5GL).

title: In context to Database management system which of the following

text:

solution:
Query by Example (QBE) is a user-friendly, graphical database query language meant for relational databases. Instead of making users write structured code like SQL (e.g., SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Age > 25), it provides a visual grid or form template that resembles the database table structure.

Analyzing Statement I:

"A Query by example form collects all information from a user for composing query language statements for search criterion."

  • Analysis: Correct. In a QBE interface, the user specifies their search parameters directly inside a blank form or skeleton table layout. The database engine then takes these filled details (the criteria/examples provided by the user) and converts them internally into operational query statements (like SQL commands) to search and retrieve the requested data.

Analyzing Statement II:

"Query by example relieves users from remembering query language keywords and using them with correct syntax to form quires."

  • Analysis: Correct. Since QBE is completely graphical, users do not need to memorize strict keyword syntaxes, proper command nesting, or comma/semicolon rules. They simply type what they are looking for directly into the appropriate column boxes of the table view. This heavily lowers the barrier to entry for non-technical users.

Because both statements accurately define the mechanism and the fundamental purpose of QBE, Both I and II are correct.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect: This option is incomplete because Statement II is also a completely true and vital feature of Query by Example.
Incorrect: This option falsely claims both factual definitions of QBE are incorrect.
Correct: This accurately reflects that both statements correctly describe how a QBE form collects data criteria and how it eliminates the need to remember complex command-line syntax.
Incorrect: This option is incomplete because Statement I is also functionally accurate regarding how QBE builds backend queries from input forms.

title: Consider database table containing two columns and each of type
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider a database table T containing two columns X and Y each of type Integer. After the creation of the table, one record (X=1,Y=1) is inserted in the table. Let MX and MY denote the respective maximum values of X and Y among all records in the table at any point in time. Using MX and MY, new records are inserted in the table 128 times with X and Y values being MX+1,2×MY+1 respectively. It may be noted that each time after the insertion, values of MX and MY change. What will be the output of the following SQL query after the steps mentioned above are carried out?

SELECT Y FROM T WHERE X=7;
solution:
A recurrence relation defines each new term purely from the previous one via a fixed rule. When a rule such as Y_new = 2 × Y_old + 1 is applied once per insertion alongside X simply incrementing by 1, the value tied to any particular X must be built up step by step from the initial record — it cannot be read off directly. A SELECT ... WHERE query on such a table then just reports the Y stored in the one record whose X matches the target.

Applying this to the table: it starts with the single record (X = 1, Y = 1). Each insertion sets the new X to (current maximum X) + 1 and the new Y to 2 × (current maximum Y) + 1, so the record carrying X = 7 is the 6th record inserted (X goes 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7). Tracking Y through each of these six insertions:

  1. X = 2: Y = 2 × 1 + 1 = 3

  2. X = 3: Y = 2 × 3 + 1 = 7

  3. X = 4: Y = 2 × 7 + 1 = 15

  4. X = 5: Y = 2 × 15 + 1 = 31

  5. X = 6: Y = 2 × 31 + 1 = 63

  6. X = 7: Y = 2 × 63 + 1 = 127

So the record with X = 7 carries Y = 127, and SELECT Y FROM T WHERE X = 7; returns 127.

Independent check: every record in this sequence satisfies Y = 2X − 1 (X = 1 gives 21 − 1 = 1; X = 2 gives 22 − 1 = 3; …; X = 7 gives 27 − 1 = 127), matching every step traced above and confirming the answer independently. The remaining options do not belong to this sequence: 15 is the Y value at the earlier step X = 4 rather than X = 7, while 129 and 257 never occur in the sequence generated by this recurrence.

optionFeedback.html: The value 127 is one less than 128 and has the seven-bit binary representation 1111111.
The value 15 is one less than 16 and has the four-bit binary representation 1111.
The value 129 is one more than 128 and has the eight-bit binary representation 10000001.
The value 257 is one more than 256 and has the nine-bit binary representation 100000001.

solution: The SELECT statement is used to retrieve specific columns and rows from a database table. Its basic syntax includes SELECT column_name FROM table_name WHERE condition.

INSERT INTO adds new rows to an existing table. It does not select or retrieve specific columns and rows from the database as requested.

title: Which of the following statement contains an error?
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following statement contains an error?
solution:
Concept

Every standard SQL SELECT query that reads values from a stored table must name that table in a FROM clause. The FROM clause is what tells the engine which table the column names and the WHERE filter belong to. Omit it while still referencing table columns and the statement is syntactically invalid.

Applying it here

Walk each statement and check whether the table it reads from is declared:

  • Select * from EMP where EMPID = 15; — names the table with from EMP, so every column and the filter resolve against EMP. Valid.

  • Select EMPID from EMP where EMPID = 15; — selects one column from the declared table EMP and filters on it. Valid.

  • Select EMPID from EMP; — selects a column from EMP with no filter, returning that column for all rows. Valid.

  • Select EMPID where EMPID = 15 and LASTNAME = 'Singh'; — selects EMPID and filters on EMPID and LASTNAME, but never declares a FROM clause. There is no table for those columns to come from, so the parser rejects it. This is the statement with the error.

Cross-check

The rule is: literals and expressions can be selected without a FROM (e.g. SELECT 1+1), but the moment you reference a base-table column such as EMPID or LASTNAME, a FROM clause naming that table becomes mandatory. The faulty statement breaks exactly this rule.

optionFeedback.html: This references columns through the * projection and a where condition, and the clause from EMP names the table those columns are taken from. Trace each clause to a table: the from EMP clause supplies one, so every referenced column has a declared source.

Here the projected column EMPID and the where condition both name columns, and the clause from EMP names the table supplying them. Trace each clause to a table: the from EMP clause supplies one, so every referenced column has a declared source.

This references the single column EMPID in its projection and carries no where condition, and the clause from EMP names its table. Trace each clause to a table: the from EMP clause supplies one, so every referenced column has a declared source.

Here the projected column EMPID and the where condition on EMPID and LASTNAME reference columns, but no from clause names a table for them. Trace each clause to a table: there is no from clause, so the referenced columns have no declared source.

title: Which of the following SQL queries correctly selects records where
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following SQL queries correctly selects records where the First_Name contains a specific pattern, the Last_Name also matches a pattern using LIKE, and the City does not match a given pattern using NOT LIKE?

options.html:
SELECT * FROM Employee
WHERE First_Name LIKE '%A%'
AND Last_Name LIKE '%K%'
AND City NOT LIKE '%Delhi%';

SELECT * FROM Employee
WHERE First_Name IN '%A%'
AND Last_Name IN '%K%'
AND City NOT IN '%Delhi%';

SELECT * FROM Employee
WHERE First_Name LIKE '%A%'
OR Last_Name LIKE '%K%'
OR City NOT LIKE '%Delhi%';

SELECT * FROM Employee
WHERE First_Name NOT LIKE '%A%'
AND Last_Name LIKE '%K%'
AND City LIKE '%Delhi%';

solution:
The requirement is a single query that filters the Employee table on three conditions joined by AND: First_Name matches a pattern with LIKE, Last_Name matches a pattern with LIKE, and City does NOT match a pattern with NOT LIKE.

In SQL, the LIKE operator performs pattern matching, where % is a wildcard standing for zero or more characters and _ stands for exactly one character. NOT LIKE returns the rows that do not match the pattern. The = / != operators do an exact literal comparison, so a % inside them is treated as a literal percent character, not a wildcard. IN tests membership in a list and must be followed by a parenthesised set of values, e.g. IN ('A','B') — it cannot be used for pattern matching.

Only Option (a) uses LIKE / LIKE / NOT LIKE with the wildcard % and joins all three predicates with AND, so every selected record must satisfy all three conditions. Hence Option (a) is correct.

Option (b) uses = and != with '%', which compares literally instead of pattern-matching. Option (c) misuses IN, which needs a parenthesised list and does not do pattern matching. Option (d) joins the predicates with OR, so a record matching any single condition is selected, which is not what is required. Option (e) inverts the logic (NOT LIKE on First_Name and LIKE on City).

optionFeedback.html: Correct. This query uses LIKE for both name patterns and NOT LIKE for the city, all combined with AND, so every returned record matches the two name patterns and excludes the city pattern — exactly what is asked.
Incorrect. The = and != operators perform exact literal comparison, so '%A%' is matched as the literal three-character string, not as a wildcard pattern. Pattern matching requires LIKE/NOT LIKE.
Incorrect. IN tests whether a value belongs to a parenthesised list, e.g. IN ('Delhi','Pune'). The syntax IN '%A%' is invalid and IN does not perform wildcard pattern matching at all.

Incorrect. Although it uses LIKE/NOT LIKE correctly, the three predicates are joined with OR. That selects a record if it satisfies any single condition, whereas the question requires all three conditions to hold together.
Incorrect. The logic is reversed: it applies NOT LIKE to First_Name and LIKE to City. The question needs First_Name to match its pattern and City to be excluded, which is the opposite of this query.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q4
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which SQL keyword is used to eliminate duplicate tuples from the result relation?
solution:
Concept

A SELECT query normally returns every row produced by its projection and filtering steps, including repeated rows.

The DISTINCT modifier applies set-style duplicate elimination to the selected result rows; it does not delete rows from the stored table.

Application

  1. Suppose a column contains the values Delhi, Delhi, and Jaipur.

  2. SELECT city FROM centres returns all three rows, so Delhi appears twice.

  3. SELECT DISTINCT city FROM centres compares the projected city values and returns Delhi and Jaipur once each.

Contrast

  • DELETE removes stored rows that satisfy a condition; it is not a modifier for deduplicating a query result.

  • NON DUPLICATE is not a standard SQL keyword.

  • EXISTS tests whether a subquery returns at least one row; it does not collapse repeated result rows.

Result

Therefore, the keyword used to eliminate duplicate tuples from the result relation is DISTINCT.

optionFeedback.html: DELETE is a data-modification statement that removes stored rows satisfying a condition.
DISTINCT is a SELECT modifier that collapses repeated projected rows into one result row.
NON DUPLICATE is not a standard SQL keyword and has no defined query-processing operation.
EXISTS is a predicate that reports whether a subquery returns at least one row.

title: Which SQL clause is used to restrict the rows returned
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which SQL clause is used to restrict the rows returned by a query in Oracle?
solution: The correct answer is Option A: WHERE. In Oracle and standard SQL, the WHERE clause is used to filter and restrict individual rows from a table based on a specified condition before any grouping occurs. Only rows that satisfy the WHERE condition are returned in the final result set.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The WHERE clause applies a conditional filter directly to raw table rows to selectively include or exclude them from the query output.
Incorrect. The GROUP BY clause does not restrict individual rows; instead, it aggregates or groups rows that have the same values into summary rows (e.g., finding totals per department).
Incorrect. While HAVING also restricts data, it filters grouped data or summary rows created by a GROUP BY clause based on aggregate functions, rather than restricting individual raw rows.
Incorrect. The ORDER BY clause is used strictly to sort the returned result set in ascending or descending order; it does not filter or reduce the number of rows returned.

text: Which of the following is not a valid relational operator used with WHERE clause in SQL?
solution: In SQL, the WHERE clause uses relational operators to compare values. The valid operators include: > (greater than), < (less than), >= (greater than or equal to), <= (less than or equal to), = (equal to), and <> (not equal to). The symbol '=>' is not a valid relational operator in standard SQL. It is often confused with '>=', but the correct syntax for 'greater than or equal to' is two characters without an arrow.

optionFeedback.html: The greater-than symbol (>) is a standard relational operator in SQL. It is commonly used in the WHERE clause to filter records where a column value is strictly greater than a specified value.
The less-than-or-equal-to symbol (<=) is a valid relational operator in SQL. It allows filtering data where a column value is less than or equal to a specific threshold.
The symbol '=>' is not a valid relational operator in standard SQL. While it resembles '>=', the correct syntax for greater-than-or-equal-to uses two characters without the arrow.
The not-equal-to symbol (<>) is a valid relational operator in SQL. It is widely used to select records where a column value is different from a specified value.

title: Which of the following statements about the “DELETE” command is
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following statements about the “DELETE” command is FALSE?

options.html: It removes tuples as well as the relation (table).
A missing WHERE clause specifies that all tuples in the relation are to be deleted.
Depending on the number of tuples selected by the condition in the WHERE clause, zero, one or several tuples can be deleted by a single DELETE command.

solution:
Concept

The DELETE command is a Data Manipulation Language (DML) statement. By definition, DML operates on the DATA stored inside a relation (table) — it inserts, updates, or removes tuples (rows) — but it never alters the relation's SCHEMA or definition. Removing the table object itself (its structure and metadata) is the job of a Data Definition Language (DDL) command, namely DROP TABLE.

Applying it to each statement

We are asked for the statement that is FALSE about DELETE. Test each claim against the definition above:

  • "It removes tuples from a relation" — TRUE: removing rows is exactly what DELETE does.

  • "It removes tuples as well as the relation (table)" — FALSE: DELETE only clears the rows; the empty table and its definition remain. Dropping the relation needs DROP TABLE, not DELETE.

  • "A missing WHERE clause deletes all tuples" — TRUE: DELETE FROM t; with no WHERE removes every row, leaving an empty table.

  • "Zero, one, or several tuples may be deleted depending on the WHERE condition" — TRUE: the count of affected rows equals the number of rows matching the WHERE predicate.

Cross-check

Contrast DELETE with the related commands: DELETE removes selected rows (DML, can use a WHERE clause); TRUNCATE removes all rows but keeps the structure; DROP removes the rows AND the structure. Only the claim that DELETE itself removes the relation contradicts this hierarchy, confirming it is the false statement.

optionFeedback.html: The DELETE statement names its target relation in a FROM clause and removes the rows that satisfy any WHERE condition supplied; those rows are the tuples the statement acts on.
A relation's catalog entry — its name, column definitions, and constraints — and the data rows currently held in it are two separate kinds of information stored inside a database.
A DELETE statement's WHERE clause is an optional component; when a statement is written without one, no per-row condition is evaluated during that statement's execution.
A DELETE statement's WHERE clause is evaluated against each row individually at execution time, and the set of rows found to satisfy it becomes the set the statement acts on.

title: In relational database, which term represents missing, unknown, or unavailable
subject: Data Base Management System
text: In a relational database, which term represents a missing, unknown, or unavailable attribute value?
solution:
Concept

In the relational model (defined by E. F. Codd), a NULL is a special marker placed in a column to indicate that an attribute value is missing, unknown, inapplicable, or simply not yet available. It is not a value in the ordinary sense — it represents the absence of any known value.

Application

The question asks for the term that represents a missing, unknown, or unavailable attribute value. That is exactly the definition of a NULL, so "Null value" is the term the relational model uses for an attribute whose value is absent or undetermined.

Why NULL is not the same as "nothing"

A common pitfall is to equate NULL with zero or with an empty string. NULL means "no value recorded"; because it is unknown, any arithmetic or comparison involving NULL yields UNKNOWN (three-valued logic) rather than a definite true/false. By contrast, 0 and an empty string are concrete, known values.

Contrast with the other terms

Term

Why it does not fit

Empty table

A relation that currently holds no rows — describes the whole table being empty, not a single attribute whose value is unknown.

Derived value

A value computed from other stored values (e.g. age from a birth date) — a known, calculated value, not a missing one.

Default value

A predefined value the system substitutes when none is supplied — a definite, known value chosen in advance, the opposite of "unknown".

Zero value

The number 0, a concrete known quantity — storing 0 asserts an actual value, which differs from asserting the value is unknown.

optionFeedback.html: "Empty table" describes a relation that holds no rows at all; it characterises the table as a whole, not an individual attribute whose value is unknown or unavailable. The term being asked for applies at the level of a single attribute value.
A "derived value" is computed from other stored data (for example, total = price × quantity). It is a known, calculated result, so it cannot stand for a value that is missing or unknown.

"Null value" is precisely the relational-model marker for an attribute whose value is missing, unknown, inapplicable, or not yet available — it denotes the absence of a known value, which is what the question describes.
A "default value" is a predefined value the system fills in when none is supplied. It is a definite, known substitute decided in advance — the opposite of an unknown or unavailable value.
"Zero value" is the concrete number 0, a known quantity. Recording 0 asserts an actual value, which is different from indicating that the value is unknown or absent.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2019 — Q10

text: Which Oracle-recommended data type should be used to declare a variable-length character column?
solution:
Concept

A variable-length character datatype stores text up to a declared maximum length while using only the space required by the stored value.

In a database definition, the datatype name and its length limit together specify how the column stores character data.

Application

Oracle documents VARCHAR2(size) as its built-in datatype for variable-length character strings and recommends using VARCHAR2 rather than VARCHAR to avoid possible future semantic changes.

Contrast

  • VARCHAR is currently a synonym of VARCHAR2 in Oracle, but Oracle reserves the right to redefine it with different comparison semantics in a future release.

  • VARCHAR3 is not an Oracle built-in SQL character datatype.

  • VARCHAR2 declares variable-length character data and requires a maximum size, such as name VARCHAR2(100).

  • None of these does not apply because VARCHAR2 is present among the offered values.

Cross-check

The declaration name VARCHAR2(100) allows up to 100 characters or bytes according to the chosen length semantics, which matches the required variable-length column behavior.

Result: The Oracle-recommended datatype is VARCHAR2.

optionFeedback.html: VARCHAR is documented by Oracle as a character-type name whose comparison semantics may change in a future release.
VARCHAR3 has no entry in Oracle's documented set of built-in SQL character datatype names.
Oracle documents the declaration syntax VARCHAR2(size), in which the size parameter supplies the column limit.
None of these is a set-level negation: it excludes the entire offered set rather than naming a datatype.

title: Consider this statement: CREATE TABLE Orders (OrderID INT, OrderDate DATE,
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Consider this statement: CREATE TABLE Orders (OrderID INT, OrderDate DATE, CustomerID INT NOT NULL);. What does the NOT NULL constraint on CustomerID enforce?

options.html: It sets a default value for CustomerID.
It ensures that CustomerID must always have a value.

solution: The NOT NULL constraint in SQL enforces a column to always contain a value. This means you cannot insert a new record or update an existing record without providing a valid, non-null value for the CustomerID column. It prevents missing data in critical fields.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The NOT NULL constraint does not assign values automatically. To set a default fallback value when no data is provided, you must use the DEFAULT constraint (for example: CustomerID INT DEFAULT 0).

Correct. This is the exact purpose of NOT NULL. It is an integrity constraint that prevents NULL (empty/missing) entries from being inserted into this column, ensuring that every record in the table contains a valid value for CustomerID.
Incorrect. It does the exact opposite. By default, SQL columns allow NULL values unless you explicitly restrict them by adding the NOT NULL constraint.

Incorrect. NOT NULL only enforces that a value must exist; it does not care if that value has been used before. If you want to prevent duplicate IDs, you need to use a UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint. Under NOT NULL alone, multiple orders can still share the exact same CustomerID.

title: Roll_no is the primary key of student table, Dept_id is
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Roll_no is the primary key of the Student table, Dept_id is the primary key of the Department table, and Student.Dept_id is a foreign key that refers to Department.Dept_id. What will happen if we try to execute the following two SQL statements?

(i) Update Student set Dept_id = Null where Roll_no = 12;

(ii) Update Department set Dept_id = Null where Dept_id = 12;
solution:
Concept: Two integrity rules decide whether an UPDATE that sets a column to NULL succeeds. The Entity Integrity Rule says a primary-key column can never hold NULL in any row, with no exception. The foreign-key nullability rule says a foreign-key column may hold NULL (meaning "no reference yet") unless that column itself was explicitly declared NOT NULL; standard SQL treats a NULL foreign-key value as trivially satisfying the constraint.

Application:

  1. Student.Dept_id is declared only as a foreign key referencing Department.Dept_id; nothing in the schema description adds a NOT NULL constraint to it. By the foreign-key nullability rule, statement (i), Update Student set Dept_id = Null where Roll_no = 12, is permitted, so it succeeds.

  2. Department.Dept_id is the primary key of Department. By the Entity Integrity Rule, no primary-key column may ever be NULL, regardless of any declaration. Statement (ii), Update Department set Dept_id = Null where Dept_id = 12, is therefore rejected by the database, so it fails.

Cross-check: If Student.Dept_id had instead been declared NOT NULL, statement (i) would fail too — but no such constraint is stated here, so the default nullable foreign key applies. The primary-key prohibition on NULL for Department.Dept_id is unconditional: it does not depend on whether any Student row currently references Dept_id = 12, so statement (ii) fails purely on entity-integrity grounds.

Result: Statement (i) succeeds and statement (ii) fails.

optionFeedback.html: This option pairs a rejected outcome for statement (i) with a rejected outcome for statement (ii): it states that the attempt to set the foreign-key column Student.Dept_id to NULL for Roll_no = 12 is refused, and the attempt to set the primary-key column Department.Dept_id to NULL for Dept_id = 12 is also refused.

This option pairs a rejected outcome for statement (i) with an accepted outcome for statement (ii): it states that the attempt to set the foreign-key column Student.Dept_id to NULL for Roll_no = 12 is refused, while the attempt to set the primary-key column Department.Dept_id to NULL for Dept_id = 12 goes through.

This option pairs an accepted outcome for statement (i) with a rejected outcome for statement (ii): it states that the attempt to set the foreign-key column Student.Dept_id to NULL for Roll_no = 12 goes through, while the attempt to set the primary-key column Department.Dept_id to NULL for Dept_id = 12 is refused.

This option pairs an accepted outcome for statement (i) with an accepted outcome for statement (ii): it states that the attempt to set the foreign-key column Student.Dept_id to NULL for Roll_no = 12 goes through, and the attempt to set the primary-key column Department.Dept_id to NULL for Dept_id = 12 also goes through.

title: Consider two table with relational database Update Student set Dept_id=
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the two tables of a relational database shown above, together with the following SQL statements.

  • S1. UPDATE Student SET Dept_id = NULL WHERE Roll_no = 1;

  • S2. UPDATE Department SET Dept_id = NULL WHERE Dept_id = 1;

Note: Roll_no is the primary key of the Student table, Dept_id is the primary key of the Department table, and Dept_id in the Student table is a foreign key referring to Dept_id in the Department table.

Which of the following is true if we execute the above statements?
solution:
Concept: Entity integrity forbids any part of a primary key from holding NULL — a NULL key value could not identify a row — so a PRIMARY KEY column is implicitly NOT NULL and a DBMS rejects any attempt to store NULL in it. A foreign key carries no such rule: unless the column is separately declared NOT NULL it may hold NULL, and referential integrity is simply not enforced on a NULL reference, because NULL there means "refers to no row at all".

Applying the two rules, statement by statement:

  1. S1 assigns NULL to Student.Dept_id for Roll_no = 1. That column is a foreign key referring to Department.Dept_id, and the schema does not declare it NOT NULL, so NULL is a legal value for it. Once the reference is NULL, no matching Department row is required and the referential-integrity check does not apply, so the row (1, Suresh, 1) simply becomes (1, Suresh, NULL).

  2. S2 assigns NULL to Department.Dept_id for Dept_id = 1. That column is the primary key of Department, so entity integrity forbids the value NULL there and the DBMS rejects the statement before any data is changed.

  3. A second, independent constraint also blocks S2: the Student row with Roll_no = 2 still holds Dept_id = 1, so erasing that key value would leave a dangling reference and violate referential integrity as well.

Cross-check — the two statements side by side:

Statement

Column set to NULL

Role of that column

Outcome and reason

S1

Student.Dept_id

Foreign key referring to Department.Dept_id

Executes — NULL is a legal foreign-key value and referential integrity is not enforced on a NULL reference

S2

Department.Dept_id

Primary key of Department

Fails — entity integrity forbids NULL in a primary key

So the two statements come out differently: S1 executes and S2 fails, which is the outcome pair "S2 will fail, S1 will execute".

Contrast with the other outcome pairs:

  • "Both will execute" would require Department.Dept_id to accept NULL, which entity integrity does not permit.

  • "Both will fail" would require a foreign-key column to be barred from holding NULL, which is true only when that column is explicitly declared NOT NULL — and this schema does not declare it so.

  • "S2 will execute, S1 will fail" swaps the two rules, treating the primary key as nullable and the foreign key as non-nullable.

optionFeedback.html: This pairing asserts that the update to Dept_id in Department, which is the primary key of that table, does not take effect, while the update to Dept_id in Student, which is a foreign key referring to it, does take effect.

This pairing asserts that the update to Dept_id in Department, which is the primary key of that table, does take effect, while the update to Dept_id in Student, which is a foreign key referring to it, does not take effect.

This pairing asserts that neither update takes effect: neither the one to Dept_id in Department, which is the primary key of that table, nor the one to Dept_id in Student, which is a foreign key referring to it.

This pairing asserts that both updates take effect: both the one to Dept_id in Department, which is the primary key of that table, and the one to Dept_id in Student, which is a foreign key referring to it.

solution: The commands used to control access over objects in a relational database are part of the Data Control Language (DCL). The primary DCL commands are GRANT, which assigns privileges to users, and REVOKE, which removes those privileges.

subject: Data Base Management System

solution: DELETE is a DML command that logs row deletions, allowing transactions to be rolled back. In contrast, TRUNCATE is a DDL command that deallocates pages and typically auto-commits, preventing data retrieval via rollback.

TRUNCATE operations typically commit immediately as a DDL command, making data retrieval via rollback impossible. Only DELETE supports transactional recovery of data.
DELETE is a DML command that logs row deletions, allowing transactions to be rolled back. TRUNCATE is a DDL command that deallocates data pages and typically auto-commits, preventing rollback.

title: Which SQL statement is used in embedded SQL to fetch
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which SQL statement is used in embedded SQL to fetch data into host variables?
solution: In embedded SQL, the SELECT INTO statement is used to fetch data from a database and store it directly into host variables. This allows the application to retrieve specific data from a table and use it in the host program. The syntax is: SELECT column1, column2 INTO :host_var1, :host_var2 FROM table_name WHERE condition; The INTO clause specifies the host variables where the retrieved data will be stored. This is essential for retrieving data in a structured way within a host language like C or COBOL.

optionFeedback.html: Step 1: INSERT INTO is used to add new records into a table. Step 2: It does not retrieve data into host variables. Step 3: This statement is for data insertion, not data fetching.
Step 1: UPDATE modifies existing records in a table. Step 2: It does not fetch data into host variables. Step 3: This statement is for updating data, not retrieving it.

title: Which set of SQL language commands is used to query
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which set of SQL language commands is used to query and update a database?

options.html: Both Data Control Language (DCL) and Data Definition Language (DDL)

solution:
SQL statements are grouped into sub-languages by function:

Sub-language

Commands

Operates on

Data Definition Language (DDL)

CREATE, ALTER, DROP

Schema objects — tables, columns, structure

Data Manipulation Language (DML)

SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE

The data rows themselves — read and write

Data Control Language (DCL)

GRANT, REVOKE

User access permissions

Transaction Control Language (TCL)

COMMIT, ROLLBACK

Transactions

Only DML's commands act on the data rows themselves — SELECT reads them (a query) and INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE write them (an update). This question asks for the command set that does BOTH — query the database AND update it.

  • Data Definition Language (DDL) only defines or alters schema objects such as tables and columns — it never reads or writes the data rows stored inside them.

  • Data Control Language (DCL) only manages who may access the database by granting or revoking permission — it never reads or writes data rows itself.

  • Combining DCL and DDL still leaves no command that reads or writes data rows, so that pairing cannot query or update data either.

  • “Question not attempted” is not a command language at all; it simply marks the item as unanswered.

Therefore, the correct set of commands for querying and updating a database is Data Manipulation Language (DML).

optionFeedback.html: DDL commands — CREATE, ALTER, DROP — work at the schema level, shaping tables, columns, and other structural objects.
DCL commands — GRANT, REVOKE — work at the permissions level, governing who may access the database, while DDL commands — CREATE, ALTER, DROP — work at the schema level, shaping tables and columns.
DCL commands — GRANT, REVOKE — work at the permissions level, governing who may access the database.
DML commands — SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE — work at the data level, reading and writing the rows stored inside database tables.
This choice marks the response as unanswered.

title: Includes query language and commands to insert tuples into, delete

solution: Data-manipulation language (DML) provides the functional capability to query data and perform modifications like inserting, deleting, or updating records (tuples) within the table structure. Unlike DDL, which defines the schema, DML interacts directly with the data itself. The correct option is B.

title: Which statement creates new user in ORACLE?
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which statement creates a new user in ORACLE?
solution:
Concept

In Oracle, a user account is created with the CREATE USER statement, and the syntax requires stating how the account will authenticate: CREATE USER username IDENTIFIED { BY password | EXTERNALLY | GLOBALLY }, or — for a schema-only account with no login — NO AUTHENTICATION. Oracle needs one of these: an authentication clause or an explicit NO AUTHENTICATION, so a bare CREATE USER name; that supplies neither is not a complete, valid statement.

Application

  • CREATE USER Susan IDENTIFIED BY blue; — well-formed: it names the user and supplies password authentication via IDENTIFIED BY. This is the standard way to create a local user.

Why the other statements fail

  • CREATE USER Susan; — omits the required IDENTIFIED clause, so Oracle has no authentication method and rejects it.

  • CREATE OR REPLACE USER Susan; — Oracle has no CREATE OR REPLACE form for users (that syntax is for views, procedures, etc.), and it still lacks IDENTIFIED.

  • CREATE NEW USER Susan DEFAULT; — NEW USER and a trailing DEFAULT are not valid Oracle DDL keywords here.

Cross-check

Per the Oracle SQL reference, CREATE USER requires either an IDENTIFIED clause (BY password, EXTERNALLY, or GLOBALLY) or an explicit NO AUTHENTICATION — none of which the other three statements in this question supply. Among the four given, only the one using IDENTIFIED BY blue is syntactically complete and creates an authenticatable local account.

optionFeedback.html: CREATE USER Susan; begins correctly by naming the user, but it stops there and so remains an incomplete account-creation statement that Oracle will not accept as written.
CREATE OR REPLACE USER Susan; borrows the CREATE OR REPLACE pattern used for views and procedures, but Oracle provides no such form for users, so the statement is rejected for an account.
CREATE NEW USER Susan DEFAULT; reads like plain English, but NEW USER is not an Oracle keyword and a trailing bare DEFAULT is not valid syntax, so the statement fails to parse.
CREATE USER Susan IDENTIFIED BY blue; names the user and pairs it with a password via IDENTIFIED BY, which is the complete statement form Oracle uses to create a local account.

title: Under standard DBMS transaction theory used in basic SQL classification,
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Under standard DBMS transaction theory used in basic SQL classification, which of the following commands is generally rollback-able before COMMIT?
solution:
Concept

SQL commands fall into categories that behave differently inside a transaction. DML commands (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) only stage row-level changes, so they remain part of the open transaction and can be undone with ROLLBACK until COMMIT. DDL commands (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) carry an implicit COMMIT in standard SQL, so they finalise immediately and cannot be rolled back. SELECT reads data without changing it, and COMMIT is the act of finalising — neither leaves anything to undo.

Applying it

  1. Classify each command: SELECT is a read (DQL), COMMIT is transaction-control (TCL), CREATE and ALTER are DDL, DELETE is DML.

  2. Apply the transaction rule: only DML changes are held open and reversible before COMMIT.

  3. DELETE is the only DML command among the choices, so it is the command that ROLLBACK can undo before COMMIT.

Cross-check

  • SELECT: returns rows but writes nothing, so there is no change for ROLLBACK to reverse.

  • COMMIT: permanently finalises the transaction; once issued there is no pending work left to undo.

  • CREATE / ALTER: DDL statements trigger an implicit COMMIT in standard SQL, finalising the schema change on execution.

  • DELETE: stages row removals within the transaction, which ROLLBACK restores while the transaction is still open.

optionFeedback.html: SELECT only retrieves rows and makes no change to the data, so there is nothing for ROLLBACK to reverse — it is not a write that a transaction holds open.
COMMIT is the command that finalises a transaction; it ends the unit of work rather than staging a reversible change, so it is not something ROLLBACK can undo.
DELETE is a DML statement: it stages row removals inside the open transaction, and those staged changes are exactly what ROLLBACK restores while the transaction has not yet been committed.
CREATE is a DDL statement, and DDL triggers an implicit COMMIT in standard SQL — the schema change is finalised on execution, leaving nothing pending for ROLLBACK.
ALTER is a DDL statement that carries an implicit COMMIT in standard SQL, so the schema modification takes effect immediately and cannot be held open for ROLLBACK.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q88
subject: Data Base Management System
text: In Oracle SQL authorization, which privilege allows a user to create a table in another user's schema?
solution:
Oracle SQL privilege scope works on two levels: an ordinary privilege (for example, CREATE TABLE) applies only within the grantee's own schema, while the same action prefixed with ANY (for example, CREATE ANY TABLE) extends that action to every schema in the database. Predefined roles such as RESOURCE and DBA are administrative bundles of many such privileges rather than a single named privilege.

The question asks for the one privilege that specifically authorizes creating objects (tables) inside another user's schema. That is CREATE ANY TABLE — its ANY qualifier is exactly what extends table-creation rights beyond the grantee's own schema into any schema in the database.

  • ALTER SYSTEM controls instance-wide configuration parameters; it is unrelated to schema object creation.

  • RESOURCE is a predefined role granting ordinary object-creation privileges (CREATE TABLE, CREATE PROCEDURE, CREATE SEQUENCE, and similar) that apply only to the grantee's own schema — it carries no ANY-schema scope.

  • DBA is a predefined role bundling a very large set of system privileges, including several ANY-scoped ones, for full administrative control; it is a broad role rather than the single targeted privilege.

Oracle's privilege documentation uses the ANY qualifier precisely to denote "in any schema" scope, which is why CREATE ANY TABLE — and not RESOURCE or DBA — is the privilege that fits this question.

optionFeedback.html: CREATE ANY TABLE is granted with the statement GRANT CREATE ANY TABLE TO <username> and is classified as a system privilege, listed in Oracle's DBA_SYS_PRIVS catalog view.

ALTER SYSTEM is granted with the statement GRANT ALTER SYSTEM TO <username> and is classified as a system privilege, listed in Oracle's DBA_SYS_PRIVS catalog view alongside instance-management privileges.
RESOURCE is granted with the statement GRANT RESOURCE TO <username> and is one of Oracle's original predefined roles, listed in the DBA_ROLES catalog view.
DBA is granted with the statement GRANT DBA TO <username> and is Oracle's built-in administrative role, listed in the DBA_ROLES catalog view alongside RESOURCE.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q155
subject: Data Base Management System
text: SQL command used to remove a table from the database is
solution:
SQL commands span several categories — DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL — grouped by what they act on. Two of those categories matter here: Data Definition Language (DDL) commands change the STRUCTURE of a database object — creating, altering, or removing an entire table, view, or index. Data Manipulation Language (DML) commands change only the DATA (rows) stored inside an object that already exists, without touching its structure.

DROP is the DDL command that eliminates a table object completely — its structure, its stored rows, and any indexes or constraints defined on it — from the database, so DROP is the command used to remove a table.

Command

Effect on the table object

DROP

Removes the table object itself — its structure, its stored rows, and the indexes and constraints defined on it — from the schema.

DELETE

Removes only the rows chosen by an optional WHERE clause; the table object, with its column definitions and constraints, stays in the schema.

TRUNCATE

Empties every row in one bulk operation; the table’s columns, indexes and constraints remain defined.

REMOVE

Not a keyword defined by the SQL standard, so no database engine executes a ‘REMOVE TABLE’ command.

This can be cross-checked by the effect on a later query: after DROP TABLE, querying that table name fails because the object no longer exists in the schema; after an unqualified DELETE (no WHERE clause) or after TRUNCATE, the same query still succeeds and returns zero rows, because the table itself still exists — only its rows are gone. Only DROP removes the table, confirming it as the correct command.

optionFeedback.html: DELETE is a Data Manipulation Language statement that acts on the rows held inside a table: an optional WHERE clause chooses which rows go, each removal is written to the transaction log, and the table's column definitions, indexes and constraints stay registered in the schema afterwards.

DROP is a Data Definition Language statement that acts on a whole schema object such as a table, view or index: the object's definition, the data it holds and the indexes and constraints built on it all cease to exist, and its name is deleted from the data dictionary.

TRUNCATE is a Data Definition Language statement that clears a table's stored rows in one bulk operation by deallocating its data pages instead of logging each row removal, and the emptied table stays defined, with its columns, indexes and constraints still in place.

REMOVE belongs to file-system and programming-API vocabularies rather than to the statement keywords defined by the SQL standard, so a relational engine's parser raises a syntax error on a statement that begins with it.

solution:
Concept

A data-manipulation command changes the contents of rows, whereas a data-definition command changes the structure of a table.

In SQL, UPDATE is the statement for assigning new values to columns of existing rows. Its core form is UPDATE table_name SET column_name = value, with an optional WHERE condition.

Apply the command definition to this item:

  1. Identify the target operation: values in rows already stored in a table must change.

  2. Choose the SQL data-manipulation statement designed for that operation: UPDATE.

  3. Use SET to specify the new column value and WHERE to limit the affected rows, for example: UPDATE employees SET salary = 50000 WHERE id = 7.

Contrast

  • MODIFY is a general verb and also appears in some vendor-specific schema-alteration syntax; it is not the data-manipulation statement required here.

  • NEW describes a prospective value or row image in some database contexts; it does not perform the operation.

  • UPDATE is the SQL data-manipulation statement that assigns new values to columns of existing rows.

Cross-check

The PostgreSQL command reference defines UPDATE as changing specified column values in rows that satisfy a condition, which matches the operation in the stem.

Result

Therefore, the required command is UPDATE.

title: What happens if you execute DROP DATABASE sales_db; while users
subject: Data Base Management System
text: What happens if you execute DROP DATABASE sales_db; while users are connected to the database?

options.html: The database is dropped, and all users are automatically disconnected.
Only tables are dropped; the database structure remains.
SQL prevents the drop until all connections are terminated.

solution: When you execute DROP DATABASE sales_db; while users are actively connected, the database engine explicitly blocks the command and raises an error. Relational database management systems treat active client sessions as open states that could be performing read or write operations. To prevent sudden application failures, data corruption, or broken transactions, the system holds a lock on the database and mandates that all active connections must be cleared out before a destructive schema change can happen.

optionFeedback.html: Most standard relational database engines (like PostgreSQL or SQL Server) will not automatically boot active users off the system just because someone issued a drop command. Doing so could cause sudden application crashes and uncommitted data corruption.

The DROP DATABASE command is an all-or-nothing statement. Its explicit job is to completely delete the entire catalog, schemas, files, and physical directories associated with that database. It never leaves a partial empty shell behind.

This is the standard safety behavior. When a drop command is executed, the database management system (DBMS) checks its internal connection pools. If any active user sessions or application background threads are still attached to that specific database, the system halts the operation and throws an error.

SQL database management systems do not fail silently. If a command cannot be completed due to active sessions, the engine will explicitly reject the query and return a diagnostic error message, such as "database is being accessed by other users."

title: ‘AS’ clause is used in SQL for
subject: Data Base Management System
text: ‘AS’ clause is used in SQL for
solution:
Answer: The AS clause assigns an alias (a temporary name) to a column or table.

Key points:

  • Column alias: gives a new name to a column in the query result. Example: SELECT ENO AS EMPLOYEE_NO FROM EMP;

  • Table alias: gives a short name to a table (useful in joins). Example: SELECT e.ENO FROM EMP AS e;

  • AS is often optional in many SQL dialects, so aliases can sometimes be written without AS (e.g., SELECT ENO EMPLOYEE_NO FROM EMP or SELECT e.ENO FROM EMP e).

Clarification: AS performs renaming (aliasing). It does not perform selection, join, or projection operations themselves, though it is commonly used alongside those operations to make results clearer.

The output of the above query will be ?
solution:
Concept: COUNT(*) counts every row of the result set regardless of NULL values in any column, because it counts rows, not a column's values. COUNT(column-expr) and AVG(column-expr), by contrast, are evaluated only over the rows where that expression is NOT NULL — a NULL value in the named column is skipped both from the count and from the sum used inside AVG. This NULL-skipping behavior applies to every aggregate function except COUNT(*).

Step-by-step computation: Apply the rule above to each aggregate over the 7 rows of R.

  1. COUNT(*) = 7 — all 7 rows of R are counted, since COUNT(*) does not look at any column's value.

  2. COUNT(x) = 4 — only the rows where x is NOT NULL are counted: x = 2, 2, 4, 4 (four rows); the three rows with x = NULL are skipped.

  3. COUNT(y) = 2 — only the rows where y is NOT NULL are counted: y = 4, 4 (two rows); the five rows with y = NULL are skipped.

title: Which SQL feature allows calculations to be performed across group
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which SQL feature allows calculations to be performed across a group of related rows while still returning each individual row separately, typically using the PARTITION BY clause?
solution:
The correct answer is Window Function.

A window function performs a calculation across a set of rows that are related to the current row — called a "window" — without collapsing those rows into a single output row. It is written with the OVER clause, and the optional PARTITION BY clause divides the rows into groups (partitions) over which the calculation is applied independently. For example: SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) returns, on every employee row, the total salary of that employee's department, while still listing each employee separately.

This is exactly what distinguishes a window function from a GROUP BY aggregate. GROUP BY collapses each group into one summary row and discards the individual rows, so per-row detail (like an employee's name or id) is lost. A window function keeps every original row and simply attaches the group-level value alongside it.

Why the other options are wrong: a nested query (subquery) only composes one query inside another; a trigger is a procedure auto-fired on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE; a scalar function returns one value per row in isolation and cannot span a partition; and "Aggregate Constraint" is not a real SQL feature. None of these provide the PARTITION BY, per-row-preserving behaviour the question describes.

optionFeedback.html: A nested query (subquery) is a query placed inside another query, used to feed a value or a set of values to the outer query. It is a query-composition technique, not a row-level calculation feature, and it has no PARTITION BY clause.

A trigger is a stored procedure that the database automatically executes in response to a data-modification event (INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE) on a table. It enforces rules or audits changes; it does not compute running totals or rankings across a set of rows in a SELECT.

A scalar function (such as UPPER, ROUND or ABS) takes one or more inputs and returns a single value for each individual row in isolation. It cannot look across a group of related rows or use a PARTITION BY clause.

"Aggregate Constraint" is not a standard SQL feature. SQL constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK, NOT NULL) restrict the data a column may hold; they do not perform calculations across rows in a query.

Correct. A window function uses the OVER clause (commonly with PARTITION BY) to compute a value across a window of related rows while still returning every individual row separately — exactly the behaviour described in the question.

solution:
The INSTR() string function (in MySQL, Oracle, and similar SQL implementations) returns the position of the first occurrence of a substring within a string.

SQL strings are 1-indexed: the first character is at position 1 (not 0), so the default starting index returned for a match at the very beginning of the string is 1. By default the search begins at the first character. In MySQL, INSTR() takes only two arguments (the string and the substring) and has no start_position parameter; Oracle's INSTR() additionally accepts an optional start_position argument, which itself defaults to 1.

When the substring is not present in the target string, INSTR() returns 0 (zero). It does not return -1 (a 0-based convention used by some programming languages) or NULL (NULL is returned only when an argument itself is NULL).

Therefore the correct answer is: starts from 1, and returns 0 if the substring is not found.

title: Which of the following is an aggregate function in SQL?
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following is an aggregate function in SQL?
solution:
Concept

In SQL, an aggregate function takes a set (column) of values across many rows and collapses it into a single summary value. Common aggregates are AVG, SUM, COUNT, MIN and MAX. They differ from scalar functions, which operate on one value (per row) and return one value per row.

Applying it here

Examine what each function does and whether it summarises many rows into one value:

  • AVG() takes a column of numeric values across rows and returns their single arithmetic mean, so it is an aggregate function.

  • CONCAT() joins two or more strings within a single row and returns one string per row.

  • SUBSTRING() extracts a portion of one string and returns one string per row.

  • LENGTH() returns the character count of one string, one value per row.

  • NOW() returns the current date and time and is unrelated to summarising rows.

Conclusion

Only AVG() consumes a group of rows and produces a single aggregated result, so AVG() is the aggregate function.

optionFeedback.html: CONCAT() is a scalar string function: it joins two or more strings within one row and returns a value for each row rather than summarising a group of rows.
AVG() operates over a whole column of values across rows and returns their single arithmetic mean, which is exactly the behaviour of an aggregate function.
SUBSTRING() is a scalar string function: it extracts part of a single string per row, so it processes one value at a time instead of collapsing many rows.
LENGTH() is a scalar string function: it returns the character count of one string per row, producing a result per row rather than one summary over many rows.
NOW() is a scalar date/time function: it returns the current timestamp and does not take a set of rows or reduce them to a single summary value.

title: Consider the following relational schema: Suppliers (sid:integer, sname:string, saddress:string) Parts

text:
Consider the following relational schema: 

Suppliers (sid:integer, sname:string, saddress:string)
 Parts (pid:integer, pname:string, pcolor:string)
