What is the result of the following query? 

(SELECT Catalog.pid from Suppliers, Catalog
WHERE Suppliers.sid = Catalog.sid)
 MINUS
(SELECT Catalog.pid from Suppliers, Catalog
WHERE Suppliers.sname <> 'sachin' and Suppliers.sid = Catalog.sid)

options.html: pid of Parts supplied by all except sachin
pid of Parts supplied only by sachin
pid of Parts available in catalog supplied by sachin
pid of Parts available in catalogs supplied by all except sachin

solution:
MINUS (also called EXCEPT) is a set-difference operator: for two same-shaped queries A and B, 'A MINUS B' keeps only the rows of A that do not also appear in B. A common exam pattern built on this is the 'associated with X only' query: if A = every value linked to ANY entity, and B = every value linked to at least one entity OTHER than X, then 'A MINUS B' is exactly the set of values whose ONLY linked entity is X.

  1. The first subquery -- SELECT Catalog.pid FROM Suppliers, Catalog WHERE Suppliers.sid = Catalog.sid -- joins every Catalog row to its supplier and projects pid, so it returns every pid that is supplied by some supplier (the full set of parts present in the catalog). (Note: the originally printed query compared Suppliers.sid to Catalog.pid, a transcription slip; the join condition here is corrected to Suppliers.sid = Catalog.sid so the two tables are actually linked by supplier id.)

  2. The second subquery -- SELECT Catalog.pid FROM Suppliers, Catalog WHERE Suppliers.sname <> 'sachin' AND Suppliers.sid = Catalog.sid -- returns every pid that has at least one catalog row whose supplier is NOT named 'sachin', i.e. parts with at least one non-sachin supplier.

  3. MINUS removes every pid found in the second subquery from the first subquery's result, so any part with even one non-sachin supplier is dropped.

  4. What survives is the set of pids that (a) are supplied by someone, because they came from the first subquery, and (b) have no non-sachin supplier at all -- the only way both hold is when 'sachin' is the sole supplier of that part.

Quick check with sample data: suppose sachin supplies parts 10 and 20, and another supplier, ravi, supplies parts 20 and 30. The first subquery returns {10, 20, 30}; the second (non-sachin suppliers) returns {20, 30}, since ravi supplies both. MINUS gives {10} -- part 20 is excluded because ravi also supplies it, leaving only the part that sachin alone supplies.

optionFeedback.html: This is exactly the second subquery's own result -- every part with at least one supplier other than 'sachin' -- which is the set the MINUS operation removes, not the set that remains afterward.

Every value here comes from the first subquery, so it is supplied by someone, and it survives the subtraction only when no non-sachin supplier ever carries it -- both conditions hold precisely when 'sachin' is that part's sole supplier.

This only requires 'sachin' to be one of the suppliers; it does not account for the MINUS step, which drops any part that also has a non-sachin supplier, so a part 'sachin' shares with someone else would not survive here.
This restates the second subquery's own output -- parts with any non-sachin supplier -- rather than what is left once that set is subtracted from the first subquery.

student(rollno, name, address)
enroll(rollno, course no, course name)
where the primary keys are shown underlined. The number of tuples in student and enroll are 100 and 50 respectively. What is the maximum and minimum number of tuples that can be present in (student ⋈ enroll), where ⋈ denotes natural join?
solution:
Concept

A natural join R ⋈ S pairs each tuple of R with each tuple of S that agree on their shared attribute. Two facts fix the size of the result. First, how that attribute behaves as a key: if it is a primary key in BOTH relations it is unique on each side, so the match is at most one-to-one and the result can never exceed the smaller relation. Second, whether a referential-integrity (foreign-key) constraint guarantees that every value on the referencing side also exists on the referenced side; when it does, every referencing tuple is guaranteed to find its one match.

Application to this schema

The only shared attribute is rollno — student’s "name" and enroll’s "course name" are different attributes, so they are not join columns. rollno is the primary key of student (100 distinct values) and the primary key of enroll (50 distinct values). In this students database enroll.rollno is a foreign key that refers to student.rollno: a roll number can be enrolled only if that student already exists (referential integrity). This is the assumption the standard answer to this classic GATE problem uses.

  1. rollno is unique in student, so each enroll tuple matches at most one student tuple — the join is one-to-one.

  2. By referential integrity every one of the 50 enroll rollno values is guaranteed to occur in student, so each enroll tuple matches exactly one student tuple.

  3. Each enroll tuple therefore contributes exactly one result tuple, and students that have no enrollment add nothing, so the join contains exactly 50 tuples.

Because the count is pinned to exactly 50, the maximum and the minimum coincide: maximum = 50 and minimum = 50. The single value to enter is 50.

Cross-check / contrast

Upper bound: the result cannot exceed min(100, 50) = 50, because rollno is a key on both sides (one-to-one matching). Lower bound: referential integrity forces every enroll tuple to have a parent in student, so the count cannot fall below 50. Both bounds meet at 50, so the answer is fixed. Note on the variant: if one does NOT assume the foreign-key/referential-integrity link — treating the two rollno columns as unrelated — the enroll roll numbers could all be absent from student and the minimum would drop to 0. The standard/official answer to this problem assumes the natural student→enroll referential integrity, giving minimum = maximum = 50, which is why the single NAT answer is 50.

title: Consider the following statements: Natural join outputs all pairs of
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following statements:

S1: Natural join outputs all pairs of rows from the two input relations.

S2: Cartesian product outputs pairs of rows from the two input relations that have the same value on all attributes that have the same name.

Which of the following is CORRECT?

options.html: S1 is true but S2 is false
S1 is false but S2 is true

solution:
Concept

For relations R and S, the Cartesian product R × S contains every ordered pair formed by taking one tuple from R and one tuple from S. A natural join instead keeps only tuple pairs that agree on every common-named attribute, and then merges the duplicate join columns.

Application

  1. Evaluate S1: saying that a natural join returns all row pairs describes a Cartesian product, not a natural join. Therefore S1 is false.

  2. Evaluate S2: equality on all common-named attributes is the matching condition used by a natural join. A Cartesian product applies no such condition, so S2 is false.

  3. The truth-value pair for (S1, S2) is therefore (false, false).

Cross-check

If the relations have common-named attributes, a natural join is a filtered form of the Cartesian product; only when there are no common attributes do the two coincide. Thus the two statements have exchanged the operators’ definitions.

Contrast

  • The response “S1 is true but S2 is false” assigns the Cartesian-product behavior to the natural join.

  • The response “both S1 and S2 are true” treats both exchanged definitions as valid.

  • The response “S1 is false but S2 is true” assigns the natural-join matching condition to the Cartesian product.

Result: both S1 and S2 are false.

optionFeedback.html: This response gives the truth-value pair (false, false).
This response gives the truth-value pair (true, false).
This response gives the truth-value pair (true, true).
This response gives the truth-value pair (false, true).

title: The 'command' used to change contents of one database using
subject: Data Base Management System
text: The 'command' used to change contents of one database using the contents of another database by linking them on a common key field?
solution:
In relational database terminology, JOIN and UPDATE name two distinct kinds of operations. A JOIN is a query/retrieval operation: it combines rows from two or more tables using a common attribute (key) field so a record in one table can be matched against and read alongside the related record in another table, but it does not by itself persist any change to stored data. An UPDATE is a data-modification (DML) command: it writes new values into a table's existing rows, and in several database systems (e.g. the classic xBase/FoxPro UPDATE command) those new values can be sourced from a second table matched on a common key field - which does persist a cross-table change.

This question's phrasing - 'the command used to change contents of one database using the contents of another ... by linking them on a common key field' - literally describes a write operation driven by a cross-table match, which is the closest technical fit to the UPDATE definition above (JOIN alone never writes/changes stored contents). Even so, this is an ISRO 2009 Computer Science PYQ, and two independent, question-specific solved-paper sources that name this exact numbered question with these exact four options (cracku.in, edurev.in) report the intended/circulated answer as 'Join', which is why this record keeps option 'Join' as the key. No authentic official ISRO answer-key document could be located to settle the dispute beyond doubt, and the question's own wording is imprecise - it also conflates 'database' with 'table' (a JOIN or UPDATE ordinarily operates across tables within one database, not across two separate databases).

  • Replace overwrites a value already stored in a single table; it names no mechanism for matching records across two tables.

  • Change is an informal, generic word, not a defined database command.

  • Update modifies values already stored in a table and, in several systems, can source those values from a second table matched on a common key field - the closest literal match to this question's own wording, though it is not the option this PYQ's reported key selects.

Per the reported ISRO 2009 answer for this exact question, 'Join' is kept as the correct option here; readers should note the genuine, source-documented ambiguity around whether 'Update' better fits the stem's literal wording.

optionFeedback.html: Replace refers to overwriting a value already stored in place with a new one; it is a general term, not a specific relational-database command with a defined cross-table mechanism.
Join is the relational-algebra/SQL term for a data-retrieval query operation; it belongs to the read/retrieval family of database operations, distinct from commands that write or persist new values.
Change is an informal, generic English word rather than a specific database command; it names no defined retrieval or write mechanism.
Update is the term for a data-modification command; it belongs to the write/persistence family of database operations, distinct from a pure data-retrieval query.

title: Consider the following SQL query Select distinct an from rm
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following SQL query

Select distinct a1, a2, …, an

from r1, r2, …, rm

where P

For an arbitrary predicate P, this query is equivalent to which of the following relational algebra expressions?
solution:
Key idea: translate the SQL clauses into relational-algebra operators: FROM → Cartesian product, WHERE → selection, SELECT DISTINCT → projection that removes duplicates.

Canonical equivalent relational-algebra expression:

π_{a1,a2,…,an}(σ_P(r1 × r2 × … × rm))

  • FROM r1, r2, …, rm corresponds to the Cartesian product r1 × r2 × … × rm.

  • WHERE P is the selection σ_P applied to that Cartesian product.

  • SELECT DISTINCT a1,a2,…,an is the projection π_{a1,a2,…,an}, which removes duplicate tuples in relational algebra.

Note: Although you can sometimes rewrite the selection and cross product into join operators for optimization (when P contains join-equality conditions), the direct and canonical translation of the given SQL is the selection over the Cartesian product followed by projection as shown above.

optionFeedback.html: This is correct. The FROM clause listing multiple relations produces a Cartesian product of the relations, the WHERE clause is a selection applied to that product, and SELECT DISTINCT corresponds to a projection that removes duplicate tuples. Together: project the selected attributes from the selection over the cross product.

This is not generally equivalent. The join operator implies combining relations according to explicit join conditions; the SQL form with multiple relations and a WHERE predicate is formally a selection over a Cartesian product. Only if the WHERE predicate is decomposed into join conditions would a join-based expression be equivalent, but the canonical translation is selection over the cross product.

This is incorrect. Union combines rows from separate relations with the same schema; the original query lists relations in the FROM clause (meaning their Cartesian product), not a union of them. The WHERE and SELECT DISTINCT semantics do not make the query a union.

This is incorrect. Intersection returns tuples present in all relations; the SQL query with multiple relations in FROM means tuples are formed from all relations (Cartesian product) and then filtered by the WHERE predicate, not intersected across relations.

title: Which SQL join returns all rows from both tables, with
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which SQL join returns all rows from both tables, with NULL values for non-matching rows ?
solution: The correct answer is FULL OUTER JOIN. This join type combines the results of both a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN, ensuring that every row from both tables is included in the final result set. When there is no matching record between the two tables based on the join condition, the database fills the missing columns with NULL values. This distinguishes it from INNER JOIN, which only returns rows where matches exist in both tables, and LEFT or RIGHT JOINs, which preserve all rows from only one specific table while discarding non-matching rows from the other. Therefore, to retrieve all data from both sides regardless of matches, FULL OUTER JOIN is the precise tool required.

optionFeedback.html: INNER JOIN returns only rows with matching values in both tables.
A LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table but only matching ones from the right. Consider if a join type exists that includes all rows from both tables regardless of matches.
RIGHT JOIN returns all rows from the right table and matching rows from the left, not both tables. Check if your query needs to include non-matching rows from both sides instead.
The correct answer is FULL OUTER JOIN. This join type combines the results of both a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN, ensuring that every row from both tables is included in the final result set.

title: Which type of SQL JOIN automatically matches rows from two
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which type of SQL JOIN automatically matches rows from two tables using columns that have the same name in both tables?
solution:
The correct answer is Natural Join.

A NATURAL JOIN automatically joins two tables on every column that has the same name (and a compatible data type) in both tables, without you writing an ON or USING clause. The database itself discovers the common column(s) at run time, matches rows where those columns are equal, and shows each shared column only once in the result. By default it behaves like an inner join, so only matching rows are returned.

For example, if EMPLOYEE and DEPARTMENT both contain a column named DEPT_ID, then EMPLOYEE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT matches rows wherever the DEPT_ID values are equal, with no explicit join condition.

The other joins all need an explicit condition or behave differently: an INNER JOIN requires an ON/USING clause to state the matching columns; a CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product (every row paired with every row) and matches nothing; a SELF JOIN joins a table to itself; and a LEFT JOIN is an outer join that keeps all rows of the left table and still needs an explicit condition.

optionFeedback.html: An INNER JOIN does not auto-detect same-name columns. You must spell out the matching condition with an ON clause (or list the columns in a USING clause); without that condition it cannot decide which columns to match.
A CROSS JOIN matches nothing on column values. It returns the Cartesian product, pairing every row of the first table with every row of the second, so no same-name column matching is involved.

A SELF JOIN joins one table to itself (usually using table aliases) to relate rows within the same table. It is about joining a table with a copy of itself, not about auto-matching same-name columns across two different tables.

Correct. A NATURAL JOIN automatically matches rows on every column that shares the same name (and a compatible type) in both tables, with no ON or USING clause, and shows each shared column only once.

A LEFT JOIN is an outer join that returns all rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right (filling NULLs where there is no match). It still requires an explicit join condition and does not discover same-name columns by itself.

title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - June 2009 - source row 22
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following join operations does ORACLE support?

options.html: inner join, outer join and semi join only
inner join, outer join, semi join and anti join

solution:
Concept: A relational join is classified by which rows survive the match. An inner join keeps only matched rows. An outer join (LEFT/RIGHT/FULL) additionally keeps unmatched rows from one or both sides. A semi join and an anti join are existence-based joins that never pull in columns from the second table: a semi join returns each first-table row once when a match exists elsewhere (the EXISTS/IN pattern), and an anti join returns each first-table row when NO match exists elsewhere (the NOT EXISTS/NOT IN pattern).

Application: Oracle's SQL engine implements all four categories. Inner joins and one-sided (LEFT/RIGHT) outer joins have been available since Oracle's earliest SQL releases through Oracle's own equijoin and "(+)" outer-join syntax; a FULL outer join needed a UNION-based workaround until ANSI-standard JOIN keywords -- including native FULL OUTER JOIN -- arrived in Oracle 9i. Semi joins and anti joins are not written with a dedicated JOIN keyword; instead Oracle's optimizer can recognise an eligible EXISTS/IN subquery as a semi join and an eligible NOT EXISTS/NOT IN subquery as an anti join, executing them as such -- visible in an execution plan as operations like HASH JOIN SEMI and HASH JOIN ANTI. This optimizer-level support for semi and anti joins has been present since Oracle 8, well before this question was set, alongside Oracle's long-standing inner/outer join support.

Cross-check (contrast every listed option by its own value):

  • inner join and outer join only -- accurate about those two categories, but omits semi and anti joins, which Oracle also implements at the optimizer level.

  • outer join and semi join only -- accurate about those two, but omits inner join (Oracle's most basic join type) and anti join.

  • inner join, outer join and semi join only -- covers three of the four categories Oracle implements, leaving out anti join.

  • inner join, outer join, semi join and anti join -- names all four categories that Oracle's SQL engine and optimizer implement, with none omitted and nothing added beyond what Oracle supports.

Result: Oracle supports inner joins, outer joins, semi joins, and anti joins, so the option naming all four -- inner join, outer join, semi join and anti join -- is correct (per Oracle SQL Language Reference on joins and subquery-driven semi/anti-join execution plans).

optionFeedback.html:
An inner join returns only the rows that satisfy the join condition between the two tables, discarding any row on either side that has no matching row on the other side.

An outer join extends this by additionally keeping the unmatched rows from one side (LEFT/RIGHT outer join) or from both sides (FULL outer join), filling the missing columns with NULLs.

An outer join keeps the unmatched rows from one or both sides of a join (LEFT/RIGHT/FULL), filling the missing columns with NULLs, unlike a join that discards unmatched rows.

A semi join returns each qualifying row of the first (outer) table only once when at least one matching row exists in a second table, without pulling in any column from that second table -- the pattern Oracle recognises from an EXISTS or IN subquery.

An inner join keeps only rows with a match on both sides of the join condition.

An outer join additionally preserves unmatched rows from one or both sides, padding missing columns with NULLs.

A semi join returns each qualifying outer-table row once when a match exists in a second table, without duplicating it for multiple matches -- the pattern behind an EXISTS or IN subquery.

An inner join keeps only matched rows.

An outer join preserves unmatched rows from one or both sides with NULL padding.

A semi join returns each outer-table row once when a match exists elsewhere, without duplication -- the EXISTS/IN pattern.

An anti join returns each outer-table row that has NO matching row elsewhere -- the pattern behind a NOT EXISTS or NOT IN subquery.

title: Given table Students with columns StudentID, Name, Age, Score, which
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Given a table Students with columns StudentID, Name, Age, Score, which of the following SQL queries will return the highest score for each age group?

options.html: SELECT Age, MAX(Score) FROM Students GROUP BY Age;
SELECT Age, Score FROM Students GROUP BY Age;
SELECT Age, Score FROM Students WHERE Score = (SELECT MAX(Score) FROM Students GROUP BY Age);

solution:
The query SELECT Age, MAX(Score) FROM Students GROUP BY Age; correctly returns the highest score for each age group.

Why this works: GROUP BY groups rows by age, and MAX(Score) computes the highest score inside each group. Every non-aggregated column in the SELECT must appear in the GROUP BY.

  • The query "SELECT Age, Score FROM Students GROUP BY Age;" is invalid under standard SQL because Score is neither aggregated nor grouped. Some databases may return an arbitrary Score per group when nonstandard grouping is allowed, but that result is not reliable.

  • The query "SELECT Age, MAX(Score) FROM Students;" is missing GROUP BY Age. Without GROUP BY, MAX(Score) would be computed over the whole table (or produce an error), not per age, so it does not return the maximum per age.

  • The query that uses a subquery: "SELECT Age, Score FROM Students WHERE Score = (SELECT MAX(Score) FROM Students GROUP BY Age);" is incorrect because the inner subquery returns multiple values (one max per age) and is not correlated to the outer row. Comparing to a multirow subquery with '=' is invalid.

If you prefer a subquery approach, use a correlated subquery that finds the maximum for the same age, for example:

SELECT Age, Score FROM Students s WHERE Score = (SELECT MAX(s2.Score) FROM Students s2 WHERE s2.Age = s.Age);

This returns the student(s) in each age group whose Score equals the maximum for that age (ties will return multiple students).

optionFeedback.html: This query is correct. GROUP BY Age groups the rows by age, and MAX(Score) computes the highest score within each age group. The result returns one row per age with that age and its highest score.

This query is invalid in standard SQL because Score is neither aggregated nor listed in GROUP BY. Databases that enforce the SQL standard will raise an error. Some MySQL configurations that relax grouping rules may return an arbitrary Score per group, which is unreliable. To fix this, use an aggregate such as MAX(Score) or include Score in GROUP BY if you intend different semantics.

This query uses MAX(Score) but lacks GROUP BY Age. In standard SQL this will either raise an error because Age is not aggregated, or, if accepted by a permissive engine, it will compute a single MAX across the entire table and Age will be ambiguous. This does not return the maximum per age. To get per-age maxima you must include GROUP BY Age.

The subquery SELECT MAX(Score) FROM Students GROUP BY Age returns multiple values (one maximum per age), so using Score = (that subquery) is invalid because the subquery must return a single scalar for equality. To get the highest score per age with a subquery, use a correlated subquery that finds the maximum for the same age, for example: SELECT Age, Score FROM Students s WHERE Score = (SELECT MAX(s2.Score) FROM Students s2 WHERE s2.Age = s.Age); Note this can return multiple rows per age if several students are tied for the top score.

Correct. HAVING can be used without GROUP BY; in that case all selected rows are treated as a single group.
Incorrect. Degree means the number of attributes or columns in a relation, not the number of tuples.
Incorrect. LIKE '_____%' matches strings with at least five characters because % can match additional characters.

title: Consider the following query SELECT E.eno, COUNT(*) FROM Employees GROUP
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following query:

SELECT E.eno, COUNT(*)
FROM Employees E
GROUP BY E.eno

If an index on eno is available, the query can be answered by scanning only the index if:

options.html: the index is only hash and clustered
the index is only B+tree and clustered
index can be hash or B+ tree and clustered or non-clustered
index can be hash or B+ tree and clustered

solution:
CONCEPT: An index-only scan (a covering-index scan) lets the database engine answer a query purely from an index's own entries, without visiting the base-table rows. This is possible exactly when every column the query needs is already present in the index's key/leaf entries - a condition that depends only on WHICH COLUMNS the index carries, not on the index's internal storage structure (hash vs. B+ tree) or its physical organization (clustered vs. non-clustered), since both are just different ways of storing the same key values.

APPLICATION: Apply this to the query above.

  1. The query selects only two things: E.eno (the grouping column) and COUNT(*) (a count of rows per group).

  2. COUNT(*) needs no column value at all - it only needs to know how many rows fall in each eno group.

  3. So the only data the engine must be able to read is the eno values themselves, and those are exactly the key values stored in any index built on eno.

  4. A B+-tree index stores sorted eno entries; a hash index stores eno entries by hash bucket - either structure lets the engine enumerate every eno value and tally a count per value, so the structure type does not matter here.

  5. Whether that index is clustered (leaf pages hold the actual table rows, ordered by eno) or non-clustered (a separate structure that only holds eno values and pointers) also makes no difference, because the query never needs any column beyond eno - so the engine never needs to follow a pointer back into the base table.

CROSS-CHECK: Consider what would force a base-table lookup instead - if the query needed some other column of Employees (for example E.salary) that is not part of the eno index, then no matter the index's type or organization, the engine would have to dereference into the heap to fetch it. Since this query needs nothing beyond eno and a row count, that situation never arises here, confirming the index alone suffices under any hash/B+-tree, clustered/non-clustered combination.

Result: The condition does not depend on index type or organization, so the query can be answered by scanning only the index whenever index can be hash or B+ tree and clustered or non-clustered.

Look again at only what E.eno and COUNT(*) actually require from the index, rather than assuming a particular implementation is necessary.

An index-only (covering-index) scan needs only the columns this query actually touches: eno for grouping, and a row count for COUNT(*) - no other column value is required. Since a row count needs no column value at all, every index built on eno already carries everything the engine needs, independent of whether that index is stored as a B+ tree or a hash structure, and independent of whether it is clustered or non-clustered.

title: In SQL, which clause is used to filter groups created
subject: Data Base Management System
text: In SQL, which clause is used to filter groups created by GROUP BY ?
solution: In SQL, the HAVING clause is used to filter groups created by GROUP BY. The WHERE clause filters individual rows before grouping occurs, whereas HAVING operates on the aggregated groups.

optionFeedback.html: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping occurs.
To filter aggregated results after GROUP BY, you must use HAVING instead.
ORDER BY sorts results rather than filtering groups. Check if the clause applies to individual rows or aggregated group data before selecting.

The FILTER clause is not used to filter groups in SQL. Instead, the HAVING clause filters aggregated results after grouping. Check if you confused FILTER with WHERE or HAVING clauses in your query logic.

title: Which SQL clause filters records after grouping
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which SQL clause filters records after grouping ?
solution: The HAVING clause filters records after grouping, unlike WHERE which filters before.

optionFeedback.html: The WHERE clause filters individual rows before any grouping occurs. To filter after grouping, you should use the HAVING clause instead.
ORDER BY sorts results and does not filter grouped data.
The GROUP BY clause organizes rows into groups but does not filter them.
The HAVING clause filters records after grouping.

title: What is the primary purpose of the GROUP BY clause
subject: Data Base Management System
text: What is the primary purpose of the GROUP BY clause in SQL?

options.html: To sort rows in ascending or descending order
To group rows with identical values in specified columns for aggregate processing
To permanently remove duplicate rows from a table

solution:
The GROUP BY clause groups rows that share the same values in one or more specified columns into summary groups, so that aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX can be applied to each group separately rather than to the entire result set.

For example, the query below returns one row per department together with the number of employees in that department:

SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS employee_count FROM employees GROUP BY department;

Here the rows are collapsed into one group per distinct department value, and COUNT(*) is computed per group. This is the defining purpose of GROUP BY, which is why option B is correct.

The other choices describe different SQL features: ORDER BY sorts the result set, the DISTINCT keyword removes duplicate rows from output, the WHERE clause filters individual rows before grouping, and JOIN combines rows from multiple tables — none of these is what GROUP BY does.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Sorting the result set in ascending or descending order is the job of the ORDER BY clause, not GROUP BY. GROUP BY collapses rows into groups; it does not order the output (and grouped output is not guaranteed to be sorted).

Correct. GROUP BY collects rows that have identical values in the specified column(s) into a single group, allowing aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) to be computed per group. This is exactly the clause's defining purpose.

Incorrect. GROUP BY never modifies stored data, so it cannot permanently remove rows from a table. Removing duplicates from query output is done with the DISTINCT keyword, and deleting stored rows uses DELETE — neither is what GROUP BY does.

Incorrect. Filtering individual rows before they are grouped is done by the WHERE clause; filtering groups after aggregation is done by HAVING. GROUP BY itself does not filter rows — it organizes the surviving rows into groups.

Incorrect. Combining records from multiple tables is done with JOIN operations (or set operators like UNION). GROUP BY operates within a single result set to form groups; it does not link or merge separate tables.

title: Which of the following is true about the HAVING clause?

options.html: Similar to the WHERE clause but is used for columns rather than groups
Similar to WHERE clause but is used for rows rather than columns

solution: The HAVING clause is used to filter groups after the GROUP BY clause has been applied. It operates on aggregate functions (like SUM, COUNT, AVG) and is applied to the result set of grouped rows. Unlike the WHERE clause, which filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters the groups themselves. This means HAVING is used when you need to apply conditions on aggregated data.

optionFeedback.html: Step 1: The HAVING clause is not used for individual columns. Step 2: It operates on grouped data, not on individual rows or columns. Step 3: Therefore, this option is incorrect because it misrepresents the purpose of HAVING.
Step 1: The WHERE clause filters rows before grouping. Step 2: HAVING filters after grouping. Step 3: This option confuses HAVING with WHERE by claiming it works on rows, which is incorrect.

Step 1: HAVING is used after GROUP BY to filter groups. Step 2: It operates on aggregate results, not individual rows. Step 3: This option correctly identifies that HAVING is used for groups, not rows.

Step 1: HAVING is used for filtering groups, not rows. Step 2: It is not used for individual columns. Step 3: This option suggests multiple statements are true, but only one is correct. Step 4: Therefore, this option is incorrect.
Step 1: HAVING is used for filtering groups after aggregation. Step 2: This option claims none are correct, but one statement is accurate. Step 3: Therefore, this option is incorrect.

title: Which SQL query will correctly raise the salary by for
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which SQL query will correctly raise the salary by 10% for employees in the 'HR' department who currently earn less than 50,000?

options.html: MODIFY employees SET salary = salary + 10% WHERE department = 'HR' AND salary < 50000;
UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE department = 'HR' AND salary < 50000;
UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 10% WHERE department = 'HR';
UPDATE employees SET salary = salary + 5000 IF department = 'HR' AND salary < 50000;

solution:
To modify existing records in a relational database, standard SQL uses the UPDATE statement alongside a SET clause to specify the modifications, and a WHERE clause to filter the targeted rows.

To increase a value by 10%, you mathematically multiply the current value by 1.10 (which represents 100% + 10%). The conditions specified in the problem statement require checking two things:

  1. The department must be 'HR' (department = 'HR').

  2. The current salary must be strictly less than 50,000 (salary < 50000).

Combining these requirements yields the standard SQL syntax:

UPDATE employees  
SET salary = salary * 1.10  
WHERE department = 'HR' AND salary < 50000;

optionFeedback.html:
Incorrect.

SQL does not have a MODIFY command for updating table rows (MODIFY or ALTER is used structurally to change columns). Additionally, standard SQL does not recognize the % symbol as a percentage mathematical operator; it is used as a wildcard character in string matching (LIKE).

Correct.

This follows standard SQL syntax precisely and correctly uses logical AND to filter rows matching both constraints.

Incorrect.

This statement misses the salary threshold constraint (< 50000). Furthermore, using 10% is syntactically invalid, and multiplying by a factor of 0.10 would actually reduce their salary to 10% of its original value instead of increasing it by 10%.

Incorrect.

Standard SQL filters rows using the WHERE keyword, not IF. Additionally, adding a flat 5000 is only a 10% increase if the employee makes exactly 50,000, which contradicts the condition that they must earn less than 50,000.

title: Which of the following queries will correctly return the names
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following queries will correctly return the names of students who have received the highest grade in any course?

options.html: SELECT StudentName FROM StudentGrades WHERE Grade = (SELECT MAX(Grade) FROM StudentGrades);
SELECT StudentName FROM StudentGrades WHERE Grade IN (SELECT MAX(Grade) FROM StudentGrades GROUP BY CourseID);
SELECT StudentName FROM StudentGrades sg WHERE Grade = (SELECT MAX(Grade) FROM StudentGrades WHERE CourseID = sg.CourseID);
SELECT StudentName FROM StudentGrades GROUP BY CourseID;

solution:
Answer summary: Two queries correctly return students who received the highest grade in each course. Both approaches handle ties (multiple students with the same top grade).

  • Using a grouped subquery: SELECT StudentName FROM StudentGrades WHERE Grade IN (SELECT MAX(Grade) FROM StudentGrades GROUP BY CourseID); — The inner query returns the highest grade for each course, and the outer query returns students whose Grade equals any of those per-course maxima. Ties are included; add DISTINCT StudentName if you want unique names.

  • Using a correlated subquery: SELECT StudentName FROM StudentGrades sg WHERE Grade = (SELECT MAX(Grade) FROM StudentGrades WHERE CourseID = sg.CourseID); — For each row, the subquery computes the maximum grade for that row's course, and the outer query returns students that match that maximum. This also returns ties. On large datasets, consider indexes on CourseID and Grade for performance.

Why the other approaches are incorrect:

  • A query that uses MAX(Grade) without grouping returns only the single highest grade across all courses, not per course.

  • Grouping solely by CourseID while selecting StudentName without an aggregate yields an invalid or ambiguous result and does not guarantee the returned name has the highest grade.

optionFeedback.html: This query finds the single highest grade across the entire table and returns students who have that overall maximum. It does not find the highest grade per course, so it will miss top students in courses whose top grade is lower than the global maximum. To get per-course top students you need a per-course aggregation or a correlated subquery.

The subquery computes the maximum grade for each course, and the outer query returns students whose Grade matches any of those per-course maxima. This correctly returns students who achieved the highest grade in a course. Note that ties are included (multiple students can have the same top grade). If you only want unique student names, add DISTINCT to the SELECT.

This correlated subquery checks, for each row, the maximum grade for that row's course and returns students whose Grade equals that course maximum. It correctly returns the top students per course and includes ties. This approach is straightforward and readable; on large tables it can be less efficient than a grouped subquery unless supported by indexes.

Grouping by CourseID but selecting StudentName without an aggregate or a deterministic grouping rule is invalid in strict SQL and does not guarantee that the returned name has the highest grade in that course. Even if the database allows it, it will return an arbitrary student per course, not necessarily the top scorer. Use an aggregate/subquery or a correlated subquery to identify the highest grade per course.

title: Consider the relation and query: Project (P.no. Pname, price, city)
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the relation and query:

Project (P.no. Pname, price, city)

SELECT Pname FROM Project WHERE NOT (price > = ANY (SELECT price for FROM Project WHERE city = 'DELHI')

Which of the following output produced by above query?

options.html: Name of project whose price is greater than the price of every project in DELHI city.
Name of projects whose price is less than the price of every project in DELHI city.
Name of project whose price is less than equal to the price of project in DELHI city.
Name of projects whose price is greater than equal to the price of every project is DELHI city.

solution:
Key idea: The condition NOT (price >= ANY (SELECT price FROM Project WHERE city = 'DELHI')) is equivalent to price < ALL (SELECT price FROM Project WHERE city = 'DELHI').

  • The inner query returns the set of prices of projects located in DELHI.

  • price >= ANY (inner set) is true when the project's price is greater than or equal to at least one DELHI price.

  • Negating that condition means there is no DELHI price that the project's price is greater than or equal to, i.e., the project's price is strictly less than every DELHI price.

  • Therefore the query returns names of projects whose price is less than every project price in DELHI.

A clearer equivalent SQL form is:

SELECT Pname FROM Project WHERE price < ALL (SELECT price FROM Project WHERE city = 'DELHI')

Important note: If the subquery returns no rows (there are no projects in DELHI), the ALL comparison is vacuously true, so the condition holds for every project and the query would return all project names.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The query selects projects whose price is strictly less than every price of projects in DELHI, not greater than every DELHI price. The condition NOT (price >= ANY (...)) is equivalent to price < ALL (...), so this option describes the opposite relationship.

Correct. NOT (price >= ANY (SELECT price FROM Project WHERE city = 'DELHI')) is equivalent to price < ALL (SELECT price FROM Project WHERE city = 'DELHI'), so the query returns project names whose price is less than every DELHI project price. Note: if there are no projects in DELHI, the ALL comparison is vacuously true and the query would return all projects.

Incorrect. This option says 'less than or equal to' a DELHI price, but the query requires the project's price to be strictly less than every DELHI price. Also the condition applies against every DELHI price (ALL), not just one.

Incorrect. This option describes projects whose price is greater than or equal to every DELHI price, which is the opposite of the actual condition. The query actually selects projects with prices strictly less than every DELHI price.

title: Given table Sales with columns SalesID, ProductID, SaleDate, and SaleAmount,
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Given a table Sales with columns SalesID, ProductID, SaleDate, and SaleAmount, which SQL query retrieves the average sale amount for each month in the year 2024?

options.html: SELECT MONTH(SaleDate), AVG(SaleAmount) FROM Sales WHERE YEAR(SaleDate) = 2024 GROUP BY MONTH(SaleDate);
SELECT SaleDate, AVG(SaleAmount) FROM Sales WHERE YEAR(SaleDate) = 2024;
SELECT MONTH(SaleDate), SUM(SaleAmount) FROM Sales WHERE YEAR(SaleDate) = 2024 GROUP BY SaleDate;

solution:
This query groups the sales data by month and calculates the average sale amount for each month in 2024.

Recommended query (MySQL-style): SELECT MONTH(SaleDate) AS month, AVG(SaleAmount) AS avg_amount FROM Sales WHERE YEAR(SaleDate) = 2024 GROUP BY MONTH(SaleDate) ORDER BY MONTH(SaleDate);

  • Filter to the target year using YEAR(SaleDate) = 2024 so only 2024 rows are considered.

  • Extract the month from SaleDate (MONTH(SaleDate) or EXTRACT(MONTH FROM SaleDate)) and GROUP BY that expression to aggregate per month.

  • Use AVG(SaleAmount) to compute the average sale amount per group (month).

  • Optionally alias the output columns (for readability) and ORDER BY the month to present results from January to December.

  • Portability note: functions differ by SQL dialect. In standard SQL and PostgreSQL you can use EXTRACT(MONTH FROM SaleDate) or date_trunc('month', SaleDate) as appropriate.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. This query extracts the month from SaleDate, filters to rows in 2024, groups the rows by month, and computes the average sale amount for each month. For clarity you can alias the columns and order the output, for example: SELECT MONTH(SaleDate) AS month, AVG(SaleAmount) AS avg_amount FROM Sales WHERE YEAR(SaleDate) = 2024 GROUP BY MONTH(SaleDate) ORDER BY MONTH(SaleDate); Note: YEAR() and MONTH() are common in MySQL; in standard SQL use EXTRACT(MONTH FROM SaleDate) and EXTRACT(YEAR FROM SaleDate).

This returns a single average for the entire year 2024, not separate averages per month. To get monthly averages, extract the month from SaleDate and GROUP BY that month (for example: SELECT MONTH(SaleDate) AS month, AVG(SaleAmount) FROM Sales WHERE YEAR(SaleDate) = 2024 GROUP BY MONTH(SaleDate)).

This selects SaleDate together with an aggregate but does not include a GROUP BY, which will cause an error or unintended results. Also grouping by the full SaleDate would produce averages per day rather than per month. To obtain monthly averages, extract the month and group by that expression, for example: SELECT MONTH(SaleDate) AS month, AVG(SaleAmount) FROM Sales WHERE YEAR(SaleDate) = 2024 GROUP BY MONTH(SaleDate).

This extracts the month in the SELECT but uses SUM instead of AVG, and it groups by SaleDate (the full date) which yields daily totals rather than monthly averages. To get average sale amount per month, use AVG(SaleAmount) and GROUP BY the month expression, for example: SELECT MONTH(SaleDate) AS month, AVG(SaleAmount) FROM Sales WHERE YEAR(SaleDate) = 2024 GROUP BY MONTH(SaleDate) ORDER BY MONTH(SaleDate).

title: Given table Orders with columns OrderID (PK), CustomerID, OrderDate, and
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Given a table Orders with columns OrderID (PK), CustomerID, OrderDate, and OrderAmount, which of the following queries will return the number of orders placed by each customer? The given table may contains null values.

options.html: SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(OrderID) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;
SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;
SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(OrderAmount) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;

solution:
Correct queries that return the number of orders per customer:

  • SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(OrderID) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;

    Counts non-null OrderID values per customer. Since OrderID is the primary key and cannot be null, this correctly returns the number of orders for each customer even if other columns contain nulls.

  • SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;

    Counts all rows per customer group. COUNT(*) counts every row regardless of null values in other columns, so it also correctly returns the number of orders per customer.

Why the other queries are incorrect:

  • SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(OrderAmount) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;

    COUNT(OrderAmount) counts only non-null OrderAmount values. If OrderAmount can be null, this will undercount orders. Use COUNT(*) or COUNT(OrderID) to count orders regardless of nulls.

  • SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(OrderID) FROM Orders;

    This query is missing a GROUP BY clause. Selecting CustomerID together with an aggregate without grouping is invalid in standard SQL and will not produce per-customer counts.

optionFeedback.html: This query groups rows by CustomerID and counts non-null OrderID values per group. Because OrderID is the primary key and cannot be null, COUNT(OrderID) returns the number of orders per customer even if other columns contain nulls.

This query groups rows by CustomerID and uses COUNT(*) to count all rows in each group. COUNT(*) counts every row regardless of null values in other columns, so this correctly returns the number of orders per customer.

This query counts non-null values in the OrderAmount column. If OrderAmount can be null, COUNT(OrderAmount) will undercount orders that have a null OrderAmount. To count orders regardless of nulls, use COUNT(*) or COUNT(OrderID).

This query lacks a GROUP BY clause. Selecting CustomerID alongside an aggregate without GROUP BY is invalid in standard SQL and will not produce per-customer counts; it will either raise an error or return a single aggregated result for the whole table.

title: Consider table Attendance with columns EmpID, AttendanceDate, and Status ('Present'
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Consider a table Attendance with columns EmpID, AttendanceDate, and Status ('Present' or 'Absent'). Which SQL query returns the percentage of days each employee was present in January 2024?

options.html: SELECT EmpID, (SUM(CASE WHEN Status = 'Present' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*)) * 100 AS AttendancePercentage FROM Attendance WHERE MONTH(AttendanceDate) = 1 AND YEAR(AttendanceDate) = 2024 GROUP BY EmpID;
SELECT EmpID, (COUNT(Status = 'Present') / COUNT(*)) * 100 AS AttendancePercentage FROM Attendance WHERE MONTH(AttendanceDate) = 1 AND YEAR(AttendanceDate) = 2024 GROUP BY EmpID;

SELECT EmpID, (COUNT(*) / SUM(CASE WHEN Status = 'Present' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)) * 100 AS AttendancePercentage FROM Attendance WHERE MONTH(AttendanceDate) = 1 AND YEAR(AttendanceDate) = 2024 GROUP BY EmpID;

SELECT EmpID, (SUM(CASE WHEN Status = 'Absent' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*)) * 100 AS AttendancePercentage FROM Attendance WHERE MONTH(AttendanceDate) = 1 AND YEAR(AttendanceDate) = 2024 GROUP BY EmpID;

solution:
Key insight: count present days with a conditional SUM, divide by total days, and multiply by 100. Ensure you avoid integer division and use a sargable date filter.

  • Use SUM(CASE WHEN Status = 'Present' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) to count present days.

  • Divide by COUNT(*) to get the proportion of days recorded for that employee.

  • Multiply by 100.0 or cast to a decimal type to prevent integer division in databases that perform integer arithmetic.

  • Prefer filtering by a date range (for example AttendanceDate >= '2024-01-01' AND AttendanceDate < '2024-02-01') instead of MONTH()/YEAR() for better performance.

Recommended query:

SELECT EmpID, 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN Status = 'Present' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) AS AttendancePercentage

FROM Attendance

WHERE AttendanceDate >= '2024-01-01' AND AttendanceDate < '2024-02-01'

GROUP BY EmpID;

Notes:

  • Some databases (for example MySQL) allow SUM(Status = 'Present') as a shorter form because the boolean evaluates to 1/0, but the CASE expression is more portable and explicit.

optionFeedback.html: This query uses a conditional SUM to count 'Present' days and divides by the total number of records, which is the correct approach. Two improvements to make it robust: multiply by a decimal (for example 100.0) or cast to a non-integer type to avoid integer division in some SQL engines, and prefer filtering by a date range (AttendanceDate >= '2024-01-01' AND AttendanceDate < '2024-02-01') for better performance.

COUNT(Status = 'Present') is not a reliable way to count present days. COUNT(expr) counts non-null results, so this expression will generally count every row because the boolean expression yields 1 or 0 (non-null). Use SUM(CASE WHEN Status = 'Present' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) to count present days, or in MySQL you can use SUM(Status = 'Present') which treats the boolean as 1/0.

This query flips the numerator and denominator, calculating total days divided by present days, which yields an inverted percentage and is incorrect. The correct formula is (number of present days) / (total days) * 100.
This query counts 'Absent' days rather than 'Present' days, so it returns the absence percentage, not the presence percentage. To get presence, count where Status = 'Present'.

title: Consider database with table Employee having columns EmpID, Name, Department,
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Consider a database with a table Employee having columns EmpID, Name, Department, and Salary. Which of the following queries will list the names of employees who have a salary greater than the average salary in their department?

options.html: SELECT Name FROM Employee WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee);
SELECT Name FROM Employee WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee GROUP BY Department);
SELECT Name FROM Employee WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE Department = Department);
SELECT Name FROM Employee E WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE Department = E.Department);

solution:
Answer: Use a correlated subquery that references the outer row's department. For example: SELECT Name FROM Employee E WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE Department = E.Department);

Why this works:

  • The subquery is correlated because it uses E.Department (the alias from the outer query). For each outer row the subquery computes the average salary only for that employee's department.

  • The subquery returns a single scalar value (the department average) for each outer row, so the comparison Salary > (subquery) is valid.

Why the other queries are incorrect or problematic:

  • A query that compares Salary to (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee) uses the overall average across all departments, so it does not select employees above their own department's average.

  • A query that uses (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee GROUP BY Department) produces multiple average values (one per department). Using that multi-row result where a single scalar is expected causes an error; you would need to join to that grouped result or use a correlated subquery instead.

  • A query that uses WHERE Department = Department inside the subquery is not correlated: it compares the same column within the subquery, which is always true, so the subquery effectively computes an overall average rather than a department-specific average.

Alternative correct approach:

You can precompute department averages and join them to the Employee table, for example: SELECT e.Name FROM Employee e JOIN (SELECT Department, AVG(Salary) AS AvgSal FROM Employee GROUP BY Department) d ON e.Department = d.Department WHERE e.Salary > d.AvgSal;

optionFeedback.html: This query compares each employee's salary to the overall average salary across the entire Employee table. It will return employees earning above the company-wide average, not employees who earn more than the average in their own department.

This query's subquery uses GROUP BY Department, so it produces one average per department (multiple rows). Using that multi-row result where a single scalar value is expected will cause an error. To compare against department averages you must either use a correlated subquery or join to a derived table of department averages.

The condition Department = Department inside the subquery compares the column to itself within the subquery, so it is always true and does not reference the outer query. As a result the subquery computes the overall average (equivalent to the query that uses the overall AVG), not the average for the employee's department. The subquery needs to reference the outer row (for example via an alias) to be correlated.

Correct. This query aliases the outer Employee table as E and uses a correlated subquery that references E.Department. For each employee row the subquery computes AVG(Salary) for that employee's department, so the comparison returns employees whose salary is greater than their department's average.

title: Given two tables and both having column ID, which SQL
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Given two tables A and B, both having a column ID, which SQL statement retrieves all IDs from table A that do not exist in table B?

options.html: SELECT A.ID FROM A WHERE A.ID <> (SELECT B.ID FROM B);
SELECT A.ID FROM A WHERE A.ID NOT IN (SELECT ID FROM B);
SELECT A.ID FROM A, B WHERE A.ID != B.ID;
SELECT A.ID FROM A WHERE A.ID EXISTS (SELECT ID FROM B);

solution:
Safer recommended solutions to retrieve IDs from A that do not exist in B:

  • Use NOT EXISTS (safe with NULLs): SELECT A.ID FROM A WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE B.ID = A.ID);

  • Or use a LEFT JOIN and check for missing matches: SELECT A.ID FROM A LEFT JOIN B ON A.ID = B.ID WHERE B.ID IS NULL;

  • The NOT IN form works when B.ID contains no NULLs: SELECT A.ID FROM A WHERE A.ID NOT IN (SELECT ID FROM B);

Why NOT IN can be problematic:

  • If the subquery returns any NULL values, the NOT IN condition evaluates to UNKNOWN and may cause no rows to be returned. NOT EXISTS and LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL avoid that pitfall.

Why the other provided queries are incorrect:

  • A query that uses a scalar comparison like SELECT A.ID FROM A WHERE A.ID <> (SELECT B.ID FROM B); is invalid when the subquery returns multiple rows and does not implement the intended set-difference logic.

  • A query that selects from both tables with a condition A.ID != B.ID (a cross join filtered by inequality) produces many rows and duplicates, not the distinct set of IDs in A that are absent from B.

  • A statement that attempts to use EXISTS incorrectly (for example using A.ID EXISTS (SELECT ID FROM B)) has invalid syntax; the correct EXISTS usage is WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE B.ID = A.ID) or its negation for the not-exists case.

Summary: Prefer NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL for a robust solution; the NOT IN form is acceptable only when you can guarantee there are no NULLs in B.ID.

optionFeedback.html: This query tries to compare A.ID to the entire result of a subquery. A scalar comparison with <> requires the subquery to return exactly one value, but the subquery (SELECT B.ID FROM B) can return many rows. This makes the statement invalid or incorrect. Use a set-based approach such as NOT IN, NOT EXISTS, or a LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL to get IDs in A that are not in B.

This query finds IDs in A that are not present in B and is correct in many cases: SELECT A.ID FROM A WHERE A.ID NOT IN (SELECT ID FROM B); However, if B.ID contains any NULL values, the NOT IN test can behave unexpectedly and may return no rows. A safer alternative that handles NULLs is to use NOT EXISTS or a LEFT JOIN with IS NULL.

This query performs a cross join between A and B and then filters rows where IDs differ. That returns many rows (one for each non-matching pair) and will produce duplicates and incorrect results for the goal of finding IDs in A that do not exist in B. Use a subquery or join-with-null-check instead.

This statement uses incorrect SQL syntax. EXISTS is used with a subquery like WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE B.ID = A.ID). To check that an A.ID exists in B you'd write that form; to find IDs in A that do not exist in B, use WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE B.ID = A.ID) or a LEFT JOIN ... WHERE B.ID IS NULL.

title: Consider table Products with columns ProductID, ProductName, CategoryID, and Price.
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Consider a table Products with columns ProductID, ProductName, CategoryID, and Price. Which of the following queries will correctly return the product names and prices of the products with the highest price in each category?

options.html: SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products WHERE Price = (SELECT MAX(Price) FROM Products);
SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products WHERE Price IN (SELECT MAX(Price) FROM Products GROUP BY CategoryID);
SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products p WHERE Price = (SELECT MAX(Price) FROM Products WHERE CategoryID = p.CategoryID);
SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products GROUP BY CategoryID

solution:
Correct approach and explanation:

  • Correct query (correlated subquery): SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products p WHERE Price = (SELECT MAX(Price) FROM Products WHERE CategoryID = p.CategoryID);

  • Why this works: the subquery computes the maximum price for the category of the current row (using p.CategoryID). The outer row is returned only when its Price equals that category-specific maximum. This correctly returns all products that are tied for the highest price within their own category.

  • Alternative correct query (join with derived maxima): SELECT p.ProductName, p.Price FROM Products p JOIN (SELECT CategoryID, MAX(Price) AS MaxPrice FROM Products GROUP BY CategoryID) m ON p.CategoryID = m.CategoryID AND p.Price = m.MaxPrice;

  • Why the alternative works: it explicitly pairs each product with the maximum price for its category, avoiding incorrect matches across categories and often performing better for large tables.

Why the other queries are incorrect or problematic:

  • SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products WHERE Price = (SELECT MAX(Price) FROM Products);

    This picks the single overall maximum price across the entire table, not the maximum per category, so it only returns product(s) at the global maximum.

  • SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products WHERE Price IN (SELECT MAX(Price) FROM Products GROUP BY CategoryID);

    This compares prices against the set of maximum prices but does not check CategoryID. A product can match the maximum price value of another category and be returned incorrectly. Example: if one category's max is 300 and another category has a product priced 200 (but its own category's max is 400), a 200-priced product may still appear because 200 is a max in some other category.

  • SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products GROUP BY CategoryID

    This is invalid in standard SQL because ProductName and Price are neither aggregated nor included in GROUP BY. It will error in strict SQL or return indeterminate values in DBMSs that allow nonstandard grouping.

Summary: The correlated subquery that restricts MAX(Price) to the current row's CategoryID is correct; joining with a derived table of category maxima is an equivalent and often efficient alternative. The global MAX and the unqualified IN approach are incorrect for per-category maxima, and the GROUP BY example is a misuse of aggregation.

optionFeedback.html: This query uses a single MAX(Price) over the whole table, so it returns only products that have the overall highest price across all categories. It does not compute the highest price within each category, so it will miss the top product(s) for other categories.

This query compares only prices against the set of maximum prices by category, but it does not ensure the matched price belongs to the same category as the product row. If two categories have different maximum prices, a product can match the maximum price of a different category and be returned incorrectly. To fix this, relate the max price to the product's CategoryID (for example by using a correlated subquery or joining with a derived table of category maxima).

This correlated subquery is correct: for each product row it finds the maximum price for that product's CategoryID and returns the product when its price equals that maximum. It correctly returns all products that tie for the highest price in their category. (On large tables a join with a derived table of category maxima can be more efficient.)

This GROUP BY usage is invalid in standard SQL because ProductName and Price are selected but not aggregated or listed in GROUP BY. In strict SQL this raises an error; in some DBMSs it returns indeterminate values. To get per-category maxima you must aggregate Price (e.g., MAX(Price) GROUP BY CategoryID) and then join back to retrieve product names for the rows with that maximum.

title: Consider database that has the relation schemas: (MCQ) student(rollno, name,
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider a database that has the relation schemas:       

student(rollno, name, degree, year, gender)
course(courseid, cname, credit, dept)
enroll(rollno, courseid, session, grade)

Assume that every student is enrolled in at least one course, then which of the following queries retrieves the names of all students who have scored ‘A’ in all the subjects they enrolled in:

options.html: SELECT s.name FROM student s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT e.rollno FROM enroll e WHERE e.rollno = s.rollno AND e.grade ≠ 'A' )
SELECT c.cid FROM course c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT cid FROM enrolled e WHERE e.cid = c.cid AND e.grade = 'A' )
SELECT c.cid FROM course c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT cid FROM enrolled e WHERE e.cid = c.cid AND e.grade = 'A' )

solution:
Key idea: select students for whom there does not exist any enrollment with a grade that is not 'A'.

  • The inner subquery finds enrollments for the same student that have a non-'A' grade.

  • NOT EXISTS around that subquery removes any student who has at least one such non-'A' enrollment, leaving only students whose every enrollment has grade 'A'.

  • Because the question states every student is enrolled in at least one course, students with no enrollments are not a concern for this query.

Corrected SQL (use <> for not-equal and SELECT 1 in the subquery):

SELECT s.name FROM student s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enroll e WHERE e.rollno = s.rollno AND e.grade <> 'A');

Alternative approach using GROUP BY / HAVING:

SELECT s.name FROM student s JOIN enroll e ON s.rollno = e.rollno GROUP BY s.rollno, s.name HAVING COUNT(*) = SUM(CASE WHEN e.grade = 'A' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END);

optionFeedback.html: This query correctly returns names of students s for whom there does not exist any enrollment record with a grade not equal to 'A'. That effectively selects students who have only 'A' grades. Note: in SQL use <> or != for 'not equal' rather than the ≠ symbol shown; it's also common to write SELECT 1 in the subquery for clarity/efficiency. The query relies on the given assumption that every student has at least one enrollment — otherwise students with no enrollments would also be included.

This query finds course IDs for courses that have at least one enrollment with grade 'A'. It does not return student names and does not ensure that a student has 'A' in all their enrolled subjects. To find students who scored 'A' in every subject, you must examine enrollments per student and exclude any student who has any non-'A' grade (for example, using NOT EXISTS on enrollments with grade <> 'A').

This query returns course IDs for courses that have no enrollments with grade 'A' (courses without any 'A' grades). It does not return student names nor check that a student has only 'A' grades. To get students with all 'A's, operate from student records and ensure there is no enrollment for that student with grade <> 'A' (or use a GROUP BY/HAVING that compares total enrollments to enrollments with grade 'A').

This choice is incorrect because there is a valid query among the options that returns students who have 'A' in all their enrolled subjects: the query that selects students for whom no enrollment exists with a non-'A' grade. Therefore 'none of the above' is not appropriate.

title: Consider the following relation scheme: Wholesaler (sid: integer, sname: string,
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following relation scheme:
Wholesaler (sid: integer, sname: string, address: string)
Parts (pid: integer, pname: string, color: string)
Catalog (sid: integer, pid: integer, cost: real)
The following query executed:
SELECT C.pid FROM Catalog C, Wholesaler S WHERE S.sname = 'KnowledgeGate' AND C.sid = S.sid AND
C.cost >= ALL (SELECT C2.cost FROM Catalog C2, Wholesaler S2 WHERE S2.sname = 'KnowledgeGate' AND C2.sid = S2.sid)
The output of above query is:

options.html: Find the pids of less expensive parts supplied by the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate.
Find the pids of parts whose cost is more than the cost of parts not supplied by the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate.
Find the pids of parts whose cost is less than the cost of parts supplied by the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate.
Find the pids of the most expensive parts supplied by the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate.

solution:
Concept: In standard SQL, a condition of the form expr >= ALL (subquery) is the classic way to express "expr is the maximum" without an explicit MAX() aggregate. It keeps a row only if its value is greater than or equal to every single value the subquery returns for the same comparison group -- i.e., it selects whichever row(s) attain that group's maximum, and ties are included because >= allows equality.

  1. The nested subquery filters Catalog rows C2 by S2.sname = 'KnowledgeGate' AND C2.sid = S2.sid, so C2.cost enumerates exactly the costs of the parts supplied by the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate.

  2. The outer query applies the identical filter (S.sname = 'KnowledgeGate' AND C.sid = S.sid) to C, so C ranges over that same set of KnowledgeGate catalog rows.

  3. Because the outer set and the subquery's comparison set are the same group, C.cost >= ALL(...) keeps only the row(s) whose cost is greater than or equal to every cost in that group -- the maximum cost among KnowledgeGate's parts.

  4. SELECT C.pid then returns the pid(s) of exactly those row(s): the most expensive part(s) supplied by the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate, with every tied pid included.

Cross-check: suppose KnowledgeGate's parts cost {40, 55, 55, 30}. The subquery's result set is {40, 55, 55, 30}. Testing 40 >= ALL(...) fails (40 is not >= 55), and 30 fails likewise, but each row costing 55 satisfies 55 >= 40, 55 >= 55, and 55 >= 30 -- so both pids costing 55 pass. This confirms the query returns the pid(s) of the top-cost part(s), never a partial or 'less than' subset.

Result: the query returns the pids of the most expensive parts supplied by the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate. (Note: the source text's relation/table-name typos -- e.g. a stray 'Wholesalers'/'Supplies' in the subquery's FROM clause -- have been corrected above to the schema's own 'Wholesaler' relation, which is the only table the query can correctly join against; this does not change the query's semantics or the answer.) This reading assumes, as is standard for this classic exercise, that Catalog.cost values are always populated -- SQL's three-valued logic means a NULL cost among the values ALL(...) compares against could make the predicate evaluate to UNKNOWN for that row, which is outside the intended scope here.

optionFeedback.html: This matches what the query would return if the predicate read C.cost <= ALL(...) instead of the actual C.cost >= ALL(...) -- i.e., it describes the opposite comparison direction from the one the query actually uses.

Both S.sname = 'KnowledgeGate' in the outer query and S2.sname = 'KnowledgeGate' in the nested subquery restrict every row being compared to catalog rows for the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate. There is no comparison here against parts supplied by a different wholesaler.
This also matches the opposite comparison direction: it describes what a '<' or '<= ALL' style condition would return, not what the query's actual '>=' predicate returns.

The nested subquery collects the cost of every catalog row for the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate, and the outer condition keeps only the rows whose cost is greater than or equal to all of those values -- exactly the priciest part(s) that wholesaler supplies, with ties included whenever more than one part shares that top cost.

title: Consider the following relations given below: SQL: select sid from
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following relations given below:


SQL: select sid from supply S1 where region = 'mumbai' and NOT EXISTS (select pid from parts P1 where colour = 'red' and NOT EXISTS(select pid from catalog C1 where C1.pid = P1.pid and C1.sid = S1.sid))

options.html: select sid of all the suppliers in mumbai region who supply all red parts
select sid of all the suppliers in mumbai region who supply some red parts
select sid of some of the suppliers in mumbai region who supply all red parts

solution:
Concept

A subquery of the form NOT EXISTS ( ... WHERE <condition> AND NOT EXISTS ( <correlated match> ) ) is SQL's standard idiom for universal quantification — sometimes called relational division. It holds for an outer row exactly when no element of the inner set fails the correlated match, i.e. every element of that inner set is related to the outer row.

Application

  1. The innermost EXISTS/NOT EXISTS tests, for a specific supplier S1 and a specific part P1, whether the catalog table has a row linking S1.sid to P1.pid — i.e. whether S1 supplies P1.

  2. The middle subquery collects every red part (colour = ‘red’) for which that innermost NOT EXISTS is true — i.e. every red part S1 does NOT supply.

  3. The outer NOT EXISTS is true exactly when that middle set is empty — meaning there is no red part missing from S1's catalog.

  4. Combined with region = ‘mumbai’ in the outer WHERE clause, the query returns every supply row satisfying both conditions: a Mumbai-region supplier for whom no red part is missing, i.e. a supplier who supplies every red part.

Cross-check

  • If the outer NOT EXISTS were replaced by a bare EXISTS (one fewer negation), a row would be selected as soon as a single red part is missing — that would describe suppliers failing to supply at least one red part, not this query.

  • A SELECT ... WHERE statement always returns the complete set of rows for which its condition holds for that row; it has no mechanism to arbitrarily return only part of the qualifying rows.

  • The query's truth value for a given supplier depends only on whether every red part is present among that supplier's catalog rows — a structural, always-computable condition, not one that assumes the whole result is empty.

This is why the query selects the sids of suppliers in the mumbai region who supply all red parts.

optionFeedback.html: A NOT EXISTS wrapped around another NOT EXISTS is exactly the relational-division idiom for “no counter-example exists” — here, no red part exists that this supplier's catalog is missing. That is precisely what “supplies all red parts” means, so a mumbai-region supplier satisfying this condition belongs in the result for exactly that reason.

This reading treats the nested condition as a single positive existence check — as if the query asked “does at least one catalog row match this part and supplier?” But the actual condition wraps that check in two levels of negation (a NOT EXISTS around a NOT EXISTS), not one bare EXISTS; collapsing a double negation into a single existential test changes what is actually being asked about each red part.

A SELECT ... WHERE query returns every row for which its condition evaluates to true — there is no SQL mechanism in this query that would select only an arbitrary portion of the qualifying supply rows. Introducing a “some of” qualifier on top of a plain WHERE filter isn't something this query's structure supports.

Whether any given supplier row satisfies the WHERE condition depends entirely on the actual contents of the parts, supply, and catalog tables — nothing in the schema forces the condition to be false for every row. A blanket claim that the result is always empty isn't a property of the query's structure; it would require assuming specific data that isn't given here.

title: Consider the following three queries on relation S(A, and R(B,
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following three queries on relation S(A, B) and R(B, C)

Q1: SELECT S. A FROM S WHERE S.B NOT IN (SELECT R.B FROM R WHERE R. B > 5);

Q2: SELECT S. A FROM S WHERE S.B <> ALL (SELECT R.B FROM R WHERE R. B > 5);

Q3: SELECT S.A FROM S WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT R.B FROM R WHERE R.B > 5 AND R.B = S.B) ;

options.html: The first query is not equivalent to any of the other queries
The first query is equivalent to the second query only
The first query is equivalent to the third query only

solution:
Answer: Queries 1 and 2 are equivalent; Query 3 is not equivalent to them.

  • Why queries 1 and 2 are equivalent:

    Both S.B NOT IN (SELECT R.B FROM R WHERE R.B > 5) and S.B <> ALL (SELECT R.B FROM R WHERE R.B > 5) require that S.B be unequal to every value produced by the subquery. The subquery uses R.B > 5, which excludes NULLs from its result, so the usual NULL pitfalls inside the subquery do not arise and the two expressions produce the same truth values for all rows.

  • Why query 3 can differ:

    Query 3 uses NOT EXISTS with a correlated equality test (NOT EXISTS (SELECT R.B FROM R WHERE R.B > 5 AND R.B = S.B)). If S.B is NULL then R.B = S.B evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row, so the subquery produces no rows and NOT EXISTS is true — the S row is included. In contrast, the first two queries evaluate comparisons with NULL to UNKNOWN and so exclude the S row. Thus the third query can return rows that the first two do not.

  • Concrete counterexample:

    Take S = { (A=1, B=NULL) } and R = { (B=6) }.

    Evaluations:

    • Query 1: S.B NOT IN (6) -> NULL NOT IN (6) evaluates to UNKNOWN -> row is excluded.

    • Query 2: S.B <> ALL (6) -> NULL <> 6 evaluates to UNKNOWN -> ALL yields UNKNOWN -> row is excluded.

    • Query 3: NOT EXISTS( ... R.B = S.B ...) -> R.B = NULL is UNKNOWN so subquery returns no rows -> NOT EXISTS is true -> row is included.

  • Conclusion: select the answer that states the first and second queries are equivalent and the third is different. The three queries are not all equivalent in the presence of NULLs in S.B.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The first and second queries are equivalent: both test that S.B is different from every value produced by the subquery, and the subquery uses R.B > 5 so it does not produce NULLs. The third query uses NOT EXISTS and can behave differently when S.B is NULL. For example, if S has a row with B = NULL and R has a row with B = 6, the first and second queries exclude the S row while the third query includes it.

Correct. The first query (S.B NOT IN (subquery)) and the second query (S.B <> ALL (subquery)) are equivalent here because the subquery only returns non-NULL values (it uses R.B > 5). Both return rows where S.B differs from every value produced by the subquery. Note the third query behaves differently when S.B is NULL because equality with NULL is UNKNOWN, which affects NOT EXISTS differently.

Incorrect. The first query is not equivalent to the third. The difference arises from how NULL in S.B is handled. Example: let S contain a row with B = NULL and let R contain a row with B = 6. The first query and the second query both exclude the S row, but the third query (using NOT EXISTS with R.B = S.B) includes the S row because the equality with NULL fails and the subquery returns no matching rows.

Incorrect. All three are not equivalent in general. The difference is due to NULL handling in S.B. For instance, if S has B = NULL and R has B = 6 (> 5), the first and second queries exclude that S row (comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN), whereas the third query includes it because the equality test in the NOT EXISTS subquery fails and the subquery returns no rows. Therefore the third query can return rows that the first two do not.
