title: Which of the following SQL query deletes all tuples in
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following SQL queries deletes all tuples in the teacher relation for teachers associated with a department located in the building named 'CSE', as recorded in the department relation?

options.html:
DELETE FROM teacher
WHERE dept_name IN (
SELECT dept_name
FROM department
WHERE building = 'CSE');

solution:
A DELETE statement's WHERE clause can only test columns belonging to the table it deletes from. When the filtering condition instead depends on an attribute stored in a DIFFERENT relation, the standard, portable way to express this is a subquery: first resolve the qualifying values from that other relation, then match the outer DELETE's WHERE...IN clause against the resulting set. (Some dialects also allow a correlated EXISTS or a joined DELETE/USING form for the same logic, but the subquery form is the one offered here.)

  1. The inner subquery, SELECT dept_name FROM department WHERE building = 'CSE', resolves to the set of department names whose department is located in the CSE building.

  2. The outer query, DELETE FROM teacher WHERE dept_name IN (...), then removes every teacher row whose dept_name is a member of that resolved set -- this is the query that satisfies the requirement.

Checking why every other option fails:

  • A query that compares dept_name directly to the building's name 'CSE' mixes two different attributes from two different relations, and is not a syntactically valid IN condition either way.

  • A query that deletes rows from the department relation itself removes department records, not the associated teacher records the question asks for.

  • Since a valid query does satisfy the requirement, the option stating that none of the given queries works does not hold.

The subquery-based DELETE is therefore the query, among those offered, that correctly performs the required deletion.

optionFeedback.html: This deletes from the correct teacher relation, but it compares that relation's department-name attribute directly to 'CSE' -- a BUILDING name from a different attribute in a different relation. The two values belong to different domains, and IN also needs a set (a subquery or list), not a bare string literal.
This deletes rows from the department relation itself, not the associated teacher records the question asks for.

The inner subquery resolves every dept_name whose department is located in the CSE building, and the outer DELETE removes exactly the teacher rows whose dept_name falls in that resolved set -- the two-step subquery pattern used here whenever a DELETE's filter depends on a column that lives in a different relation (some dialects also support a correlated EXISTS or joined DELETE form for the same logic).
A syntactically valid query that satisfies the requirement is present among the other options, so this option does not hold.

title: Logical data independence is the ability to change schema without
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Logical data independence is the ability to change ______ schema without having to change ______ schema.

Logical data independence is the capacity to change the conceptual schema without affecting the external schema (view level). It isolates user applications from structural modifications made at the logical level.

Therefore, the correct choice is conceptual; external. Correct option is C.

Incorrect. The internal schema resides below the conceptual schema; modifications to the conceptual layer do not require changes to the underlying storage structure.
Correct. This accurately fulfills the definition of logical data independence within the standard ANSI-SPARC three-level architecture.
Incorrect. Changing the internal schema without changing the conceptual schema defines physical data independence, not logical data independence.

title: Consider the following relation schema along with the tuples. Employee(name,
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following relation schema R along with the tuples.

Employee(name, salary) = {<e1, 10000>, <e2, 5000>, <e3, 2500>, <e4, 7500>, <e5, 8900>, <e6, 9800>}

What is the output of following SQL query?

SELECT name, MAX(salary) FROM Employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee);
solution:
Concept: A scalar subquery inside a WHERE clause is fully evaluated first, producing a single value that the outer query then filters against. Once the WHERE clause has filtered the rows, any aggregate function (MAX, MIN, COUNT, etc.) in the outer SELECT operates only on that filtered subset of rows, not on the whole table.

Application: working through the query step by step —

  1. Evaluate the inner subquery first: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee scans all six tuples and returns 10000 (the salary of e1).

  2. Apply the outer WHERE filter: keep only rows with salary < 10000. This keeps e2 (5000), e3 (2500), e4 (7500), e5 (8900), and e6 (9800); it drops e1 (10000) because 10000 is not strictly less than 10000.

  3. Apply the outer aggregate MAX(salary) over exactly this filtered set of five tuples — the largest value among {5000, 2500, 7500, 8900, 9800} is 9800, contributed by e6.

  4. So the query returns the single row <e6, 9800>.

Cross-check: sorting the filtered salaries — 2500, 5000, 7500, 8900, 9800 — confirms 9800 is the unique largest value in that set, so no other filtered tuple could produce a larger MAX(salary). (Note: strict ANSI SQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, and MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY reject this query outright, since name is not functionally dependent on the aggregate without a GROUP BY. A dialect such as SQLite, which specifically permits a bare column alongside MIN/MAX and deterministically returns the row that produced the extreme value, DOES guarantee this exact pairing — non-strict MySQL, by contrast, only guarantees the aggregate value and leaves the paired name officially unspecified. This question follows that SQLite-style / exam-convention reading, under which the row of the extreme salary is returned together with it — exactly the concept these PYQ-style subquery questions are testing.)

optionFeedback.html: 2500 is the smallest salary in the entire table — the opposite extreme from what MAX(salary) computes. The filtered set (rows below the overall maximum) still contains several salaries larger than this one, so this cannot be the aggregate maximum.

8900 does pass the WHERE filter (it is below 10000), but merely passing that filter does not make a row the aggregate maximum of the filtered set — computing MAX(salary) requires comparing every qualifying row against each other, a step this option skips by stopping at the first plausible-looking value.

9800 is the highest salary among the tuples that satisfy salary < 10000 — i.e., after the one tuple equal to the overall maximum has been excluded by the WHERE clause. That is exactly the value the outer MAX(salary) aggregates to once filtering is applied.

10000 equals the overall maximum salary, so it fails the strict inequality salary < 10000 in the WHERE clause and is excluded from the filtered set entirely — it never reaches the outer aggregation step.

solution:
Understanding Nested Queries

A nested query, also known as a subquery, is a query embedded within another SQL query. It acts as a complete select-from-where block used to provide data for the outer query's conditions.

This structure allows the database to process the inner query first, using its results to filter or validate data in the outer query. It enables complex logic within a single statement.

optionFeedback.html: Nested queries refer to a query embedded within another query. They function as complete select-from-where blocks used to filter or retrieve data based on results from the outer query. This structure allows complex logic within a single statement.

SQL queries is a general term for any command executed in a database. It does not specifically describe the structural relationship of one query being contained within another. This option lacks the necessary specificity regarding nested structures.

Update queries are used to modify existing records in a table. They do not inherently describe a block structure contained within another query. This option refers to a specific operation rather than a nested architectural pattern.

Select queries retrieve data from a database table. While they can be part of a larger structure, the term itself does not define a block within another query. This option describes the action, not the nesting relationship.

title: Consider the following given relations: student(rollno,name,degree,year gender) course(cid,cname,deptno) enrolled(rollno,cid,grade) Which

Which of the following retrieve the ‘name of students who have scored A in all the enrolled subjects’ :

options.html: {s.name | student(s) Λ (∀e)((enroll(e) V e.rollno=s.rollno)→ e.grade = A)}
{s.name | student(s) Λ (∀e)((enroll(e) Λ e.rollno=s.rollno)→ e.grade = A)}
{s.name | student(s) Λ (∃e)((enroll(e) Λ e.rollno=s.rollno)→ e.grade = A)}
{s.name | student(s) Λ (∃e)((enroll(e) V e.rollno=s.rollno)→ e.grade = A)}

solution:
(∀e)((enroll(e) Λ e.rollno = s.rollno) → e.grade = A)

Explanation:

  • The universal quantifier (∀e) ranges over enrollment tuples.

  • The antecedent (enroll(e) Λ e.rollno = s.rollno) restricts e to records that are enrollments of the specific student s.

  • The implication requires that for every such enrollment tuple, the grade is A, which exactly captures "scored A in all enrolled subjects."

  • Note: under classical logic this formula is vacuously true for students with no enrollments. If you want to exclude those students, add an existence condition such as: (∃e)(enroll(e) Λ e.rollno = s.rollno) in conjunction with the universal requirement.

optionFeedback.html: This formula uses a disjunction (enroll(e) OR e.rollno = s.rollno) in the antecedent. That incorrectly makes the antecedent true for many tuples not belonging to the given student, forcing unrelated enrollment records to have grade A. The correct restriction is to require both that e is an enrollment record and that it belongs to the student (use a conjunction), so this expression is incorrect.

This is correct: the universal quantifier with a conjunction in the antecedent ((enroll(e) AND e.rollno = s.rollno) → e.grade = A) restricts e to the student's enrolled courses and requires each such course to have grade A. Note: under classical logic this formula is vacuously true for students with no enrollments; if you want to exclude students with no enrollments, add an existence condition requiring at least one enrollment for the student.

This uses an existential quantifier with an implication. That only requires there exists some tuple e for which the implication holds; because implications are true when the antecedent is false, this formula can be satisfied trivially and does not ensure the student has grade A in every enrolled subject. To express "A in all enrolled subjects" you need a universal quantifier over the student's enrollments.

This expression combines an existential quantifier and a disjunction in the antecedent, so it similarly fails to restrict e to the student's enrollments and can be trivially true. It does not ensure the student has grade A in every enrolled subject. The correct approach is to universally quantify over enrollment tuples that belong to the student and require grade A for each.

title: Given the following relational schemas Employee (empId, name, age, sex,
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Given the following relational schemas

Employee (empId, name, age, sex, deptId, advisor)

Department (deptId, DName, head, phoneNo)

Which of the following will be the TRC query to obtain the department names that do not have any female employee?
solution:
Concept

In Tuple Relational Calculus, a universal quantifier must be paired with an implication, (∀s)( P(s) → Q(s) ) — read as 'for every tuple s, IF s satisfies P then s also satisfies Q.' The antecedent P(s) is what restricts the quantification to the tuples of interest (here, the employees of a given department); only those tuples are required to satisfy Q. Pairing ∀ with a bare conjunction instead, (∀s)( P(s) ∧ Q(s) ), asserts something different: that every tuple s in the ENTIRE domain satisfies both P and Q — this is essentially never true for a real database, since tuples that fail P (rows of other relations, employees of other departments, etc.) immediately violate the conjunction. An existential quantifier, by contrast, is correctly paired with a conjunction: (∃s)( P(s) ∧ Q(s) ) = 'there exists some s satisfying both.' De Morgan's law connects the two forms: ¬(∃s)(P(s)) ⇔ (∀s)(¬P(s)).

Application

  1. The requirement: return department names d such that no employee of department d has sex = 'F'.

  2. Correctly written with a universal quantifier, this is (∀s)( (employee(s) ∧ s.deptId = d.deptId) → s.sex ≠ 'F' ) — the implication restricts s to employees of department d before requiring sex ≠ 'F'.

  3. By De Morgan's law this is equivalent to ¬(∃s)(employee(s) ∧ s.deptId = d.deptId ∧ s.sex = 'F') — 'there is no employee of department d with sex = F'.

  4. The given option that negates an existential quantifier with the predicate sex = 'F' is written in exactly this equivalent negated-existential form, so it correctly computes the required department names.

  5. The given option that uses a universal quantifier is written as (∀s)(employee(s) ∧ s.deptId = d.deptId ∧ s.sex ≠ 'F') — a bare conjunction, not an implication. As written it requires every tuple in the entire domain (not just employees of department d) to simultaneously be an employee of department d and non-female. Since the domain always contains tuples that fail this, the query as written is not equivalent to the correct implication form and does not answer the requirement.

  6. The given option that negates an existential quantifier with the predicate sex ≠ 'F' identifies departments with no non-female employee — i.e. departments that are all-female or empty — the opposite of the required condition.

  7. 'None of these' is therefore not correct, since one of the given queries (the negated-existential form with sex = 'F') already correctly answers the requirement.

Cross-check

  • Department with employees Alice (sex='F') and Bob (sex='M'): (∃s)(employee(s) ∧ deptId=d ∧ sex='F') is true (Alice), so the negated form is false — department correctly excluded.

  • Department with only Bob (sex='M'): no employee has sex='F', so the existential is false and the negated form is true — department correctly included.

  • Department with zero employees: the existential is trivially false (no employee exists), so the negated form is trivially true — an empty department is correctly included too, exactly as an empty set vacuously has no female employee. This vacuous inclusion is a shared, harmless property of the correct negated-existential form; it is NOT what disqualifies the conjunction-based universal option — that option is disqualified because a bare conjunction under ∀ forces the entire domain (not just department d's employees) to satisfy both conditions.

Conclusion: department names with no female employee are correctly obtained only by the negated-existential form (¬∃s, sex = 'F'). The universal-quantifier option is a common ∀+AND trap and, as written, is not equivalent to the correct implication form; the negated-existential option with the opposite predicate (¬∃s, sex ≠ 'F') answers a different question (all-female-or-empty departments); and since a correct option exists among the choices, 'None of these' is also wrong.

optionFeedback.html: This expression is true for department d exactly when every staff member of d (if any) has sex = 'F' — that is, when the department is all-female or has no staff at all. The task asks for departments with no female staff member (all-male or empty departments should qualify), which is a different, in fact opposite, condition. So this expression identifies a different set of departments than the ones asked for.

As written, this expression pairs a universal quantifier with a bare conjunction over three conditions on tuple s: s is a staff record, s belongs to department d, and s is non-female — joined with AND, not an implication. That requires every tuple s in the ENTIRE domain — not just the staff of department d — to simultaneously satisfy all three conditions at once. Since the domain always contains tuples that fail this (staff of other departments, the Department tuples themselves, and so on), this expression is false for essentially any real database, independent of whether department d itself has any staff. A universal quantifier needs an implication (if-then) to restrict the claim to just the staff of department d; a bare conjunction changes the meaning entirely. So this expression identifies a different set of departments than the ones asked for.

This expression is true for department d exactly when department d has no staff member with sex = 'F' — a department with zero female staff, including one with no staff at all (there is then no female staff member to find, which trivially satisfies the test). That is precisely the condition asked for. So this expression identifies exactly the departments asked for.

"None of these" would only hold if none of the other three expressions matched the departments asked for. One of them already identifies exactly the departments asked for, so a qualifying expression exists among the choices and "None of these" does not apply.

title: In TRC, which of the following expressions correctly retrieves all
subject: Data Base Management System
text: In TRC (Tuple Relational Calculus), which of the following expressions correctly retrieves all tuples from the Employee relation where the attribute salary is strictly greater than 50,000?
solution:
We need a Tuple Relational Calculus (TRC) expression of the form {t | P(t)} that returns exactly the Employee tuples whose salary exceeds 50000.

A safe TRC filter combines two parts with conjunction (∧): the membership predicate Employee(t), which binds t to tuples of the Employee relation, and the condition t.salary > 50000.

Therefore the correct expression is: {t | Employee(t) ∧ t.salary > 50000}.

Why the others fail: using ∨ (OR) admits any tuple that is an Employee OR earns more than 50000, so it neither filters Employees nor stays safe. Using → (implication) is vacuously true for every non-Employee tuple, again admitting unwanted tuples. σ salary>50000(Employee) is relational algebra, not TRC. And {t : salary > 50000 || Employee(t)} is malformed (salary is not bound to t) and uses OR.

Hence the answer is {t | Employee(t) ∧ t.salary > 50000}.

optionFeedback.html: Uses disjunction (∨). "Employee(t) ∨ t.salary > 50000" is satisfied by any tuple that is an Employee OR has salary > 50000, so it does not filter Employees down to the high-salary ones; with an unbounded tuple variable it is also an unsafe (potentially infinite) expression.

This is relational algebra, not relational calculus. σ is the selection operator of relational algebra; while the result set is right, it is the wrong formalism for a TRC question, which must be written as {t | P(t)}.

Malformed. The condition "salary > 50000" is not bound to the tuple variable t (it should be t.salary), and "||" expresses OR, which again admits tuples that are not Employees. The expression does not correctly restrict to Employee tuples with salary > 50000.

Uses implication (→). "Employee(t) → t.salary > 50000" is logically TRUE for every tuple that is NOT an Employee (vacuous truth), so it admits arbitrary non-Employee tuples and is an unsafe expression rather than a filter.

Correct. The predicate Employee(t) restricts t to tuples of the Employee relation, and the conjunction (∧) with t.salary > 50000 keeps only those whose salary exceeds 50000 — the standard, safe TRC form {t | R(t) ∧ condition(t)}.

title: Amongst the ACID properties of transaction, the 'Durability' property requires
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Amongst the ACID properties of a transaction, the 'Durability' property requires that the changes made to the database by a successful transaction persist. ISRO(2023) GATE(2005)

options.html: Except in case of an operating system crash
Except in case of a disk crash
Except in case of a power failure
Always, even if there is a failure of any kind

solution:
Concept

Durability is one of the four ACID properties of a database transaction. It guarantees that once a transaction commits, its effects become permanent -- the changes it made are never lost, no matter what happens to the system afterward. This guarantee is unconditional: it must hold across every kind of subsequent failure (an operating-system crash, a disk or storage failure, or a power outage), not just some of them. It is implemented by writing changes to non-volatile, stable storage as part of commit -- typically through write-ahead logging, checkpointing, and a redo/recovery procedure that replays committed work after any failure.

Application

The stem describes exactly this guarantee and asks which statement correctly captures it. Because durability's promise is unconditional across failure types, the description that matches the ACID definition is the one stating that the committed changes persist always, regardless of what kind of failure occurs -- an operating-system crash, a disk crash, or a power failure are precisely the scenarios durability is built to survive, not exceptions carved out of it.

Cross-check

Each of the other three descriptions carves out one specific failure type as an exception where durability supposedly does not hold -- but durability is built to survive all three:

  • Operating-system crash: recovery logging replays every committed transaction's write-ahead log on restart, so this is not a gap.

  • Disk crash: stable or redundant storage plus archived logs protect committed data against storage-level failure, so this is not a gap either.

  • Power failure: the log is force-written to stable storage before commit acknowledgement, so an immediate power loss still leaves the log intact for replay.

Since durability is designed to survive all three of these cases, not just some, none of the restricted descriptions can be correct, and only the unconditional description -- persisting through any kind of failure -- matches the ACID definition.

optionFeedback.html: Durability's recovery mechanism specifically covers an operating-system crash: on restart, the recovery manager replays the write-ahead log for every committed transaction, restoring every committed change, so no operating-system-crash exception exists in the guarantee.

Durability's recovery mechanism specifically covers a disk crash: replicated or stable storage, periodic backups, and archived logs protect committed data against storage-level failure, so no disk-crash exception exists in the guarantee.

Durability's recovery mechanism specifically covers a power failure: the log is force-written to stable storage before a commit is acknowledged, so even an immediate power loss leaves the log intact for replay during recovery, meaning no power-failure exception exists in the guarantee.

Durability's recovery mechanism covers every one of these failure types together: the same write-ahead logging and stable-storage protocol that survives an operating-system crash, a disk crash, and a power failure applies without exception, so committed changes persist regardless of which failure occurs.

title: ACID is set of properties that guarantee that database transactions
subject: Data Base Management System
text: ACID is a set of properties that guarantee that database transactions are processed reliably. Here A stands for
solution:
Concept

In a database, a transaction is a logical unit of work made up of one or more operations. The ACID properties are the four guarantees a transaction system must provide so that data stays valid even when errors, crashes, or power failures occur. ACID is an acronym: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

Applying it to this item

The letter A in ACID stands for Atomicity. Atomicity means a transaction is treated as a single, indivisible "all-or-nothing" unit: either every operation inside it completes successfully and is committed, or — if any operation fails — the whole transaction is rolled back and the database is left exactly as it was before the transaction started. There is no partial result.

Example: a bank transfer debits one account and credits another. Atomicity guarantees that you can never end up with the debit applied but the credit lost — both happen, or neither does.

Why the other terms are not "A"

  • Consistency — the C in ACID; a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, preserving all rules and constraints.

  • Isolation — the I in ACID; concurrent transactions do not interfere with one another, as if each ran alone.

  • Durability — the D in ACID; once a transaction is committed, its effects survive any later system failure.

So among the choices, Atomicity is the property denoted by A; "Access", "Algorithm", and "Affiliation" are not part of the ACID model at all.

optionFeedback.html: "Access" is not one of the four ACID properties. This choice usually comes from confusing ACID with access control or permissions — a database security topic about who is allowed to read or modify data, which is unrelated to the transaction-reliability guarantees that ACID describes.

Atomicity is exactly what the A in ACID denotes: a transaction runs as one indivisible all-or-nothing unit — every operation commits together, or the whole transaction rolls back leaving the database unchanged. This is the standard, widely documented meaning of the A property.

"Algorithm" is a general computing term for a step-by-step procedure to solve a problem. It is not a transaction property and does not appear anywhere in the ACID acronym, which names guarantees about transaction behaviour rather than a method of computation.

"Affiliation" refers to association or membership and has no meaning in database transaction theory; it is not part of the ACID model. It is offered here only as a distractor because it happens to begin with the letter A.

title: Which ACID property ensures that transaction is executed entirely or
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which ACID property ensures that a transaction is executed entirely or not executed at all, so that partial updates are not permanently applied if a failure occurs during execution?
solution:
Correct answer: Atomicity.

Atomicity is the ACID property that guarantees a transaction is treated as a single, indivisible unit of work — it is either executed entirely (all of its operations commit) or not executed at all. It is popularly called the “all-or-nothing” rule.

If a failure (system crash, power loss, error, or explicit abort) occurs midway through a transaction, the recovery mechanism rolls back every change the transaction has already made, so no partial updates are left permanently in the database. The classic example is a fund transfer: debiting account A and crediting account B must both succeed; if the credit fails after the debit, atomicity ensures the debit is undone so money is never lost.

The other ACID properties solve different problems: Consistency keeps the database in a valid state with respect to all rules and constraints, Isolation keeps concurrently running transactions from interfering with one another, and Durability guarantees that once a transaction commits, its effects survive subsequent failures. (Recoverability is a schedule property, not one of the four ACID properties.) Hence the property described here is Atomicity.

optionFeedback.html: Consistency guarantees that a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, preserving all defined rules, constraints, and invariants. It is about correctness of state with respect to integrity rules, not about whether a transaction runs fully or is undone on failure, so it does not match a description focused on all-or-nothing execution.

Isolation ensures that concurrently executing transactions do not interfere with each other, so each transaction behaves as if it were running alone. It addresses concurrency effects (dirty reads, lost updates, etc.), not the all-or-nothing handling of a single transaction during a failure.

Recoverability is a property of schedules (it concerns whether a transaction commits only after the transactions it read from have committed), not one of the four ACID properties. It is therefore not the term that answers a question asking for the ACID property guaranteeing complete-or-nothing execution.

Correct. Atomicity is the “all-or-nothing” ACID property: a transaction is executed entirely or not at all. If a failure occurs mid-way, every change made so far is rolled back so no partial update is permanently applied — exactly the behaviour described in the question.

Durability guarantees that once a transaction has committed, its changes are permanent and survive subsequent failures such as crashes or power loss. It is about persistence of committed results after commit, not about undoing partial work when a transaction fails before completing.

title: Which one of the following is NOT part of the
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which one of the following is NOT a part of the ACID properties of database transaction?
solution:
Concept — A transaction is one logical unit of work on a database, and the guarantees a DBMS must provide for every such unit are summarised by the four-letter acronym ACID. Each letter names a property of how a transaction executes, not a way of describing the data that happens to be stored.

Applying it here — the four letters expand as follows:

  • A — Atomicity: the unit of work is indivisible; either all of its operations take effect or none of them do, with partial work rolled back.

  • C — Consistency: the unit of work carries the database from one valid state to another, leaving every declared constraint, key and trigger rule satisfied.

  • I — Isolation: concurrently running units of work do not observe one another’s intermediate states; the overall effect matches some serial order of execution.

  • D — Durability: once a commit returns, the effects survive a later crash or power loss because they are already in stable storage.

Matching the options — Atomicity, Consistency and Durability are three of those four letters. The fourth letter, Isolation, does not appear among the options at all; the term standing in its place is Instance, which belongs to a different part of DBMS vocabulary. An instance is the data actually held in the database at a given moment — the current contents whose structure the schema defines — and it changes with every insert, update and delete.

Cross-check — read each term into the sentence “the DBMS must guarantee ___ for every transaction”. Atomicity, consistency and durability read as transaction guarantees. Instance does not: a database has an instance at all times, whether or not any transaction is running, so it is a description of state rather than a guarantee about execution.

Hence the term that is not part of the ACID properties is Instance.

optionFeedback.html: Atomicity describes all-or-nothing execution of a unit of work: every operation inside it takes effect together, and a failure part-way through leaves none of them applied, the partial work being rolled back.
Consistency describes a unit of work carrying the database from one valid state to another, with every declared integrity constraint, key and trigger rule still satisfied when the unit of work ends.

An instance describes the data actually held in the database at a given moment — the current contents whose structure the schema defines — changing with every insert, update and delete that is applied to it.

Durability describes the permanence of committed effects: once a commit returns, the changes survive a crash or power loss because they are already recorded in stable storage such as the write-ahead log.

title: In transactions, write-item command includes the following steps. Arrange the
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
In transactions, a write-item (X) command includes the following steps. Arrange the following steps in correct sequence.

A. Copy item X from the program variable named X into its correct location in the buffer.

B. Store the updated block from the buffer back to disk.

C. Find the address of the disk block that contains item.

D. Copy that disk block into a buffer in main memory.

choose the correct answer from the options given below:

  1. C,D,A,B

  2. A,C,D,B

  3. C,A,B,D

  4. D,B,C,A
solution:
Correct Sequence for Write-Item Command

To perform a write-item (X) command in a database transaction system, the following logical steps must occur in a specific order to ensure data integrity and proper buffer management.

  1. Find the address of the disk block that contains item (Step C). The system must first locate the specific block on the disk.

  2. Copy that disk block into a buffer in main memory (Step D). Once the address is found, the block is loaded from the disk into a buffer in RAM.

  3. Copy item X from the program variable named X into its correct location in the buffer (Step A). The new data is then written into the specific location within the in-memory buffer.

  4. Store the updated block from the buffer back to disk (Step B). Finally, the modified block in the buffer is written back to the permanent storage on the disk.

Therefore, the correct sequence is C → D → A → B.

Loading the disk block must occur before copying data into a buffer for modification.
This sequence is incorrect because the disk block must be loaded into memory (D) before data can be copied into its buffer location (A).
This sequence is incorrect because the updated block cannot be stored back to disk (B) before the item has been copied into the buffer (A).

title: What is the primary purpose of the COMMIT operation in
subject: Data Base Management System
text: What is the primary purpose of the COMMIT operation in a database management transaction?

options.html: To permanently apply all changes made during the transaction
To temporarily save the changes for testing
To rollback the transaction to its initial state
To check the consistency of the database schema

solution:
The primary purpose of the COMMIT operation in a database management transaction is to permanently save all changes made during the transaction to the database.


Note for more understanding
In database management systems, transactions are governed by the ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability). The COMMIT operation is the mechanical trigger for both Atomicity and Durability.

  1. The Concept of a Transaction: A transaction is a bundle of multiple SQL statements that must execute as a single unit of work. For example, a bank transfer requires deducting money from Account A and adding it to Account B.

  2. Staging Area: While these operations are running, the changes are kept in a provisional state. Other database users cannot see these modifications yet (due to Isolation).

  3. Making it Permanent: If all statements within the transaction execute perfectly without errors, the application issues a COMMIT command. This tells the database engine to write these changes safely from the temporary memory buffers directly onto the hard disk transaction logs.

Once the COMMIT completes, the transaction is officially closed, the changes become permanent, visible to all users, and resilient even in the event of a sudden power failure or system crash.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The primary role of the COMMIT command is to conclude a transaction successfully and save all modifications (like INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE) permanently to the non-volatile storage of the database. Once committed, these changes cannot be undone by a rollback.

Incorrect. Changes made during a transaction are temporary and isolated from other users until they are finalized, but this temporary state is a feature of the transaction itself, not the purpose of COMMIT. COMMIT does the exact opposite—it makes them completely permanent.

Incorrect. This describes the ROLLBACK operation. ROLLBACK is used to cancel a transaction if an error occurs, erasing all temporary modifications and restoring the database to the clean state it was in before the transaction started.

Incorrect. Database consistency, structural constraints (like foreign keys or data types), and schema validations are automatically checked by the Database Management System (DBMS) engine during operation execution, not explicitly by the COMMIT command.

title: Which of the following concurrency problem exist in the above
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following concurrency problems exist in the above schedule?
solution:
Concept: A transaction schedule can exhibit three classic read/write anomalies over a shared data item. A lost update happens when two transactions each read the same original value before either writes, so one write silently overwrites the other's update. A dirty read happens when a transaction reads a value that another transaction wrote but has not yet committed. An unrepeatable read happens when a single transaction reads the same item twice within its own execution and gets two different values because another transaction updated and committed it in between.

Application: tracing the timeline

  1. T1 reads X at t0, computes X = X - N at t1, and writes the updated X at t2 — completing T1's read-modify-write sequence on X with no commit operation shown afterward.

  2. T2 reads X at t3, immediately after T1's write at t2 (not before it), so T2's read picks up the value T1 just produced rather than the value that existed before T1 started.

  3. T2 computes X = X + M at t4 and writes X at t5, again with no commit operation shown for T2.

  4. Because T2's read at t3 occurs after T1's write at t2 with no commit recorded for T1 in between, T2 has read a value that T1's transaction could still roll back — this is the defining condition of a dirty read.

Cross-check: ruling the other anomalies in or out

  • Lost update needs both transactions to read the original value of X before either writes it. Here T2's only read_item(X) happens at t3, strictly after T1's write_item(X) at t2, so T2 never sees the pre-T1 value of X.

  • Unrepeatable read needs one transaction to read the same item twice with different results. In this schedule, T1 executes read_item(X) exactly once and T2 executes read_item(X) exactly once, so no transaction observes X changing across two reads of its own.

  • Since the lost-update timing is not met and no transaction reads twice, the combined option requiring both a lost update and a dirty read together cannot hold either.

Result: the schedule exhibits a dirty read — T2 reads X immediately after T1's uncommitted write at t2.

optionFeedback.html: A lost update requires both transactions to read the same original value of X before either one writes it, so that one transaction's write overwrites the other's update. In this schedule, T1 performs read_item(X) at t0 and write_item(X) at t2, and T2 performs read_item(X) at t3 and write_item(X) at t5.

A dirty read requires a transaction to read a value that another transaction has written but not yet committed. In this schedule, T1 performs write_item(X) at t2 and T2 performs read_item(X) at t3, with no commit operation shown for T1 anywhere in the schedule.

An unrepeatable read requires a single transaction to read the same data item twice within its own execution and get two different values, because another transaction updated and committed that item in between the two reads. In this schedule, T1 performs read_item(X) once, at t0, and T2 performs read_item(X) once, at t3.

This option requires the schedule to satisfy two conditions together: both transactions reading X's original value before either one writes it, and one transaction reading a value that another transaction wrote but had not yet committed. In this schedule, T1 performs read_item(X) at t0 and write_item(X) at t2, and T2 performs read_item(X) at t3 and write_item(X) at t5, with no commit operation shown for either transaction.

title: What are the potential problems when DBMS executes multiple transactions
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
What are the potential problems when a DBMS executes multiple transactions concurrently.

1. The dirty read

2. The durability

3. The phantom read

4. The serializability
solution:
Explanation:

When multiple transactions execute concurrently, certain problems can arise due to interference between them. These include:

1. Dirty read: A transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not yet committed.

2. Unrepeatable read: A transaction reads the same data twice, but the value changes between reads due to another transaction.

3. Lost update: Two transactions update the same data, and one overwrites the other's changes.

4. Phantom read: A transaction re-executes a query and gets different sets of rows due to another transaction inserting or deleting rows.

Note: Durability and serializability are not concurrency problems. Durability ensures committed data is not lost, and serializability is a correctness property.

title: Two phase locking protocol has which of the following problem(s)?
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following problem(s) can occur in the Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL) protocol?
solution:
Two-phase locking (2PL) protocol ensures serializability by dividing transaction execution into two phases: a growing phase (acquiring locks) and a shrinking phase (releasing locks).

In Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL), all exclusive locks are held until the transaction commits or aborts.

One major issue with Strict 2PL is deadlock. Deadlock occurs when two or more transactions are waiting for each other to release locks, resulting in a standstill. For example, if transaction T1 holds a lock on resource R1 and waits for R2, while T2 holds a lock on R2 and waits for R1, neither transaction can proceed.

Cascading rollback is not a problem in Strict 2PL. Since exclusive locks are not released until commit or abort, no other transaction can read uncommitted data. Therefore, cascading rollbacks are prevented.

Hence, the primary problem associated with Strict 2PL is deadlock, while cascading rollback does not occur under Strict 2PL.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Chances of deadlock.

optionFeedback.html:
The answer "Chances of deadlock" is correct only for Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL). In Strict 2PL, exclusive locks are held until commit or abort, which prevents cascading rollbacks, but deadlocks can still occur when transactions wait for each other's locks.

Therefore, for Strict 2PL, the correct answer is: Chances of deadlock

IN Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL), then Cascading Rollback does not occur because all exclusive locks are held until the transaction commits or aborts. Therefore, "Cascading Rollback" is not the correct answer for Strict 2PL.

If the protocol is Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL), then "Neither 1 nor 2" is not the correct answer. Deadlock can still occur Cascading Rollback does not occur Therefore, for Strict 2PL, the correct answer is "Chances of deadlock", not "Neither 1 nor 2".

If the protocol is Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL), then "Both 1 & 2" is not the correct answer. Deadlock can occur Cascading Rollback does not occur because exclusive locks are held until commit or abort. Therefore, for Strict 2PL, the correct answer is "Chances of deadlock", not "Both 1 & 2".

title: Which of the following is also known as read-write conflict?
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following concurrency anomalies is also known as a read-write conflict?
solution:
Concept: Concurrency-control theory names a conflict between two transactions on the same data item by the chronological order of their two operations: a read followed later by another transaction’s write is a read-write (R-W) conflict; a write followed later by another transaction’s read is a write-read (W-R) conflict; and a write followed later by another transaction’s write is a write-write (W-W) conflict.

Application: Trace the operations for an unrepeatable read on an item X:

  1. Transaction T1 reads item X.

  2. Transaction T2 writes/updates item X and commits.

  3. T1 reads item X again, later in the same execution, and gets a different value than its first read.

The two operations on X therefore occur in the order read (T1) → write (T2), which is exactly the read-then-write ordering that defines a read-write conflict — so “read-write conflict” is the alternate name for unrepeatable read.

Cross-check against the other anomalies:

Anomaly

Operation order on the item

Conflict type

Dirty read / uncommitted dependency (same anomaly)

write (uncommitted) → read

write-read (W-R)

Lost update problem

write → write

write-write (W-W)

Unrepeatable read

read → write

read-write (R-W)

Result: Only the unrepeatable read matches the read-then-write ordering that defines a read-write conflict, so the correct answer is unrepeatable read.

optionFeedback.html: Dirty read describes a transaction reading a value that another transaction wrote but has not yet committed, so the value read may vanish from the database if that other transaction later rolls back.

The lost update problem describes two transactions concurrently updating the same data item, where one transaction's update is overwritten by the other's, so the effect of the first update never survives in the database.

Unrepeatable read describes a transaction getting two different values when it reads the same data item twice within its own execution, because another transaction changed that item in between the two reads.

Uncommitted dependency describes a transaction's later processing being based on a value written by another transaction that has not yet committed, so that basis disappears if the writing transaction aborts.

title: Which of the following is conflict equivalent serial schedule for
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Which of the following is a conflict equivalent serial schedule for the precedence graph given below involving transactions T1, T2, T3, and T4?

(1) T1, T4, T3, T2

(2) T1, T4, T2, T3

(3) T2, T1, T3, T4

(4) T2, T1, T4, T3
solution:
Conclusion: The only conflict-equivalent serial schedule is T1, T4, T2, T3.

Precedence edges:

  • T1 -> T4 (T1 must come before T4)

  • T1 -> T3 (T1 must come before T3)

  • T4 -> T2 (T4 must come before T2)

  • T4 -> T3 (T4 must come before T3)

  • T2 -> T3 (T2 must come before T3)

Deriving the order:

From the edges we must have T1 before T4, T4 before T2, and T2 before T3. Combining these constraints yields the ordering T1 before T4 before T2 before T3, i.e., T1, T4, T2, T3.

Check each candidate sequence:

  • T1, T4, T2, T3 — satisfies all edges, so it is valid.

  • T1, T4, T3, T2 — invalid because it places T3 before T2, violating T2 -> T3.

  • T2, T1, T3, T4 — invalid because it places T2 before T4 (and before T1 in this order), violating T1 -> T4 and T4 -> T2.

  • T2, T1, T4, T3 — invalid because it places T2 before T4, violating T4 -> T2 (and also conflicts with T1 -> T4).

Therefore the only conflict-equivalent serial schedule from the given choices is T1, T4, T2, T3.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The precedence graph requires T1 before T4 and T3, T4 before T2 and T3, and T2 before T3. The only serial order that respects all these constraints is T1, T4, T2, T3, so the choice that states "T1, T4, T2, T3" is valid.

Incorrect. The grouping that includes the sequence T1, T4, T3, T2 is invalid because it places T3 before T2, violating the edge T2 -> T3 in the precedence graph. Therefore the pair that claims both sequences are valid is wrong.

Incorrect. Both sequences that start with T2 are invalid because they place T2 before T4 (and before T1 in one case), but the graph requires T1 before T4 and T4 before T2. Those ordering constraints make any sequence with T2 first impossible.
Incorrect. "None of these" is wrong because the sequence T1, T4, T2, T3 does satisfy all precedence edges, so at least one of the given sequences is valid.

title: Consider the following schedule consisting of three transactions in database
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following schedule S, consisting of three transactions in a database system:
S: r1(X), w1(Y), r2(Y), w2(Z), c1, w3(X), c2, c3.
How many edges are there in the precedence graph of the given schedule?
solution:
Concept: A precedence graph (serialization graph) for a schedule has one node per transaction. For every pair of operations on the SAME data item, from DIFFERENT transactions, where at least one operation is a WRITE, an edge is drawn from the transaction whose operation appears EARLIER in the schedule to the transaction whose operation appears LATER. Read-write, write-read, and write-write pairs across transactions all create edges; a read-read pair never does. This rule depends only on the RELATIVE ORDER of the two conflicting operations: commit operations (ci) are bookkeeping markers only -- they never create an edge, and a transaction having already committed does not remove or block an edge already established by one of its earlier operations against a later operation of another transaction.

  1. Data item X: the only operations on X are r1(X) at position 1 and w3(X) at position 6, from different transactions (T1 and T3), and one of them is a write, so they conflict. Since r1(X) occurs before w3(X) in the schedule, this creates an edge T1 -> T3. c1 (the commit of T1) occurs at position 5, strictly between r1(X) and w3(X) -- but c1 is not itself a conflicting operation, so it neither creates nor removes an edge; only the relative order of r1(X) and w3(X) matters, and that order is fixed regardless of where the commit falls.

  2. Data item Y: the operations on Y are w1(Y) at position 2 and r2(Y) at position 3, from different transactions (T1 and T2), and one is a write, so they conflict. w1(Y) precedes r2(Y), so this creates an edge T1 -> T2.

  3. Data item Z: only w2(Z) touches Z, from a single transaction (T2). With no other transaction accessing Z, there is no conflicting pair on Z, so no edge is produced.

  4. Commit operations c1, c2, c3 are bookkeeping markers only and never contribute edges by themselves.

Cross-check: Cross-check by scanning every pair of transactions directly: (T1, T2) share data item Y -> one edge; (T1, T3) share data item X -> one edge; (T2, T3) share no common data item -> no possible edge. This independently confirms exactly two edges.

Note: Note on the reported confusion: c1 appearing before w3(X) in the schedule does NOT remove the T1 -> T3 edge. A precedence-graph edge is fixed purely by the order of the two conflicting read/write operations (here, r1(X) before w3(X)); it does not matter that T1 had already committed by the time T3's w3(X) executed. Commit order and conflict order are separate things -- only conflict order (the order of the actual read/write operations on the shared item) determines precedence-graph edges.

Total edges in the precedence graph: 2

text:
Consider the following read-write schedule S over three transactions T1,T2, and T3​, where the subscripts in the schedule indicate transaction IDs:

solution:
Key insight: build the precedence (conflict) graph by finding conflicting read/write or write/write operations on the same data item.

  • Conflicts on y produce edges from the transaction that writes y first to the transaction that later reads or writes y: T3's write on y precedes T2's read and write on y, giving an edge T3 → T2.

  • T3's earlier read on y also conflicts with T2's later write on y, reinforcing the same edge T3 → T2.

  • T1 accesses only z and does not conflict with T2 or T3, so T1 is independent in the precedence graph.

The resulting precedence graph has a single directed edge: T3 → T2, and is acyclic.

Conclusion: Any serial schedule that preserves the required order T3 before T2 is conflict-equivalent to the given schedule. Any serial schedule that places T2 before T3 is not conflict-equivalent.

Applying this to the listed serial schedules:

  • The serial schedule "T1 T2 T3" places T2 before T3, violating the required T3 → T2 order, so it is not conflict-equivalent.

  • The serial schedules that place T3 before T2 (for example "T1 T3 T2", "T3 T2 T1", and "T3 T1 T2") preserve the precedence and are conflict-equivalent.

That creates a precedence edge from T3 to T2, so any conflict-equivalent serial order must place T3 before T2. The serial order T1 then T2 then T3 places T2 before T3, which reverses that required order and therefore is not conflict-equivalent.

Conflict-equivalent. This serial order places the transaction that accesses y (T3) before the transaction that later accesses y (T2), preserving the conflict relation. T1 only accesses z and has no conflicts with T2 or T3, so placing it first does not break equivalence.

Conflict-equivalent. This serial order places T3 before T2, preserving the required precedence from conflicts on y. T1 is independent and can be placed anywhere without affecting conflict equivalence.

Conflict-equivalent. T3 appears before T2 here, which preserves the conflict edges arising from operations on y. T1 accesses z only and does not participate in conflicts, so this order is conflict-equivalent to the given schedule.

title: Consider following schedule with sequence of operations on data object
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following schedule on data object Q, whose initial value is 500. What will be the final value of Q after the last operation?

2. T2: Read(Q)
3. T1: Q = Q + 100
4. T2: Q = Q + 100

solution:
• Initial value: Q = 500.

    1. T1 reads Q, so local T1 = 500.
    2. T2 reads Q, so local T2 = 500. This happens before any transaction writes a new value.
    3. T1 computes Q = 500 + 100 = 600 in its local copy.
    4. T2 computes Q = 500 + 100 = 600 in its local copy.
    5. T2 writes its local value, so database Q becomes 600.
    6. T1 writes its local value last, so database Q is overwritten with 600 again.

    Final value of Q = 600. Therefore, option A is correct.

Incorrect. 700 would occur only if the second transaction read Q after the first transaction had already written 600. Here both transactions read 500 first.
Incorrect. No operation subtracts 50 or produces 550 in this schedule.
Incorrect. Q is written after both transactions compute Q + 100, so the final value cannot remain 500.

solution:

Two schedules, S1 and S2, involving the same set of transactions are defined as conflict equivalent if and only if the relative order of all conflicting operations (operations belonging to different transactions, accessing the same data item, where at least one is a write) remains identical in both schedules.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. This directly matches the fundamental database textbook definition for establishing equivalence based on preserving the relative order of conflicting execution steps.
Incorrect. "Schema equivalence" pertains to structural database designs or relational layouts matching each other, and has no contextual meaning regarding concurrent transaction schedule execution.
Incorrect. Result equivalence means two schedules produce the same final database state, which can happen by chance even if conflicting operations are reordered.

title: Consider the following transactions operating on database items and with
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following transactions operating on database items X and Y with initial values:

X = 200, Y = 100

Transaction T₁

Read X

X := X − 10

Write X

Transaction T₂

Read Y

Y := Y + 20

Write Y

Both transactions execute completely and exactly once in any serial order without rollback or failure. What will be the final values of X and Y?
solution:
Step 1 — Note the initial values: X = 200, Y = 100.

Step 2 — Identify which item each transaction modifies:

• T₁ reads X, computes X := X − 10, and writes X. It touches only X.

• T₂ reads Y, computes Y := Y + 20, and writes Y. It touches only Y.

Step 3 — Apply each operation:

• T₁: X = 200 − 10 = 190.

• T₂: Y = 100 + 20 = 120.

Step 4 — Check the effect of the serial order. T₁ works only on X and T₂ works only on Y, so the two transactions operate on disjoint data items. There is no read–write or write–write overlap between them, hence no interference. Whether the serial order is T₁ → T₂ or T₂ → T₁, the outcome is identical.

Since both transactions execute exactly once and commit without rollback, the final values are X = 190 and Y = 120.

Answer: X = 190, Y = 120.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. T₁ subtracts 10 from X (200 − 10 = 190) and T₂ adds 20 to Y (100 + 20 = 120). The transactions touch disjoint items, so every serial order gives X = 190, Y = 120.
Incorrect. X = 210 would require adding 10 to X, but T₁ subtracts 10 (X := X − 10), giving X = 190, not 210. The sign of the operation on X has been reversed here.
Incorrect. X = 190 is right, but Y = 100 ignores T₂ entirely. T₂ executes once and computes Y := Y + 20, so Y must change from 100 to 120, not stay at 100.

Incorrect. X = 200, Y = 100 are the initial values, meaning neither transaction's write took effect. The stem states both transactions execute completely without rollback, so both writes must be applied.
Incorrect. Both values are wrong: X = 210 reverses T₁'s subtraction (it should be 200 − 10 = 190) and Y = 80 subtracts 20 instead of adding it (it should be 100 + 20 = 120).

title: Suppose database schedule involves transactions Consider the precedence graph of
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Suppose a database schedule S involves transactions T1 , T2 , .............,Tn . Consider the precedence graph of S with vertices representing the transactions and edges representing the conflicts. If S is serializable, which one of the following orderings of the vertices of the precedence graph is guaranteed to yield a serial schedule ?
solution:
Main idea: If the schedule is conflict-serializable, its precedence graph has no directed cycles (it is a directed acyclic graph, or DAG).

  • A topological ordering of the DAG arranges transactions so that for every directed edge from one transaction to another, the source transaction appears earlier in the order.

  • Executing transactions serially in any topological order preserves the order of all conflicting operations, so the resulting serial schedule is conflict-equivalent to the original schedule.

  • How to obtain such an order: run any topological sort algorithm (for example, Kahn's algorithm or a DFS-based method using finishing times). If a cycle is detected, the schedule is not conflict-serializable.

Conclusion: A topological ordering of the precedence graph is guaranteed to yield a serial schedule when the schedule is serializable, because it respects all conflict dependencies.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. If the schedule is conflict-serializable, the precedence graph has no cycles (it is a directed acyclic graph). A topological ordering of that graph lists transactions so that every conflict edge goes from an earlier transaction to a later one. Executing the transactions serially in that topological order yields a serial schedule that is conflict-equivalent to the original schedule.

Not necessarily. A plain depth-first traversal (preorder) does not guarantee that all precedence edges go forward in the traversal order. A depth-first-based topological sort (using finishing times and reversing them) can produce a valid ordering, but an arbitrary depth-first visit order by itself is not guaranteed to yield a serial schedule.

Not necessarily. Breadth-first traversal visits nodes by distance from a start node and may place a successor before its predecessor with respect to conflict edges. Therefore a breadth-first order does not guarantee that every conflict is respected, so it does not ensure a serial schedule.

Not necessarily. Ordering transactions by their numeric indices is arbitrary with respect to the precedence (conflict) relationships. Such an order may violate precedence edges and thus fail to produce a serial schedule unless the indices happen to already respect the dependencies.

text:
Consider following schedules involving two transactions:

\(S_{1}: \: r_{1}(X);r_{1}(Y);r_{2}(X);r_{2}(Y);w_{2}(Y);w_{1}(X) \\ S_{2}: \: r_{1}(X);r_{2}(X);r_{2}(Y);w_{2}(Y);r_{1}(Y);w_{1}(X)\)

Which one of the following statements is correct with respect to above ?

options.html: Both 𝑆1 and 𝑆2 are conflict serializable.
𝑆1 is conflict serializable and 𝑆2 is not conflict serializable
𝑆1 is not conflict serializable and 𝑆2 is conflict serializable
Both 𝑆1  and 𝑆2 are not conflict serializable

solution:
Final answer: S1 is not conflict serializable; S2 is conflict serializable.

Analysis of schedule S1:

  • Conflicting pair: r1(Y) occurs before w2(Y), so there is an edge from transaction 1 to transaction 2.

  • Conflicting pair: r2(X) occurs before w1(X), so there is an edge from transaction 2 to transaction 1.

  • These edges create a cycle (transaction 1 -> transaction 2 -> transaction 1), so the precedence graph is cyclic and S1 is not conflict serializable.

Analysis of schedule S2:

  • Conflicting pair: r2(X) occurs before w1(X), which gives an edge from transaction 2 to transaction 1.

  • Conflicting pair: w2(Y) occurs before r1(Y), which also gives an edge from transaction 2 to transaction 1.

  • All conflict edges point from transaction 2 to transaction 1; there is no cycle, so the precedence graph is acyclic and S2 is conflict serializable.

  • Equivalent serial order: transaction 2 then transaction 1.

Tip: To determine conflict serializability, list all pairs of conflicting operations on the same data item performed by different transactions, draw edges in a precedence graph from the earlier transaction to the later one, and check the graph for cycles. A cycle means not conflict serializable; no cycle means conflict serializable.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Schedule S1 is not conflict serializable: r1(Y) occurs before w2(Y), which gives an edge from transaction 1 to transaction 2, and r2(X) occurs before w1(X), which gives an edge from transaction 2 to transaction 1; these edges form a cycle. Schedule S2 is conflict serializable (see below). A reliable way to check is to build the precedence (conflict) graph of conflicting operations.

Incorrect. Schedule S1 is not conflict serializable because it produces a cycle: r1(Y) before w2(Y) gives an edge from transaction 1 to transaction 2, and r2(X) before w1(X) gives an edge from transaction 2 to transaction 1. Schedule S2 is conflict serializable: all conflicts point from transaction 2 to transaction 1, so there is no cycle and it is equivalent to the serial order where transaction 2 runs before transaction 1.

Correct. For S1, the conflicting operations produce edges T1 -> T2 (r1(Y) before w2(Y)) and T2 -> T1 (r2(X) before w1(X)), creating a cycle, so S1 is not conflict serializable. For S2, all conflicts produce edges from transaction 2 to transaction 1 (r2(X) before w1(X) and w2(Y) before r1(Y)), so the precedence graph is acyclic and S2 is conflict serializable; the equivalent serial order is transaction 2 followed by transaction 1.

Incorrect. Schedule S2 is conflict serializable: its conflicts all point from transaction 2 to transaction 1 (for example, r2(X) before w1(X) and w2(Y) before r1(Y)), so the precedence graph is acyclic and S2 is equivalent to the serial order transaction 2 then transaction 1. Schedule S1, however, has a cycle between the two transactions and is not conflict serializable.

subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following schedules given below:

S1: r1(X),r2(Z),w2(X),w2(Y),r1(Y),r3(X),w3(Z),w1(Z),w2(Z),C2,w3(X),C3,w1(X),C1

S2: r1(Y),w1(Y),r2(Y),r3(Y),r1(X),w2(Y),w1(Z),w3(Z),C3,w1(X),C1,r2(X),C2

Which of the following is True:

options.html: S1 is cascadeless but not recoverable and S2 is cascadeless but not recoverable
S1 is not cascadeless but recoverable and S2 is not cascadeless and not recoverable
S1 is not cascadeless but recoverable and S2 is cascadeless and recoverable
S1 is cascadeless and recoverable and S2 is not cascadeless and not recoverable

solution:
Definitions:

  • Cascadeless: No transaction reads data written by another uncommitted transaction (no dirty reads).

  • Recoverable: If a transaction Tj reads a value written by Ti, then Ti must commit before Tj commits.

Analyze S1:

  • S1 contains w2(Y) followed later by r1(Y): T1 reads Y written by T2 before T2 commits → this is a dirty read, so S1 is not cascadeless.

  • Commit order: C2 (commit of T2) appears before C1 (commit of T1) and before C3. Transactions that read from T2 (T1 and T3) commit after T2, so every read-from dependency has the writer committing before the reader → S1 is recoverable.

Analyze S2:

  • S2 contains w1(Y) followed by r2(Y) and r3(Y): T2 and T3 read Y written by T1 before T1 commits → dirty reads, so S2 is not cascadeless.

  • Commit order: T3 commits (C3) before T1 commits (C1), yet T3 read T1's uncommitted write on Y. Because a reader (T3) committed before the writer (T1), S2 is not recoverable.

Conclusion: S1 is not cascadeless but is recoverable; S2 is not cascadeless and is not recoverable.

In S1, T1 reads Y after T2 wrote Y but before T2 commits (w2(Y) then r1(Y)), so S1 is not cascadeless. However, T1 commits after T2 (C2 appears before C1), so S1 is recoverable. In S2, T2 and T3 read Y written by T1 before T1 commits (w1(Y) then r2(Y) and r3(Y)), and T3 even commits before T1 (C3 before C1), making S2 not recoverable.

This statement is correct. S1 is not cascadeless because T1 reads Y written by T2 before T2 commits (w2(Y) then r1(Y)), but it is recoverable because every transaction that read from another commits after the writer (C2 appears before C1 and C3). S2 is not cascadeless because T2 and T3 read Y written by T1 before T1 commits (w1(Y) then r2(Y), r3(Y)), and it is not recoverable because T3 commits before T1 (C3 before C1) even though T3 read T1's uncommitted write.

This statement is incorrect. While S1 is correctly identified as not cascadeless and recoverable, S2 is not cascadeless and is also not recoverable. In S2, T2 and T3 read Y written by T1 before T1 commits (w1(Y) then r2(Y), r3(Y)), and since T3 commits before T1 (C3 before C1), S2 is not recoverable.

This statement is incorrect. S1 is not cascadeless because T1 performs r1(Y) after T2's w2(Y) and before T2 commits, so S1 contains a dirty read. S1 is, however, recoverable because the writer (T2) commits before the readers that read its data commit. S2 is correctly identified as not cascadeless and not recoverable.

Answer: The schedule is recoverable but not cascadeless.

  • T1 commits (C1) before T2 commits (C2). Because any transaction that reads from another commits only after the writer commits, the schedule is recoverable.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Although the schedule is recoverable, it is not cascadeless: T1 writes y (w1(y)) before T2 reads y (r2(y)), so T2 reads an uncommitted value. A cascadeless schedule forbids reading uncommitted writes.

Correct. T2 reads y that was written by T1 before T1 commits, so the schedule is not cascadeless. However, T1 commits (C1) before T2 commits (C2), so the reader commits after the writer and the schedule is recoverable.

title: Consider table bank_accounts (account_id, balance). Assume two accounts with account_id
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider table bank_accounts = (account_id, balance). Assume two accounts with account_id as A and B. Also assume that initially both accounts have a balance Rs. 5,000 each. Two transactions T1 and T2 are executed concurrently, both under REPEATABLE READ isolation level. Database uses standard locking mechanism.

  • T1: transfers Rs.1,000 from A to B. DB operation sequence is as follows: BEGIN; READ(A); READ(B); WRITE(A); WRITE(B); END

  • T2: transfers Rs.1,000 from B to A. DB operation sequence is as follows: BEGIN; READ(B); READ(A); WRITE(B); WRITE(A); END

Both transactions read the corresponding account balances, deducts Rs. 1,000 from one account, then adds Rs. 1,000 to the other account and results are written back. Assuming that all interleaving of execution of T1 and T2 are possible and that there are no extraneous factors, which of the following will never occur?

options.html: A's account balance shows Rs. 5,000 and B's account balance shows Rs. 5,000
A's account balance shows Rs. 4,000 and B's account balance shows Rs. 4,000
Deadlock is detected and T2 will be rolled back to recover
A's account balance shows Rs. 4,000 and that of B will have Rs. 6,000

solution:
Two-Phase Locking (2PL) with lock upgrades (shared to exclusive) guarantees serializability among the transactions that commit, and it does this by converting any dangerous overlap into a blocking wait (or a deadlock) rather than letting it complete silently. Concretely: a transaction must hold a shared lock to read an item and must upgrade that to an exclusive lock before writing it; the upgrade is refused for as long as any other transaction still holds a lock on the same item. So the only reachable final states are ones equivalent to a serial execution (both transactions commit) or ones where a lock conflict forces exactly one transaction to abort, leaving only the survivor's effect visible.

Trace the two operation sequences against this rule -- T1: READ(A), READ(B), WRITE(A), WRITE(B); T2: READ(B), READ(A), WRITE(B), WRITE(A):

  1. Serial-equivalent case: one transaction fully commits (and releases its locks) before the other begins its writes. Because one transfers Rs. 1,000 from A to B and the other transfers Rs. 1,000 from B to A, running them one after the other in either order cancels out, leaving A = Rs. 5,000 and B = Rs. 5,000.

  2. Reversed-order case: T1 reads A first and T2 reads B first; since shared (read) locks don't conflict with each other, each transaction can then also acquire a shared lock on the OTHER account before either attempts to write. At that point both transactions hold shared locks on both A and B, and each one's attempt to upgrade to an exclusive lock (needed to write) is blocked by the other's shared lock -- a genuine circular wait, i.e. a deadlock, which the DBMS must detect and resolve by rolling one transaction back.

  3. If the DBMS resolves that circular wait by rolling T2 back FIRST, T2's shared locks are released, T1's blocked upgrade then succeeds, and only T1 goes on to write and commit -- leaving A = Rs. 4,000 and B = Rs. 6,000 (and, symmetrically, rolling T1 back first would let T2 alone finish, leaving A = Rs. 6,000 and B = Rs. 4,000).

  4. The one outcome this locking rule structurally rules out is A = Rs. 4,000 and B = Rs. 4,000 (both accounts net LOWER). That number can only come from an uncontrolled lost update: both transactions reading the original Rs. 5,000 balances before either writes, then each independently overwriting the other's result so the Rs. 1,000 'in transit' is destroyed for both accounts. But that requires both transactions to hold read locks on both items and then write without ever waiting for the other -- exactly the situation step 2 shows is blocked (converted into a wait/deadlock) rather than allowed to complete.

Cross-check with the conservation invariant: A + B must equal Rs. 10,000 in every state reachable from a fully committed-or-rolled-back execution, since each transaction only moves Rs. 1,000 between the two accounts. 5,000 + 5,000 = 10,000 (both commit); 4,000 + 6,000 = 10,000 and 6,000 + 4,000 = 10,000 (only one transaction's transfer survives) -- all conserve the total. But 4,000 + 4,000 = 8,000 does not conserve the total, confirming it cannot be a legitimate outcome of two atomic Rs. 1,000 transfers; it is reachable only through an uncontrolled lost update, which the required lock upgrade here prevents.

So the account state that will never occur under this locking scheme is both balances showing Rs. 4,000.

optionFeedback.html: This value results whenever the two transactions run without any overlapping lock conflict -- for example when one transaction's full BEGIN...END sequence finishes and releases its locks before the other transaction starts. Since one transaction moves a fixed amount from A to B and the other moves that same amount back from B to A, executing them one after the other in either order cancels out and returns both accounts to their original starting balance, so this is a reachable final state.

Standard locking requires an exclusive lock before a write, and that upgrade is blocked for as long as another transaction still holds any lock on the same account. So both accounts ending up net lower requires both transactions to have read the original balances and then each overwritten the other's write without ever being made to wait -- but the required lock upgrade forces exactly that situation into a wait (and, given the reversed access order here, a genuine deadlock) rather than letting it complete silently. This net-loss-on-both-accounts state is therefore not reachable.

Because T1 accesses the accounts in the order A then B while T2 accesses them in the order B then A, both transactions can end up simultaneously holding shared (read) locks on both accounts before either requests a write lock. Each one's request to upgrade to an exclusive lock is then blocked by the other's shared lock, producing a genuine circular wait -- a lock-conversion deadlock -- that a standard locking scheme must detect and resolve by rolling one of the two transactions back, so this is a reachable outcome of this specific access pattern.

If the circular wait between the two transactions is resolved by rolling one of them back first (releasing its locks so the other's blocked write can then proceed and commit), only the surviving transaction's transfer remains visible. A single shift of the transfer amount from one account to the other is exactly the visible effect of one transaction completing while the other is fully undone before it, making this a reachable final state.

title: What is the primary goal of concurrency control in DBMS?
subject: Data Base Management System
text: What is the primary goal of concurrency control in DBMS?

options.html: To ensure that multiple transactions can execute concurrently without violating database consistency
To speed up database queries by allowing transactions to overlap
To allow only one transaction to be executed at a time
To guarantee that all transactions will complete anyhow

solution: The primary goal of concurrency control in DBMS is to maintain data consistency and integrity during simultaneous transaction execution. It prevents anomalies such as lost updates, dirty reads, and unrepeatable reads.

optionFeedback.html: Concurrency control mechanisms like locking or timestamp ordering manage simultaneous access to data safely. This ensures that the database remains in a consistent state even when multiple users modify records at the same time. You should verify if isolation levels are properly configured to prevent anomalies like lost updates or dirty reads during execution.

This option focuses primarily on performance rather than data integrity. Concurrency control mechanisms prioritize maintaining consistency and isolation over raw speed, often introducing overhead to prevent conflicts between simultaneous operations. Students should verify if the goal aligns with ACID properties rather than throughput optimization.

This option describes strict serialization rather than true concurrency control mechanisms used in modern systems. Concurrency aims to execute multiple transactions simultaneously while maintaining data consistency and isolation properties without unnecessarily blocking all other operations during execution.

This option ignores potential transaction failures due to conflicts or deadlocks occurring within the database system. Concurrency control manages isolation and consistency during execution, not guaranteed completion regardless of current system state or resource availability issues.

title: Consider the following schedule for transaction and r1(x), r2(y), r3(y)
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following schedule for transactions T1, T2, and T3.

S: r1(x), r2(y), r3(y), w1(x), w3(x), r2(z), w1(x)

The timestamps of T1, T2, and T3 are 30, 10, and 20, respectively.

Which of the following statements is true for this schedule?

options.html: The schedule is allowed under the basic time-stamp but not the Thomas write-stamp protocol
The schedule is not allowed under any of the basic time-stamp protocol as well as Thomas write.
The schedule is allowed under both basic time-stamp protocols as well as Thomas write.
The schedule is allowed under Thomas write time-stamp protocol but not basic time stamp protocol

solution:
Concept: Timestamp ordering executes conflicting operations in transaction-timestamp order. For a data item Q, RTS(Q) records the largest timestamp of any successful reader and WTS(Q) records that of any successful writer.

A read by Ti is permitted only when TS(Ti) is at least WTS(Q). A basic-protocol write requires TS(Ti) to be at least both RTS(Q) and WTS(Q).

Thomas write rule changes only the TS(Ti) < WTS(Q) case by ignoring that obsolete write. It does not relax the TS(Ti) < RTS(Q) rejection test.

Application:

  1. Initially, RTS and WTS are 0 for x, y, and z.

  2. r1(x) has timestamp 30, so it is accepted and sets RTS(x) = 30.

  3. r2(y) and r3(y) are accepted in sequence, so RTS(y) becomes max(10, 20) = 20.

  4. w1(x) has timestamp 30. Since 30 is not less than RTS(x) = 30 or WTS(x) = 0, the write is accepted and WTS(x) becomes 30.

  5. At w3(x), TS(T3) = 20 is less than RTS(x) = 30. This read-timestamp violation aborts T3 under the basic protocol and also under Thomas write rule.

Cross-check: The earlier r1(x) followed by w3(x) creates a conflict edge T1 → T3, but timestamp order requires T3 (20) before T1 (30). The schedule therefore violates timestamp order at the same operation.

Result: The true statement is that the schedule is not allowed under either the basic timestamp protocol or Thomas write rule.

optionFeedback.html: This statement assigns acceptance to basic timestamp ordering and rejection to Thomas write-rule timestamp ordering.
This statement assigns rejection to both basic timestamp ordering and Thomas write-rule timestamp ordering.
This statement assigns acceptance to both basic timestamp ordering and Thomas write-rule timestamp ordering.
This statement assigns rejection to basic timestamp ordering and acceptance to Thomas write-rule timestamp ordering.
