text: Which of the following concurrency control protocol ensures both conflict serializability and free from deadlock?
solution: Time Stamp Ordering (TSO) ensures conflict serializability by assigning timestamps to transactions and ordering their execution. Unlike Two Phase Locking, TSO does not use locks, which eliminates the possibility of deadlock cycles. Therefore, it satisfies both conflict serializability and freedom from deadlock.

optionFeedback.html: Time stamp ordering ensures conflict serializability by using timestamps and avoids deadlock because it does not use locks.
Two Phase Locking ensures conflict serializability but can result in deadlocks due to lock waiting cycles.
This option implies multiple protocols satisfy both conditions, which is not accurate.
This option implies no protocol satisfies both conditions, which contradicts standard concurrency control principles.

When r2(B) executes, the read timestamp of B (RTS(B)) is updated to TS(T2). Later, when T1 attempts w1(B), the protocol checks if TS(T1) < RTS(B). Since TS(T1) is less than TS(T2), T1 violates the protocol rule for writing to a data item already read by a newer transaction. Therefore, T1 must be aborted and rolled back.

In basic timestamp ordering, if an older transaction attempts to write a data item read by a newer transaction, it violates the protocol and must be aborted.
In timestamp ordering, when a younger transaction reads data before an older one writes to it, the conflict typically forces the older transaction to abort.

title: Which concurrency control protocol uses timestamp ordering
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which concurrency control protocol uses timestamp ordering ?
solution: timestamp-based concurrency control protocols use timestamps to order transactions and ensure serializability. Each transaction receives a unique timestamp upon arrival, which determines the order of execution and conflict resolution.

optionFeedback.html: Two-phase locking uses lock acquisition and release phases to ensure serializability, not timestamp ordering. Review how this protocol manages transaction conflicts through exclusive and shared locks instead of time-based sequencing.
Correct. Timestamp-based protocols use timestamp ordering to manage concurrency.

Validation-based protocols use a different approach where transactions execute first and then validate against conflicts. Check if the question specifically mentions timestamp ordering rather than validation phases.

Incorrect. While snapshot isolation also uses timestamps, it does not force a strict serialization order based on transaction arrival timestamps. Instead, it behaves like a version-control system (MVCC - Multi-Version Concurrency Control).

title: Which concurrency control protocol prevents deadlock and ensures serializability?
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which concurrency control protocol prevents deadlock and ensures serializability?
solution:
Concept

A concurrency control protocol is judged on two independent properties: whether it guarantees serializability (the concurrent schedule is equivalent to some serial order) and whether it can deadlock (transactions blocked in a cyclic wait). A protocol that NEVER makes a transaction wait for a lock cannot form a wait-cycle, so it is deadlock-free by construction.

Application

Under timestamp-ordering, every transaction is assigned a unique timestamp on arrival, and each data item carries read- and write-timestamps. Conflicting operations are forced into timestamp order:

  • A transaction whose operation would violate the timestamp order is aborted and restarted with a new timestamp — it is never blocked waiting.

  • Because no transaction ever waits on another, no wait-for cycle can form, so deadlock is impossible.

  • Serializing every conflicting pair by timestamp yields a schedule equivalent to the serial order of the timestamps, so the schedule is conflict-serializable.

Both required properties — serializability and freedom from deadlock — hold together only for timestamp-ordering among the choices.

Contrast

2PL guarantees conflict-serializability but uses blocking locks, so two transactions can wait on each other and deadlock. Strict 2PL adds cascadeless recovery on top of 2PL but is still a locking protocol and is equally deadlock-prone. “Optimistic” validation defers conflict checks to a validation phase and resolves conflicts by aborting, but it is not the classical waiting-free protocol named for this guarantee, and shared-locking alone is only one lock mode, not a complete protocol that ensures serializability.

Result

Timestamp ordering protocol is the protocol that both prevents deadlock and ensures serializability.

optionFeedback.html: Two-phase locking serializes via a growing-then-shrinking lock phase, but because transactions wait for held locks, two of them can enter a cyclic wait — so it does not by itself rule out deadlock.

Optimistic concurrency runs transactions lock-free and checks conflicts only in a final validation phase, resolving them by aborting; it is not the classical no-wait scheme defined by the deadlock-free guarantee.

Timestamp ordering fixes each transaction's order by its timestamp and aborts (rather than blocks) any operation that arrives out of that order, so transactions never wait on one another and the timestamp order keeps the schedule serializable.
Strict two-phase locking holds exclusive locks until commit for cascadeless recovery, but it is still a blocking lock scheme, so two transactions can deadlock on each other's locks.
A shared (read) lock is a single lock mode, not a complete protocol, so on its own it neither defines a serializable schedule nor governs deadlock.

title: Consider the following schedules: r1(X),w2(X),w2(Y),r1(Y),r3(X),w3(X),w1(X) r1(Y),w1(Y),r2(Y),w1(X),r2(X),w1(Z),w3(X),w3(Y) Which of the following
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following schedules:

S1: r1(X), w2(X), w2(Y), r1(Y), r3(X), w3(X), w1(X)

S2: r1(Y), w1(Y), r2(Y), w1(X), r2(X), w1(Z), w3(X), w3(Y)

Which of the following is true?

options.html: Both S1 and S2 are allowed under 2PL
Neither S1 nor S2 is allowed under 2PL
None of S1 and S2 is allowed under PL

solution:
Two-phase locking (2PL) requires every transaction to acquire every lock it will ever need before releasing its first lock — once a transaction releases any lock (starts its shrinking phase), it can never acquire a new one. A schedule can be produced by 2PL only if it is conflict-serializable (every 2PL schedule is conflict-serializable) AND a valid lock acquire/release timeline exists that obeys this growing-then-shrinking rule while matching the given operation order. When a schedule is written as ri(A)/wi(A) with no explicit lock/unlock actions, each operation is read as requiring transaction i to be holding the matching shared/exclusive lock on A at that instant — this is the standard convention for this class of question, even though lock operations are not spelled out.

Checking S1 for conflict-serializability:

  1. r1(X) occurs before w2(X) — both touch X and one is a write, so this gives an edge transaction 1 -> transaction 2.

  2. w2(Y) occurs before r1(Y) — both touch Y and one is a write, so this gives an edge transaction 2 -> transaction 1.

  3. These two edges alone form the cycle transaction 1 -> transaction 2 -> transaction 1 in the precedence graph.

A precedence graph with a cycle means S1 is not conflict-serializable. Since 2PL only ever produces conflict-serializable schedules, S1 cannot be generated by any 2PL execution, regardless of how locks are scheduled.

Checking S2 for conflict-serializability:

  1. w1(Y) occurs before r2(Y) — edge transaction 1 -> transaction 2 (on Y).

  2. w1(X) occurs before r2(X) — edge transaction 1 -> transaction 2 (on X, same direction).

  3. r2(Y) and r2(X) occur before w3(Y) and w3(X) — edge transaction 2 -> transaction 3.

  4. w1(X) occurs before w3(X) — edge transaction 1 -> transaction 3 (on X), and w1(Y) occurs before w3(Y) — edge transaction 1 -> transaction 3 (on Y) as well.

The edges are transaction 1 -> transaction 2, transaction 2 -> transaction 3, and the direct transaction 1 -> transaction 3 edges just above — still no cycle, since every edge points in the same direction consistent with the serial order T1, T2, T3. So S2 IS conflict-serializable. Conflict-serializability is necessary but not sufficient for 2PL, so the lock-holding order must also be checked.

Checking whether a 2PL lock timeline can realize S2:

  1. Transaction 1 can acquire ALL the locks it will ever need in this schedule — on Y, X, and Z — right at the very start, before its first operation, entirely within its growing phase.

  2. It then performs r1(Y) and w1(Y) using the Y lock it already holds, and releases that Y lock only afterward — just before r2(Y) needs it. Every one of its three acquisitions has already happened by this point, so this release does not come before any acquisition.

  3. w1(X) and w1(Z) later in the schedule use locks transaction 1 already acquired at the very start — these are not NEW acquisitions. Two-phase locking only forbids acquiring a lock after an earlier release; simply continuing to use a lock acquired earlier is always allowed.

  4. Transaction 1 releases its X lock, in turn, just before r2(X) needs it, and may keep or release its Z lock afterward at will, since no other transaction in this schedule touches Z.

So a valid two-phase-locking timeline for transaction 1 does exist here: acquire Y, X, and Z upfront, then release Y and later X only as the schedule requires, while continuing to use the already-held locks in between. Unlike the first schedule, the second schedule CAN be produced under (basic) 2PL after all — the requirement is only that all of a transaction's acquisitions precede its first release, not that each lock be acquired right before it is used.

Cross-check: transaction 2 needs the Y lock only from r2(Y) onward and the X lock only from r2(X) onward; transaction 1 already holds both from the very start and can hand each one over at exactly the point the schedule calls for it, and transaction 3 receives them from transaction 2 the same way afterward. At no point does the schedule require two transactions to hold a conflicting lock on the same item at once, and transaction 1 never needs to acquire a new lock after its first release.

Checked against the standard (basic) two-phase locking protocol, then: the first schedule fails outright because it is not conflict-serializable, but the second schedule is conflict-serializable AND achievable by the locking timeline above — it is allowed.

Under a stricter discipline where every write lock must be held until commit (strict two-phase locking), transaction 1 could not release its lock on Y before r2(Y) needs it, so the second schedule would fail this stricter test as well — the classification of the second schedule genuinely depends on which two-phase-locking discipline ("basic" vs "strict") is intended.

optionFeedback.html: This claims the first schedule is producible under two-phase locking, which does not hold. Building its precedence graph: r1(X) occurs before w2(X), giving an edge from transaction 1 to transaction 2, and w2(Y) occurs before r1(Y), giving an edge from transaction 2 back to transaction 1. Those two edges already form a cycle, so the first schedule is not conflict-serializable. Since every schedule produced by two-phase locking must be conflict-serializable, the first schedule cannot arise from any two-phase-locking execution — so this option's claim fails.

This claims both schedules are producible under two-phase locking. That cannot be right for at least the first schedule: its precedence graph has a cycle — r1(X) occurs before w2(X) gives one edge (transaction 1 to transaction 2), and w2(Y) occurs before r1(Y) gives the reverse edge (transaction 2 to transaction 1) — so the first schedule is not conflict-serializable, and a schedule that is not conflict-serializable can never be produced by two-phase locking. Since even one of the two schedules already fails this test, this option's claim that both are allowed cannot hold.

The first schedule cannot occur under two-phase locking: its precedence graph has a cycle — r1(X) before w2(X) gives one edge, and w2(Y) before r1(Y) gives the reverse edge — so it fails conflict-serializability outright, and no locking protocol that guarantees serializability can produce a non-conflict-serializable schedule.

Whether the second schedule is also disallowed depends on which two-phase-locking discipline is intended: under the standard (basic) protocol, transaction 1 can front-load all of its locks (on Y, X, and Z) before its first release, which makes the second schedule achievable; only under a stricter discipline (where write locks are held until commit) does the second schedule fail too.

This option names the protocol simply as 'PL', but the protocol this question is about is defined by two distinct phases — a growing phase in which a transaction may only acquire locks, followed by a shrinking phase in which it may only release them, never acquiring a new lock once releasing has begun. Plain 'PL' does not name any protocol with that two-phase structure, so this option's claim, tied to an undefined 'PL', cannot be matched to the concurrency-control rule this question is actually testing.

title: Which of the following is true?
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following is true?

options.html: In 2PL protocol if all exclusive lock are acquired by transactions in only increasing order of their addresses then 2PL protocol is deadlock free.
In 2PL protocol if all exclusive lock are acquire by transaction in only increasing order of their addresses then 2PL protocol is starvation free.

solution:
Key point: If every transaction acquires exclusive locks in a globally consistent increasing order of resource addresses, the protocol is deadlock-free.

  • Why it prevents deadlock: Acquiring resources in a single global order eliminates the possibility of a circular wait, so the wait-for graph cannot contain a cycle and deadlock cannot occur.

  • Why this does not imply starvation freedom: Starvation concerns fairness of lock granting and scheduler behavior. Even with a fixed acquisition order, a transaction might be repeatedly delayed or aborted and never make progress, so starvation is not ruled out by ordering alone.

  • Conclusion: The statement that ordering exclusive locks by increasing addresses yields deadlock freedom is correct. The claim that the same ordering guarantees starvation freedom is not guaranteed.

optionFeedback.html: True. If every transaction acquires exclusive locks in a globally consistent increasing order of resource addresses, the wait-for graph cannot contain a cycle, so deadlock cannot occur. This is the standard resource-ordering deadlock-prevention technique.

False. Acquiring locks in increasing address order prevents cyclic waiting (deadlock) but does not guarantee starvation freedom. Starvation depends on fairness of lock granting and scheduling; a transaction could still be repeatedly delayed or aborted and never complete.

Incorrect. The first statement about deadlock freedom when locks are acquired in a global increasing order is true, but the second statement about starvation freedom is not guaranteed. Therefore it is not correct that both statements are true.
Incorrect. The claim that neither statement is true is wrong because the statement asserting deadlock freedom under global ordering of exclusive locks is correct.

title: Consider the following time ordered sequence of actions performed by
subject: Data Base Management System
text:
Consider the following time ordered sequence of actions performed by the transactions T₁, T₂, T₃, and T₄. [Suffix indicates transaction number and timestamp value, BTS: Basic Time stamp, TWR: Thomas Write Rule, MVTS: Multiversion Timestamp]

W₁(A), W₂(A), W₃(A), r₂(A), r₄(A).

Which of the following is true?

options.html: T₁ is rolled back in both BTS and TWR
T₂ is rolled back in TWR, whereas T₁ is rolled back in BTS
T₂ is rolled back in both TWR and BTS
It is not allowed under BTS, TWR and MVTS as T₂ is rolled back in all

solution:
Key facts: The sequence of actions is W1(A), W2(A), W3(A), r2(A), r4(A). Transactions have timestamps TS(T1) < TS(T2) < TS(T3) < TS(T4).

BTS (Basic Timestamp Ordering) analysis:

  • Read rule: A read r_i(X) is disallowed if TS(i) < W-timestamp(X) (i.e., if a younger transaction has already written X). In that case the reading transaction must be rolled back.

  • Here, T3 has written A (W3(A)) and then T2 issues r2(A). Since TS(T2) < TS(T3) and the read occurs after T3's write, T2 violates the read rule and must be rolled back under basic timestamp ordering.

TWR (Thomas Write Rule) analysis:

  • Thomas Write Rule relaxes the write-write conflict: if a transaction attempts a write whose timestamp is older than the current write-timestamp of the data item, that older write is simply ignored (discarded) rather than causing an abort.

  • However, TWR does not change the read rule described above. Because T2 performs a read after a younger transaction (T3) has written A, T2 still violates the timestamp read rule and must be rolled back. T2's earlier write to A would be considered obsolete relative to T3's write and would be ignored by TWR, but the read violation forces T2 to abort.

MVTS (Multiversion Timestamp) analysis:

  • MVTS keeps multiple versions of each item with their write timestamps. A read by Ti returns the version with the largest timestamp ≤ TS(i).

  • In this sequence, under MVTS T2 can read the version of A corresponding to its own timestamp (or the latest version with timestamp ≤ TS(T2)) instead of the newer version written by T3. That allows T2 to avoid the read-violation and not be rolled back.

Final conclusion:

  • Under basic timestamp ordering, T2 must be rolled back because it reads a value written by a younger transaction (T3).

  • Under the Thomas Write Rule, T2's obsolete write would be ignored, but the read violation still forces T2 to be rolled back.

  • Under multiversion timestamping, T2 can read an older version and may avoid rollback. Therefore the correct statement is that T2 is rolled back under BTS and TWR, but MVTS can prevent that rollback.

optionFeedback.html: This is incorrect. Transaction T1 performed an initial write but there is no later read-by-T1 or other timestamp-order violation involving T1 in the given sequence. Nothing in the sequence forces T1 to be rolled back under basic timestamp ordering or Thomas Write Rule.

This is incorrect. The claim that the earlier transaction (T1) must be rolled back under basic timestamp ordering is not supported by the sequence. The actual conflict involves T2: T2 performs a read after a younger transaction has written A, which violates basic timestamp ordering and causes T2 to be rolled back. T2's write-related conflict under Thomas Write Rule is also resolved against T2 (see full explanation).

Correct. Under basic timestamp ordering, T2 must be rolled back because it issues a read after T3 (a transaction with a later timestamp) has already written A; a transaction that reads a value written by a younger transaction violates the read rule and must abort. Under the Thomas Write Rule, obsolete writes by older transactions that would overwrite newer values are ignored, but the read violation still forces T2 to be rolled back. Therefore T2 is rolled back under both BTS and TWR.

This is incorrect. While T2 is rolled back under basic timestamp ordering and the Thomas Write Rule (for the read-based violation), multiversion timestamping (MVTS) can avoid that rollback: MVTS keeps older versions, so T2 could read the version whose timestamp is the largest one not greater than T2's timestamp, avoiding the read-violation and thus avoiding rollback. So it is not correct to say the sequence is disallowed under all three protocols.

title: Which of the following concurrency control protocols ensure both conflict
subject: Data Base Management System
text: Which of the following concurrency control protocols ensure both conflict serializability and freedom from deadlock? (I) 2PL (Two Phase Lock) (II) Time-Stamp ordering (III) Multiple granularity protocol
solution:
Concept

A concurrency-control protocol is judged on two independent guarantees. Conflict serializability means every allowed schedule is equivalent to some serial order of the transactions. Deadlock freedom means no set of transactions can ever end up in a circular wait, each holding a resource the next needs. A protocol qualifies here only if it guarantees BOTH at once.

Applying it to each protocol

  • 2PL (Two-Phase Locking): the growing-then-shrinking lock discipline forces conflict serializability, but because transactions hold locks and wait for one another, two transactions can each wait on a lock the other holds — a circular wait. So 2PL gives serializability but NOT deadlock freedom.

  • Timestamp Ordering: each transaction gets a fixed timestamp and conflicting operations are admitted only in timestamp order, with a violating transaction aborted and restarted rather than made to wait. Ordering by timestamp guarantees conflict serializability, and because no transaction ever waits on a lock there is no circular wait — so it gives serializability AND deadlock freedom.

  • Multiple Granularity: this is a layered locking technique (intention locks over a hierarchy) that improves lock-management efficiency. It is still lock-based, so the same circular-wait possibility as ordinary locking remains; it does not guarantee deadlock freedom.

Result

Only Timestamp Ordering satisfies both properties simultaneously, so the protocol set is exactly {II}.

Cross-check

A quick consistency test: any purely lock-based scheme (2PL, multiple granularity) keeps the possibility of waiting cycles, so it cannot be deadlock-free by itself; a no-wait scheme that resolves conflicts by abort-and-restart (timestamp ordering) removes waiting entirely and is deadlock-free. That rule alone selects timestamp ordering as the single qualifying protocol.

optionFeedback.html: 2PL alone is serializable but a pure lock-based protocol: transactions hold locks and wait, so two of them can form a circular wait. Choosing only 2PL ignores the deadlock-freedom requirement that locking cannot meet.

Timestamp ordering admits conflicting operations only in timestamp order and resolves a violation by aborting and restarting rather than waiting. The fixed timestamp order delivers conflict serializability, and because no transaction ever waits on a lock there is no circular wait — both required properties hold together, so {II} is the protocol set.

Multiple granularity is a hierarchical locking technique aimed at lock-management efficiency, not a stand-alone correctness guarantee. Being lock-based, it keeps the waiting-cycle possibility, so it does not by itself guarantee deadlock freedom.

This set includes 2PL, and 2PL — being lock-and-wait based — cannot guarantee deadlock freedom, so it fails the 'both properties' test. Bundling 2PL into the answer mistakes serializability alone for the full requirement.
